News.title: Hosepipe bans extended - what is excluded, from new lawns to blue badge holders
News.content:
Hosepipe bans extended - what is excluded, from new lawns to blue badge holders

More than 18 million domestic and business customers across a swathe of southern England are now - or soon will be - subject to hosepipe bans amid the heatwave

View 3 Images You may be allowed to continue using a hosepipe to water a newly laid lawn (Image: Getty)

Thames Water has become the latest supplier to announce a hosepipe ban, impacting more than 10 million of its customers.

‌



The ban, from this Thursday, prevents domestic and business customers from using a hosepipe for a whole host of things, from watering the garden to washing the car. Five other suppliers have also imposed bans in some or all of their areas. Breaching the ban risks customers being fined up to £1,000.

‌



However, there are a number of exemptions to the ban, for a whole of reasons. These include Thames Water customers, who pay for its wastewater services - eg sewage - but get water from other suppliers, because of where they live

‌



18 million homes now under hosepipe ban as Thames Water issues update READ MORE :

Met Office reveals two UK regions facing longest spell with no rain this century READ MORE :

View 3 Images Blue badge holders could be among those exempted from new hosepipe bans (Image: Getty Images)

Thames Water

The UK’s biggest water supplier hasn’t published its full breakdown of exemptions until a legal notice is issued on Wednesday. However, it has said its own ban only applies to those who get both water (wastewater services) from the company.

It doesn't apply to those who pay for its wastewater services - eg sewage - but get water from other suppliers, because of where they live. That said, those customers’ suppliers may have hosepipe bans in place too.

‌



Thames says other exemptions are for “health and safety needs”, animal welfare, including pets, livestock, and fish, some business services and activities, and watering food crops and certain newly planted trees.

It also has a category for its Priority Services customers who cannot reasonably adjust their water use because of a disability or medical condition.

Anglian Water

Like Thames, Anglian says those on its Priority Services Register who are also unable to make reasonable adjustments because of a health condition or disability are exempt from its ban. Others excluded include if a hosepipe is needed “to protect human health and safety” or for animal welfare.

‌



A hosepipe can also be used if connected to a water butt or other recycled water storage system, rather than the mains water supply. And one can still be used for watering newly trees, hedges and saplings planted “where a watering can isn’t a practical option”. That goes the same for newly turf for the first 28 days after it has been laid, again, where this cannot be reasonably done by watering can. The same goes for newly sown grass seed for the first 28 days.

And a hosepipe can be used for food crops grown at home or on private allotments where a watering can isn’t a practical option. And sports pitches and recreational playing surfaces where watering is necessary and takes place outside peak hours (8am–10am and 5pm–9pm) is still allowed. Others include business car washes, commercially grown crops, or where water features where they are needed to keep fish healthy.

View 3 Images Most households and businesses in hosepipe ban affected areas have been ordered to heavily restrict their use

‌



Affinity Water

In areas affected by a hosepipe ban, the company says customers on the Priority Services Register, on the WaterSure tariff, and Blue Badge holders can continue to use a hosepipe if they are unable to make adjustments, such as using a watering can, due to medical reasons.

Like Anglian, an exemption applies to newly laid turf with a hosepipe for up to 28 days after it’s been laid. “Please note that this only applies to turf that was laid before the hosepipe ban was introduced”, the firm said.

What happens if you use a hosepipe during a hosepipe ban?

‌



South East Water

Again, exemptions customers registered with the South East Water’s Priority Service Register will be granted an automatic exemption to any of the restrictions. It also doesn’t apply where using a ban would cause a “risk to human or animal health or safety”.

Like others, a hosepipe can still be used when it’s connected to a water butt. And watering of new lawns at home is allowed for a period of four weeks after being laid and when undertaken outside of daily peak hours that occur 8am to 10am and 5pm to 9pm.

Watering trees, saplings and hedging planted before the ban is allowed, where it can’t reasonably done with a watering can.The same goes for watering food crops in gardens or private allotments.

Article continues below

Swimming pools and paddling pools can’t be filled but those within places of worship or community pools and when they are used as part of a religious ceremony can still be filled with a hosepipe.

News.title: Andy Burnham live: New Prime Minister sets challenge to ministers during his first Cabinet meeting
News.content:
Andy Burnham has thrown down the gauntlet, asking MPs to "take that little bit of pressure off people's shoulders" as he sets sights to help ease families facing the cost-of-living crisis

Andy Burnham today chaired his first Cabinet meeting and told his appointed ministers to examine “all possible ways” to help families struggling with high costs.

In a challenge to his top team one their applause had died down, the new Prime Minister said their task was to "take that little bit of pressure off people's shoulders" and show them help was coming so they could have some hope things were improving.

He told the meeting: "That’s the mission that we’ve got to set ourselves together” and asked his colleagues to look into what their department could do to ease cost-of-living pressures, “big and small,” saying: “We need to be a cost-of-living Government, getting that cost of living down, looking at all possible ways of doing that.”

Burnham started today by making good on his promise for “breathing space” for struggling households, a key plinth of his economic plans unveiled in his maiden speech outside No 10 on Monday. The move will see VAT removed from domestic electricity bills from October 1.

Burnham said: “Westminster has not been working for people for too long, with families struggling with the cost of living. That needs to change. I said I wanted to give people breathing space, and that’s what I’m announcing on my second day as Prime Minister. We’re taking immediate action to cut taxes on energy bills, put more money in people’s pockets and bring back hope.”

It is estimated that the change will reduce the annual Ofgem price cap by around £45 from October, with companies expected to pass the reduction onto customers.

Chancellor John Healey said: “For too long, too many people have struggled with the cost of living. Today’s energy tax cut will give families some breathing room on bills, and provide some reassurance this winter". He continued: “This measure is funded this year from cancelling the Digital ID programme, and it will help bring down inflation while supporting households in every postcode.”

The fully priced plan from Mr Healey comes as Burnham continues to pad out his cabinet, with a number of key appointments made since yesterday, including Ed Miliband receiving the FCDO brief, Angela Rayner returning as Housing Secretary, and Shabana Mahmood staying on as Home Secretary.

News.title: 'Andy Burnham's whirlwind start as PM and Cabinet shake-up ushers in new era'
News.content:
Andy Burnham is a man in a hurry.

Over a whirlwind two days, he purged his Cabinet of Keir Starmer's allies and replaced them with several eye-catching appointments, in between calls with world leaders and a flurry of announcements.

As he gathered his newly-minted top team in No10's Cabinet room, he said it was "a second chance at a first impression". What he really meant was this could be Labour's last chance to win back fed-up voters - and they need to get on with it.

The football-mad PM told his Cabinet that he was proud to see them "going out into the tunnel alongside him and on to the pitch as one team", according to No10. Who he's picked for his starting eleven tells us quite a bit about Burnham as a PM - and what he's planning to do with power.

‌



Angela Rayner's triumphant return to Cabinet after 10 months on backbenches READ MORE :

New PM Andy Burnham announces VAT cuts on household electricity bills from October READ MORE :

View 4 Images Andy Burnham arrives to host his first Cabinet meeting as Prime Minister (Image: Eddie Mulholland/Daily Telegraph/PA Wire)

A clear-out of the Starmerites had been anticipated but the scale of it sent shockwaves through Westminster. Some wags branded it the "night of the long eyelashes" as the PM sacked 11 top ministers, including Steve Reed, David Lammy, Darren Jones, Peter Kyle and Liz Kendall.

Rachel Reeves fought hard to stay on as Chancellor but she was too closely tied to the Starmer project and its most totemic failure - the cut to the winter fuel allowance. It is understood that she declined the offer of another big Cabinet job.

Starmer retired to a pub in Kentish Town, where he was joined by allies, including Reeves, for a farewell bash as their seats at the Cabinet tabled were filled. Questions have been raised about the danger of alienating so many top ministers - but it was a risk Burnham was clearly willing to take to draw a line under the old era.

‌



After weeks of hysteria over who he would choose as his Chancellor, Burnham stunned Westminster by handing control of the nation's purse strings to John Healey. Ed Miliband, who was initially seen as a favourite, was made Foreign Secretary, while Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood kept her role, despite being widely tipped to enter No11 in recent days.

Healey's appointment as Chancellor was a surprise to many but perhaps it shouldn't have been. The well-liked Labour veteran served in Gordon Brown's Treasury, and is seen as a safe pair of hands.

View 4 Images Chancellor John Healey and Energy Security and Net Zero Miatta Fahnbulleh leave No10 after Cabinet (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Much of the briefing about the next Chancellor fixated on whether Miliband was too left-wing or whether Mahmood was too right wing - but Healey is not aligned to one faction.

‌



The PM's team are clear he wants an experienced and trusted figure in the Treasury to deliver his vision. And it is his vision, as it increasingly look like the economic direction will be set by Burnham in No10.

The pair are aligned on key issues. Healey, a Yorkshire MP, shares his concern about deindustrialisation, the cost of living and backing British industry. Healey's record as a housing minister, and his commitment to overhauling forces accommodation, while he was at the Ministry of Defence, clearly chimes with Burnham's desire for a council house building boom.

Healey's decision to resign over defence spending will put him under pressure to find cash for the armed forces. But his parting swipe at Treasury orthodoxy show he's a safe pick with an edge - one who won't spook the markets but can help to drive through radical reforms.

It is a blow to Miliband, who coveted the job of Chancellor, and played a pivotal role in the new PM's rise to power. For months he was Burnham's most powerful friend in Westminster, and is said to have been the first Cabinet Minister to privately urge Keir Starmer to resign.

‌



Burnham handed him another great office of state instead. Whether it is a consolation to Miliband remains to be seen.

The PM rewarded loyalty elsewhere by appointing key ally Louise Haigh, as First Secretary of State and Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster. The former Transport Secretary, who was sacked by Starmer over a historic fraud conviction, is now one of the most powerful people in Government.

View 4 Images Louise Haigh, the new First Secretary of State, arrives in Downing Street (Image: Getty Images)

Miatta Fahnbulleh, a highly-rated 2024 intake MP who has been supplying policy ideas to Burnham, has been rewarded with the energy brief. Lisa Nandy, another MP from Wigan, stays on as Culture Secretary.

‌



Deputy Labour leader Lucy Powell, another ally, becomes Education Secretary - and one of his right-hand women, Anneliese Midgley, was named as Chief Whip. Heidi Alexander, who backed him in all three leadership bids, stays as Transport Secretary to deliver another key part of his agenda.

Angela Rayner is back in Government in her old role, Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government. She fought hard to win back this brief, which is a key priority for Burnham.

The PM kept Pat McFadden at the Department of Work and Pensions, in a sign of his commitment to fixing the welfare system and getting young people into work. He also moved experienced minister Yvette Cooper to the Department of Health, where she will drive much-needed reforms to the broken social care system.

Intriguingly, Wes Streeting was made Defence Secretary, replacing decorated former soldier Dan Jarvis. But his record in gripping the NHS at the Department of Health appears to have counted in his favour - along with his decision to set aside his own leadership ambitions to fold in behind Burnham.

‌



The Cabinet is now weighted towards the North, with seven MPs with seats in the North West, and four in Yorkshire and Humber. Only four have seats in London.

Burnham has packed his Cabinet with experienced people as well as some fresher faces to shake things up. But there is only one vision here - and it's his.

News.title: Major delays on M25 anticlockwise after lorry crashes into embankment
News.content:
There were delays of about an hour after the vehicle slammed into an embankment on the M25 at Godstone

A large section of the M25 came to a standstill after a lorry crashed into an embankment, sparking major delays with emergency services rushing to the scene.

The crash happened anticlockwise on Junction 6 at Godstone and Clacket Lane Services at around 10am this morning (Tuesday, July 21), causing the closure of two of the motorway's four lanes.

Significant queues built up in the area, with delays of up to 60 minutes and around seven miles of congestion reported.

News.title: M5 traffic live: Horror 'pile up' near Droitwich closes motorway with 90 minute delays
News.content:
National Highways has warned drivers face seven miles of queues in the lead up to crash scene near Droitwich

Part of the M5 motorway in Worcestershire is closed after a serious crash involving four vehicles. The road is shut northbound between junction 5 near Droitwich and J4A (M42) with drivers facing 90-minute delays, according to National Highways.

There are seven miles of congestion on the lead up to the scene with diversion routes in place. Emergency services and trafffic officers have rushed to the scene.

News.title: B&M fined millions over mouse infestations at Birmingham stores as firm 'deeply sorry'
News.content:
B&M fined millions over mouse infestations at Birmingham stores as firm 'deeply sorry'

B&M Retail Ltd has been fined £2m after Birmingham City Council prosecuted the retailer over food hygiene offences, including mouse infestations, identified at three of its city stores

View Image Evidence of mouse infestations was found at three Birmingham stores (Image: Google)

B&M Retail Ltd has been handed a massive £2m fine after Birmingham City Council prosecuted the retailer for food hygiene violations found across three of its city branches.

‌



The alarming breaches at St Andrews Retail Park, Priory Square Shopping Centre and The Fort Shopping Park were investigated by the council's environmental health service following complaints received between November 2024 and October last year.

‌



Evidence of mouse infestations was found at all three stores, including droppings and gnawed food products.

‌



The council revealed that inspectors visited the St Andrews Retail Park store on November 11, 2024, after reports of pests on the premises.

Officials uncovered substantial evidence of mouse activity, including mouse droppings and gnawed food products on sale. Given the threat to public health, a Hygiene Emergency Prohibition Notice was then issued, Birmingham Live reports.

An inspection was then carried out at the B&M Priory Square Shopping Centre branch after a member of the public complained of spotting a mouse inside the shop.

‌



During a visit on January 22 last year, officers uncovered evidence of an active mouse infestation, including gnawed food products, mouse droppings and urine contamination on food packaging and shelving, inadequate cleaning standards and structural defects allowing pest entry, the council confirmed.

A Hygiene Emergency Prohibition Notice was served and the store was shut down immediately. A further inspection was carried out at B&M's store at The Fort Shopping Park on 27th October last year, following a complaint alleging another mouse infestation.

Council officers uncovered widespread evidence of mouse activity throughout the premises, including mouse droppings and gnawed food products both on the shop floor and within storage areas.

‌



Mouse droppings were also discovered near children's toys on display. Given the serious risks posed to public health, the premises was also formally shut down using another Hygiene Emergency Prohibition Notice.

B&M Retail Ltd pleaded guilty to the offences at Birmingham Magistrates' Court following a sentencing hearing on July 13.

The company was ordered to pay a £2m fine, prosecution costs of £18,104, and a victim surcharge of £2,000 - each payable within 28 days.

Article continues below

Speaking after the case, Councillor Sam Forsyth, Chair of the Licensing and Public Protection Committee, said: "Residents rightly expect businesses operating in Birmingham to maintain high standards and provide safe environments for customers. The health and wellbeing of Birmingham residents will always come first, and the conditions identified by our Environmental Health officers across these stores were unacceptable and required immediate intervention to protect the public.

"I welcome the work of our Environmental Health teams in identifying these risks and taking swift action. This substantial court penalty reflects the seriousness of the offences and sends a clear message that businesses must take their responsibilities seriously. Birmingham City Council will continue to take robust enforcement action where necessary to protect residents and ensure standards are upheld across the city."

News.title: Prince William's 'troubled' teenage years were worlds away from those Prince George faces
News.content:
On the eve of his teenage years officially beginning, Prince George’s future has many similarities to that of his father, Prince William.

In September, George will follow in his father’s footsteps by starting at his new school, Eton College, while, like William before him, he is also being gradually introduced to more and more royal duties. But for the Prince of Wales, his life at 13 couldn’t have been more different to that of his eldest son, who becomes a teenager tomorrow.

Back in June 1995, William turned 13 at the height of his own parents’ bitter split, which played out in public. It came just weeks before he started at Eton College as he and brother Prince Harry shuttled between living with mum, Princess Diana and their dad, then Prince Charles.

5 View 5 Images Prince George who turns 13 today (Image: WireImage) 5 View 5 Images Prince William back when he was 13 in 1995 (Image: Tim Graham Photo Library via Getty Images)

‌



Former BBC royal correspondent Jennie Bond recalled having a long chat during a meeting with the late Diana at Kensington Palace the exact month William turned 13.

The royal expert said the princess confided in her that at that time, the burden of future Kingship weighed heavily on William’s shoulders - although he was slowly coming to terms with his future role.

However, she told the Mirror: “At this time in his life, William was troubled by a great deal more than just his destiny. He had witnessed and lived through the brutal breakup of his parents’ marriage; he had supported his mother through her distress, anger, and sadness.

“He and Harry had become used to a rather nomadic life: sometimes with their father, sometimes with their mother and much of the time at school.

‌



View 5 Images William shortly before his 13th birthday with his parents the now King Charles and the late Princess Diana (Image: Tim Graham Photo Library via Getty Images)

“Their parents’ private lives had become public. His father had admitted adultery on national television, and there was worse to come. It was only a few months after William’s 13th birthday, during his first term at Eton, that Diana recorded her now notorious Panorama interview in which she, too, admitted adultery and poured out her heart about her life and marriage. William was mortified.”

Now, William has put family life at the heart of everything he does, and today George is growing up in a more stable household away from the public spotlight - and having as normal an upbringing as possible while he gains a deeper understanding of his future duties.

And Jennie explained: “George may well feel the burden of Kingship on his shoulders, but he has two united and highly supportive parents who have always encouraged him to discuss his feelings and fears.

‌



“He has been brought up in a stable, loving household – not sent away to boarding school at the age of eight – with parents who have consciously and unashamedly put their children before their work at important times in their lives and during school holidays.

View 5 Images William with his late mother and younger brother, Prince Harry in the months after turning 13 (Image: AFP/Getty Images)

“Of course, George and his siblings have had the trauma of their mother’s shock diagnosis of cancer and the treatment which followed, which is a terrible thing for any young boy to cope with. But George has had his father at his side.”

The dawn of his teenage years will see huge changes for George as his new school, which he will enrol in September, will see him board full-time for the first time.

‌



Not only will it be a significant step for the future King, it will also be a big change for his parents and his siblings, Princess Charlotte and Prince Louis, who all attended Lambrook School together.

But Jennie said: “William - and Catherine - are bound to worry about their little boy as he becomes a teenager and sets off for boarding school. It’s a huge step and a big change in any family.

View 5 Images A 13-year-old William on his first day at Eton in September 1995 (Image: Getty Images)

‌



“But William knows exactly what life is like at Eton and he knows exactly what it’s like to be an heir to the throne. There is no one better placed to help and guide George through his teenage years.

“Diana told me the country was lucky to have William. I think George is exceptionally lucky to have the parents he has. They have given him the best, most secure start in life: he knows how much they love one another and how much they love him. He looks like a young man well equipped for this next chapter.”

News.title: Ann Widdecombe was hit on head 21 times with hammer, prosecutors say
News.content:
Ann Widdecombe was hit on the head with a hammer 21 times at her home as she ate lunch in an attack that was caught on camera, prosecutors have told Westminster Magistrates' Court.

Prosecutor Kashif Malik said the man charged with her murder, Joshua Kerry, arrived at her house on 8 July in a red Vauxhall Corsa and entered through the front door.

Kerry, who prosecutors say was in the property for two minutes and was wearing black gloves, then allegedly hit Widdecombe repeatedly with a hammer in her kitchen, tipped her from her chair and took her wallet before driving off.

The 28-year-old from South Yorkshire later also appeared at the Old Bailey and was remanded in custody.

At the Old Bailey hearing, prosecutor Alistair Richardson said the attack on Widdecombe had been carried out with a "ferocity of violence".

Malik told the court that Widdecombe did not attend a pre-arranged online interview with Channel 5's Matt Allwright show that had been scheduled for just before 13:00 BST on 8 July.

The show's production team tried to contact Widdecombe through her personal assistant, who then asked Widdecombe's gardener to check on her, the court heard.

Prosecutors said the gardener entered the house via the open front door on 9 July and found Widdecombe lying face down on her kitchen floor with a serious head injury.

News.title: Burnham tells cabinet to tackle living costs at first meeting
News.content:
Andy Burnham has promised to lead a "cost of living government," as he chaired his first cabinet meeting as prime minister.

He told his newly-assembled top team that he wanted to make living expenses a key priority, and give people a "sense that help is coming" on costs.

It comes after he announced a VAT cut to household energy bills from October, in his first major announcement since taking office.

But his plan to pay for the policy by scrapping Sir Keir Starmer's digital ID scheme led to an early row over whether the plan was properly funded.

Downing Street said the estimated Â£850m cost of the VAT cut over the rest of the financial year could come from Â£1.8bn earmarked by the previous government to roll out the digital ID scheme in the next three years.

But Darren Jones, who was among a clutch of Starmer loyalists sacked from the cabinet on Monday, said the ID programme was "unfunded" and Burnham would need to set out where the money would be found.

Opposition parties also seized on the announcement, pointing out the government's budget watchdog has previously said the money to fund digital ID was due to be found from within existing budgets.

"We are only one day in and already Labour are playing fast and loose with the public finances," said Conservative shadow chancellor Sir Mel Stride.

The PM's spokesman insisted the policy would be funded by redirecting "savings" identified by departments to cover the cost of the ID scheme.

News.title: Sackings, cabinet surprises and policies: Burnham's first 24 hours as PM
News.content:
Shortly after Andy Burnham telephoned a number of Keir Starmer's allies to sack them from the cabinet on Monday afternoon, John Healey received the signal to head to Number 10.

Wearing a suit and one of his many red ties, the former defence secretary left parliament alone via a back entrance next to a pub.

"I'm on my way to a meeting," he said with a slight smile as he marched down Whitehall.

Healey's imminent appointment as chancellor was a surprise - to him, to his Labour colleagues, and to the British public.

It was a consequential moment among a flurry of announcements from the new prime minister, including today's cut in VAT on energy bills, that demonstrate the new government's intention to move at breakneck speed - at least for now.

The Conservatives support that tax cut but have questioned its funding.

Five weeks earlier Healey had weakened Keir Starmer's grip on Downing Street by quitting as defence secretary in a row over military spending.

Soon he would be back around the cabinet table alongside two others whose recent resignations had also damaged Starmer - new defence secretary Wes Streeting and new energy secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh.

Were they rewarded for rebelling and hastening Burnham's path to office? Possibly.

But all three are also widely seen as skilled operators taking on complex roles.

News.title: Argentina's Fernandez defends team after ugly scenes in World Cup final loss to Spain
News.content:
Midfielder Enzo Fernandez has claimed Argentina represented their nation "in the best possible way" during the World Cup, despite ugly scenes during and after their final loss to Spain.

Fernandez was sent off late in normal time for two yellow cards and Spain won 1-0 after extra time on Sunday in New Jersey.

His first booking was for showing dissent towards Slovenian referee Slavko Vincic and Fernandez was later dismissed for catching Pau Cubarsi with a challenge that sent the defender cartwheeling in the air.

But, in a statement on social media, the Chelsea midfielder did not mention the red card and said: "As time goes by, you realise there is something much bigger than just a result.

"For years, this group has represented the team in the best possible way. It teaches that competing isn't just about winning; it's about giving your all for the jersey and never giving up.

"It has been a privilege to be part of a group that always stepped up, competed at the highest level, and defended these colours with pride, humility, and commitment."

News.title: Zelensky sacks Ukraine's top army commander after days of protests
News.content:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has sacked the country's commander-in-chief, Oleksandr Syrskyi.

His dismissal comes just days after the removal of popular Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov - a move that triggered street protests across the country.

Initial rumours that the end of Fedorov's tenure was related to a conflict between the two men were soon confirmed.

Fedorov, 35, has been widely praised for energising the ministry and transforming the armed forces, as well as heading a drive against corruption.

Syrskyi, 60, is seen by many in Ukraine as a Soviet-school commander reluctant to implement radical changes in the army.

News.title: Parts of the UK move closer to drought
News.content:
Summer so far has been exceptionally hot and dry across much of the UK, with three widespread heatwaves and the longest run of dry days in central England since 1995. England, Wales and eastern Scotland have been the driest areas over recent weeks, and this follows a very dry spring in similar regions.

England has received only 3% of its long-term average July rainfall with the south and east of England seeing no rain at all. Wisley in Surrey has seen 33 consecutive dry days.

Rainfall so far this summer has been below average across the UK as a whole, but there has been large regional contrast.

Up to the middle of summer - 15 July - parts of eastern and north-eastern England had received just 26% of their total expected summer rainfall. Areas of northern and western Scotland had more than average for the first half of the summer, though.

In Wales, where just 5% of July rainfall has fallen, Natural Resources Wales has moved the worst affected regions in the north and south-east into "prolonged dry weather status", the first step in its drought plan.

Comparisons are being made with last summer, when drought was declared across much of England, Wales and eastern Scotland. It officially ended just four months ago.

This year, drought has not developed as quickly because heavy rainfall recharged our aquifers, rivers and reservoirs during a very wet autumn and winter.

However, the UK Centre for Ecology and Hydrology says flash droughts, external with a sudden transition between wet and dry conditions are "likely to happen more often, and be more intense".

As the effects of human-induced climate change continue, the Met Office expects our summers to become hotter and drier, external in the future. In fact, by 2070, our summers could be up to 60% drier and 1-6C warmer compared to 1990.

News.title: Thames Water announces hosepipe ban for 10 million
News.content:
Thames Water has announced a hosepipe ban affecting 10.1 million customers after an "exceptionally warm and dry spring".

The restrictions mean, from Thursday, hosepipes should not be used for watering gardens or allotments, cleaning cars, filling paddling pools or swimming pools, or cleaning windows.

The water company said its region had seen 40% of average rainfall, and more days at or above 34C this year than ever recorded before.

Nevil Muncaster, director of strategic water resources, said: "We would not be taking this step unless it was necessary to protect water supplies for everyone and the environment."

The ban applies to all customers that Thames Water supplies with drinking water and comes into effect on Thursday.

The company provides water to customers across parts of Gloucestershire, Wiltshire, Surrey, the Thames Valley, Greater London, and the surrounding areas, external.

It provides water and wastewater services to 16 million customers overall.

It said water use was currently 10% above normal in the Thames Valley and Home Counties and 7% above normal in London, which amounted to an extra 100 million litres of water every day.

News.title: Ryanair boss says 'foreign object' may have caused plane window incident
News.content:
An incident on a Ryanair flight which saw a passenger partially sucked out of a plane window may have been caused by "foreign object damage" to an engine, said the airline's boss.

Michael O'Leary said an initial investigation into the incident on 10 July between Greece and Germany suggests "it looks like a foreign object damage to the engine on takeoff at Thessaloniki but ... we can't say that definitively".

He insisted that the engine on the 18-year-old Boeing 737 plane had been fully serviced and overhauled in the past two years.

Serbian national Ljubisa KaroviÄ's head and right shoulder were sucked out of the plane's window, leaving him "seriously injured and in shock".

His wife Svetlana GrkoviÄ MaksimoviÄ told BBC Serbia that she and two other passengers held on to his legs for several minutes.

She said: "We pulled him back together. His entire face was deformed and blood was pouring from his nose and mouth."

He was taken to hospital after the plane made an emergency landing.

Passengers told local media they heard "some kind of explosion" on board.

The aircraft was operated by Ryanair's subsidiary Malta Air.

Confirmation that the damage was caused by an external object could affect Ryanair or Boeing's liabilities over the incident.

The US National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) is investigating. O'Leary said that a draft report would be issued in about 28 days.

News.title: Russian warship carried out firing exercise off Plymouth coast
News.content:
The live-fire exercise took place in international waters and lasted for 30 minutes.

The Russian warship requested that the Royal Navy's HMS Tyne reposition to a safer distance, which it did.

The Russian frigate was also being monitored by a French military aircraft which made radio contact with the warship asking it to clarify its intentions, the BBC has been told.

BBC Verify has analysed flight and ship-tracking data which shows the position of HMS Tyne and several British military aircraft operating in and around the Channel near Plymouth on Monday.

Flight data on ADS-B Exchange indicates at least four Royal Air Force and Royal Navy aircraft were flying off the coast of Dorset mostly above the UK's territorial waters, including two Eurofighter Typhoons, a Voyager air refuelling tanker and a Super Lynx helicopter.

A French military H160M GuÃ©pard helicopter also flew out and over the Channel during the afternoon. It is not clear if this is the aircraft which made contact with the Russian warship.

Data on ship-tracking service MarineTraffic shows HMS Tyne began to broadcast its location about 40 miles off Plymouth at 13:57 BST on Monday. It remained in that location for around two hours before departing at 15:56 to return to Plymouth.

HMS Tyne has been tracking Neustrashimy since at least 16 July when both vessels were also captured in the North Sea about 36 miles miles from the port of Felixstowe in Suffolk on a satellite image.

The incident will be a reminder for the new prime minister of increased Russian naval activity near UK waters in recent months.

Last month, Royal Marine Commandos boarded a Russian "shadow fleet" oil tanker in the English Channel in a six-hour operation which was the first of its kind by UK armed forces.

Also in June, a British couple in international waters in the English Channel came across a Russian warship - Admiral Grigorovich - 23 miles off the Isle of Wight.

The frigate fired warning shots as Jane and Alan Kelvey sailed their yacht on what Russia's defence ministry said had been a "dangerous approach". However, the couple said they had not been on a "collision course".

Russian warships regularly pass through international waters in the Channel, which are separate from UK and French territorial waters.

News.title: Union plans rail strikes over train safety concerns
News.content:
A union that represents railway staff has announced plans for its members at East Midlands Railway (EMR) to take strike action over "growing safety concerns the company has failed to address".

The RMT union said it had been in dispute with EMR since April following the rollout of the 810 fleet (Aurora), which it said had been operating with a "significant number" of faults.

It said its members planned to take strike action on Saturday 1 August and the following two Saturdays.

An EMR spokesperson said any suggestion that the Hitachi Rail Class 810 fleet did not meet the required safety standards was "incorrect", and added it continued "to engage in discussions with RMT regarding this dispute".

Last week, EMR said reliability and maintenance issues with the new Aurora (Class 810) trains - made by Hitachi Rail - were to blame.

EMR has also outlined "challenges" with both the 810s and the older Class 222s, affecting the toilets, air conditioning and catering equipment.

It added the Class 222 trains had also required "additional maintenance support to accommodate increased running and operational requirements".

The operator first introduced the Aurora trains into passenger service in December, after what EMR said was a three-year delay.

News.title: Family of woman who lay dead in crash for days confronts mechanic who falsified MOT
News.content:
Angry scenes erupted outside court after the family of a woman killed in a car crash confronted a garage owner who falsified an MOT just weeks before.

Neil John Lewis, 47, pleaded guilty to fraud by false representation at Cardiff Magistrates' Court on Tuesday, and admitted he knew the car was "dangerous".

Eve Smith, 21, Darcy Ross, 21, and Rafel Jeanne, 24, died when the car given the false MOT crashed into woodland in Cardiff in March 2023. They lay undiscovered for two days. Two others survived.

As Lewis left court, the family of Ross brandished a framed photograph the dead woman, and shouted at him: "Darcy Ross, remember her name."

News.title: 'Significant hot spots' remain at Cairngorms wildfire
News.content:
Hot spots remain at a wildfire which has burned across 10 square kilometres of land in the Cairngorms over the last week, according to the fire service.

More than 100 firefighters have been involved in the operation to control and extinguish the fire, which started near Ryvoan Bothy, south of Nethy Bridge, last Wednesday.

The Scottish Fire and Rescue Service said on Sunday that they had "surrounded" the large-scale blaze.

However, they say "significant hotspots remain across a large and complex landscape" and crews will stay at the scene until the incident is brought to a safe conclusion.

News.title: Boy, 15, accused of sex attacks on eight girls
News.content:
A 15-year-old boy charged with sexual offences against eight girls, including one who was 10 years old, has appeared in court.

The complainants were aged between 10 and 15 at the time, Wellingborough Youth Court heard.

The teenager, who cannot be named because of his age, faces 22 charges relating to alleged incidents between 2023 and 2025, including rape.

He was not asked to enter any pleas during a 20-minute hearing, before the case was sent to Northampton Crown Court for 18 August.

The defendant, who was accompanied by his mother, was released on bail.

Details of where the offences took place have been withheld to protect the alleged victims' right to anonymity.

The boy has been charged with:

Twelve counts of sexually assaulting a female

Three offences of assaulting a girl under 13 by touching

Two counts of rape and a further two of making an indecent photograph or pseudo-photograph of a child

Assaulting a female by penetration

Possessing a prohibited image of a child and possessing an extreme pornographic image or images

District Judge Amar Mehta told the boy: "Your case is too serious to be tried in this court."

His bail conditions included not to contact the alleged victims and to have no unsupervised contact with females under 16.

The boy spoke only to confirm his name, date of birth and address. He also asked the judge to explain what the Youth Justice Service was.

News.title: London-based civil servants offered move to No 10 North in Manchester
News.content:
Civil servants working for government departments based in London have been offered relocation packages to encourage them to move to the North of England, the BBC understands.

It comes as the first details are emerging about the new No 10 North, which Downing Street says is already up and running.

The BBC has been told that the Northern branch of Downing Street will be overseen by cabinet minister and ally of Burnham, Louise Haigh.

Haigh, who is the first secretary of state, is thought to have been asked to lead a new Office for the Prime Minister and the Cabinet (OPMC), which will give her control of key decision-making bodies across government.

The OPMC will include No 10, No 10 North and teams within the Cabinet Office.

Addressing his cabinet for the first time, Burnham said No 10 North was "not a gimmick" and that the "time for resisting devolution was over".

A No 10 spokesman said the prime minister was expecting to work from No 10 North "at least one day a week" subject to government business.

Announcing the changes,, external which will also establish a new AI taskforce, Leader of the House of Lords, Baroness Angela Smith said No 10 North would be a "dominant driver of the UK's economy".

It is understood that the initial location of No 10 North will be Heron House in central Manchester, in the same building which houses offices for the intelligence service GCHQ. Specialist police officers have been seen guarding the building.

It is likely that the longer term base for No 10 North will be at a new government "Digital Campus" which is under construction in the Ancoats area of Manchester. It is not due for completion until 2032.

However, a good indication of what it could look like comes from a new report, released on Tuesday.

The blueprint has been authored, external by the Re:State think tank which Burnham was involved with until he stepped down as mayor of Greater Manchester.

News.title: 'We just need a bed' - Baby with 'days to live' can't access lifesaving treatment
News.content:
The parents of a three-month-old boy who they fear has just days to live say they're frustrated at being unable to access lifesaving treatment due to a lack of suitable hospital beds.

Dylan and Catrin Green from Cardiff took Macs to hospital six weeks ago after he struggled feeding.

He later suffered two cardiac arrests and was diagnosed with dilated cardiomyopathy, external, a heart condition which can lead to heart failure.

He urgently needs a "Berlin heart" - a device which could stabalise his condition while he's in intensive care awaiting a heart transplant.

The organisation which commissions specialist NHS care in Wales said funding was available but treatment was decided by clinical assessment.

Two weeks ago, Macs was transferred to a specialist unit in Bristol where his condition has since deteriorated.

He is now in an induced coma with a machine performing the usual function of the heart.

His family said he needed to be moved to one of two specialist hospitals which can offer the Berlin heart, external - a highly specialised pump which acts as a bridge to a transplant - but, at the moment, no beds were available.

News.title: B&M fined £2m over mice infestations
News.content:
B&M Retail Ltd has been fined Â£2m over mice infestations at three Birmingham stores where inspectors found rodent-gnawed foodstuffs and droppings near children's toys.

The company was prosecuted for food hygiene offences by Birmingham City Council after complaints led to inspections being carried out between November 2024 and October 2025.

Locations included St Andrew's Retail Park where officers found gnawed products on sale, the council said. Mouse infestations were also uncovered at Priory Square Shopping Centre and The Fort Shopping Park.

B&M said it was "deeply sorry for the failings identified" and had taken comprehensive action to "strengthen controls across our business".

The council said complaints included one from a member of the public "who reported seeing a mouse in the shop" at Priory Square.

Other transgressions there included urine contamination from rodents on food packaging and shelving, inadequate cleaning standards and structural defects allowing pest entry.

A Hygiene Emergency Prohibition Notice was served and the store was closed immediately, the council said.

A further inspection took place at B&M's store at The Fort Shopping Park in Erdington on 27 October 2025 following a complaint alleging a mouse infestation.

Officers found widespread evidence of mouse activity throughout the premises, including mouse droppings "in close proximity to children's toys on display", the council said.

The store was also closed due to the risks posed to public health.

Cam Newton and Karl Ravech are among the major stars exiting in the latest round of layoffs at ESPN, sources told The Athletic Tuesday.

Ravech, a 31-year veteran of the network, served as ESPN’s lead MLB play-by-play announcer, covered college basketball and anchored SportsCenter. He called the Dodgers-Phillies game Monday before reportedly learning his position was in jeopardy. When contacted by The Athletic Tuesday, Ravech said he had not yet been informed of his status.

NFL MVP Newton, longtime SportsCenter anchor David Lloyd, injury analyst Stephania Bell, former All-Pro linebacker and studio host Bart Scott and NFL Network analyst Charles Davis are also being impacted by the cuts at ESPN and NFL Network, according to The Athletic.

Newton joined ESPN as an NFL analyst in October 2024 after an 11-season NFL career that included a Super Bowl run with the Carolina Panthers. After initially appearing on First Take, he signed an expanded contract with the network in August 2025.

On Monday, ESPN announced it was parting ways with NFL analyst Ryan Clark and additional cuts are expected among behind-the-scenes staff.

open image in gallery Cam Newton signed an expanded contract with ESPN in August 2025 but was reportedly laid off Tuesday ( Getty )

open image in gallery Karl Ravech, pictured, is reportedly among those impacted by ESPN’s latest round of layoffs, sources told The Athletic Tuesday ( Getty )

Many of the cuts are reportedly connected to ESPN’s integration with NFL Network, including the expected departure of NFL insider Tom Pelissero, one of the network’s top reporters, according to the outlet.

A memo from ESPN Chairman Jimmy Pitaro to employees Tuesday morning, obtained by The Independent, did not identify those impacted by the layoffs but said the cuts followed a review of the company’s teams, resources and structure after integrating acquired NFL assets.

ESPN acquired NFL Network in late January as part of a deal with the league that also gave the NFL a 10 percent stake in ESPN.

“Over the past several months, we've made significant progress integrating the NFL assets that we acquired into ESPN. Throughout this process, we have taken the time to carefully evaluate our collective teams, resources and organizational structure to best position us for the future. As a result, we had to make some difficult decisions about job impacts that we will be communicating today,” Pitaro wrote.

“While most of the job impacts are tied to the acquisition, we will also notify colleagues in other parts of the company today that their positions have been impacted. We are committed to treating employees with compassion and respect and to providing support as they navigate this transition,” the memo continued.

“Even in moments like these, the strength of ESPN comes from our people, our teamwork and our shared mission to serve sports fans.”

open image in gallery NFL Network insider Tom Pelissero is reportedly among those impacted by ESPN’s latest round of layoffs ( Getty )

ESPN declined to provide further comment.

The network reportedly planned to announce Clark’s departure Tuesday but moved up the decision after receiving media inquiries Monday, The Athletic reported.

Clark was removed from Monday’s episode of NFL Live and informed of his dismissal directly by an executive before the news became public, sources claimed.

Clark, a former NFL safety who joined ESPN more than a decade ago, was earning more than $2 million annually, according to The Athletic. He was a prominent voice on shows including Monday Night Countdown, First Take, Get Up and NFL Live.

open image in gallery Ryan Clark’s ESPN exit was reportedly influenced by concerns over his on-air comments and conduct, including a dispute with colleague Peter Schrager ( Getty )

ESPN executives reportedly became concerned over Clark’s conduct, with tensions escalating after a dispute with colleague Peter Schrager during an episode of Get Up last season.

The disagreement followed Clark’s criticism of Schrager’s defense of Cowboys receiver CeeDee Lamb, with Clark telling Schrager, That's the non-player in you."

Clark addressed his layoff in an Instagram post Tuesday, sharing clips of his workout allegedly before he received the news. “Proof of Life…Before the madness of yesterday, I woke up, got in my Tundra, drove to Planet Fitness, and got to work,” Clark wrote.

“The rest of the day was eventful, but the journey continues. My peace is with God, and my humility comes from within. I’ll continue to build myself so the world can never strip me of what’s real. Get moving today y’all!”

Clark also showed support for his laid off colleagues on X. He wrote Tuesday: “Sending prayers and love to all those laid off today by ESPN. So many of you have poured your life into that company, & I know how you’re feeling right now. My hope is as this door closes, another opens for you all. God bless!”

Ben Stokes scored an unbeaten century in his first game since retiring from England duty as he helped Durham to a five-wicket victory over Derbyshire in the Metro Bank One Day Cup.

The former England captain has been the matchwinner so many times for his country and it did not take him long to transfer that reputation back to his county as he guided them home with 108 not out, his first list A century for Durham in 12 years.

The 35-year-old made his return to county cricket, for the first time since his international retirement in June, on the same day The Hundred also got under way.

Stokes last featured for Durham in the format in their One Day Cup final win over Warwickshire in 2014 and has not played in any 50-over format since England played Pakistan at the 2023 World Cup in India.

He previously admitted being back at his boyhood club last month, having been stood down by England during an investigation into a nightclub incident, rekindled his “affection towards cricket” and despite not getting any rewards with the ball in hand on Tuesday, he showed his quality with the bat.

Martin Andersson’s well-worked ton helped the hosts to 256 for nine but Stokes’ century helped Durham kick off their 50-over campaign in style.

Stokes struggled with cramp for much of his innings but the ‘wounded soldier’ look was a familiar sight for those who have watched him over the years, and it did not stop him knocking 10 fours and three sixes on his way to a 116-ball century.

Stokes started his first spell of bowling in the ninth over but Brooke Guest and Andersson ploughed on and produced a 112-run partnership for the second wicket before the former was dismissed on 48.

open image in gallery Ben Stokes bowled nine economical but wicketless overs (Mike Egerton/PA) ( PA Wire )

All eyes were on Stokes but Luke Robinson played the starring role with the ball, dismissing Harry Came, Wayne Madsen and Anuj Dal as the hosts fell from 181 for two to 226 for eight.

However, Andersson quietly chipped away for 112 from 118 balls to help the Falcons put a competitive total on the board. Stokes conceded only 38 runs from his nine overs.

Ben Aitchison dismissed Durham openers Graham Clark and Alex Lees inside the powerplay which brought Stokes to the crease with the score on 24 for two.

He could have been dismissed second ball when Aitchison’s delivery hit him on the thigh pad, with Derbyshire’s appeals ignored by the umpire.

It took 28 deliveries for Stokes to hit his first boundary and then two came along at once, and his first six down the ground in the 33rd over took him closer to a half-century.

open image in gallery Stokes brought up his half-century in uncomfortable fashion (Mike Egerton/PA) ( PA Wire )

Stokes edged Nick Potts for four to reach 50 but immediately fell and clutched his hamstring with what looked to be cramp before he raised his bat in the air while sitting on the ground.

Durham were edging closer but England’s Shoaib Bashir dismissed Ollie Robinson to potentially put the cat among the pigeons.

Stokes was struggling to run so he decided to stand and deliver with a flurry of boundaries, but he brought his century up with a simple single to deep midwicket before taking his side home alongside Kasey Aldridge with five balls to spare.

Durham wicketkeeper Robinson said of Stokes’ achievement: “We’re all so proud of him.

“It’s a massive boost. A man who can do what he did today back in the ranks is unbelievable. That’ll get views around the world, so good for this competition.

“He just provides us with this calmness and has this aura about him like he has done all these wonderful things, it’s amazing.”

New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill announced Tuesday that a software error at the state's motor vehicles department inadvertently registered approximately 6,600 individuals who are not U.S. citizens to vote. Despite this significant oversight, fewer than 400 of these individuals have actually cast ballots in elections since June 2023.

The Democratic governor, who assumed office in January, revealed she was informed last week about the software mistake within New Jersey's Motor Vehicle System.

This flaw, active between June 2023 and June 2024, led to the registration of people who had explicitly indicated they were not U.S. citizens. Governor Sherrill stressed that the individuals involved did nothing wrong and were mistakenly registered "through no fault of their own."

This disclosure comes as President Donald Trump has undertaken an aggressive push to identify and mitigate voting by noncitizens, particularly ahead of November's congressional elections. However, experts have long determined that non-citizen voting does not constitute a significant problem in American elections.

The Democratic governor revealed she was informed last week about the software mistake within New Jersey's Motor Vehicle System ( Reuters/Vincent Alban )

The state's preliminary analysis showed that fewer than 400 of those 6,600 - Democrats, Republicans and unaffiliated people who were scattered across the state - actually voted. Sherrill said she has ordered the removal of those individuals who were mistakenly added to the voter rolls and will replace the vendor responsible for the error, which occurred before she took office.

“As the Trump administration tries to weaponize elections for political gain, I am ensuring we protect our elections," Sherrill said in a statement. “The difference is simple: when we find a problem, we don't hide it, deny it, or invent conspiracies. We investigate it, we fix it, and we tell the public. That's what accountability and good governance look like, and that's exactly what my administration is doing."

Trump has spent years raising doubts about electoral outcomes, falsely asserting that his ​2020 loss to Democrat ⁠Joe Biden was rigged. He has also advanced other false claims, including that mail-in balloting is rife with fraud, voting machines are untrustworthy and non-citizen voting is widespread.

Numerous courts and vote recounts found no evidence of large-scale fraud in the 2020 election. A Reuters data analysis revealed that voting violations by noncitizens were often inadvertent, the result of misinformation from others or confusion on their part.

Last week, the Trump administration threatened state officials with fines and criminal charges if they do not comply with election security measures, including providing the federal government with unredacted voter rolls.

Courts have blocked Trump administration efforts to obtain states' unredacted voter rolls, which contain sensitive, personally identifiable information about residents.

Danish drugmaker Novo Nordisk filed a lawsuit against U.S. competitor Eli Lilly in a New Jersey federal court on Tuesday, alleging that the company engaged in false advertising regarding the effectiveness of its weight-loss treatments.

The suit accuses Indianapolis-based Eli Lilly of violating federal and state laws through nationwide promotional campaigns for its obesity drug Zepbound and diabetes drug Mounjaro.

Novo Nordisk, the maker of competing weight-loss injection Wegovy and diabetes drug Ozempic, is asking the court to order Eli Lilly to stop the campaign, run corrective s and pay damages derived from any profits tied to the marketing, as reported by Reuters.

“The ads are maliciously and deceptively false because Lilly knowingly cites outdated clinical trials that compare the highest doses of the Lilly medicines to lower doses of Novo Nordisk’s medicines,” according to the complaint.

Eli Lilly defended the claims, stating that its promotions were based on results from its SURMOUNT-5 clinical trial completed in 2024. A spokesperson for Eli Lilly told Reuters that the company intended to defend against the lawsuit vigorously and asserted that Novo Nordisk was seeking to block the public communication of trial results rather than compete on product merits.

Danish drugmaker Novo Nordisk is asking a federal judge to halt U.S. competitor Eli Lilly’s promotional campaign, force corrective ads, and surrender any profits earned from the misleading marketing claims ( PA )

The dispute focuses on dosage comparisons used in marketing materials. Novo Nordisk General Counsel John Kuckelman told the publication that Eli Lilly’s ads displayed average weight loss of about 50 pounds for Zepbound compared to 33 pounds for Wegovy.

Kuckelman said those figures reflected comparisons between maximum doses of Eli Lilly’s drugs and lower, older doses of Wegovy, while ignoring a 7.2-milligram dose approved by the FDA in March. Separate late-stage trials of the highest approved doses showed average weight loss of roughly 48 pounds for Zepbound and 47 pounds for Wegovy, according to Kuckelman.

Novo Nordisk issued a cease-and-desist letter in April following the approval of the higher Wegovy dose, Kuckelman said, adding that Eli Lilly subsequently inserted an inadequate disclaimer while continuing a campaign that has logged over 700 million views since late April.

Legal experts say that while pharmaceutical companies routinely sue over patents, false advertising lawsuits are far less common.

Alexandra Roberts, a professor at Northeastern University's School of Law, told Reuters that potential damages could be significant given the market size, though any financial penalty may be limited by how recently the higher Wegovy dosage entered the market.

The lawsuit comes as both drugmakers fight for control of a U.S. weight-loss market that analysts estimate could top $100 billion by 2030. Following Tuesday’s filing, Novo Nordisk shares dropped 2 percent in Copenhagen, while Eli Lilly rose slightly by 0.5 percent.

The United States and China are set to hold crucial talks on artificial intelligence in September, as the rival superpowers confront the escalating risks posed by their increasingly powerful frontier models.

The discussions, a significant outcome of the May summit between President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping, are expected to take place before President Xi’s planned visit to the U.S. on September 24, according to five individuals familiar with the matter who spoke to Reuters.

However, the exact dates remain unfinalized.

Both Beijing and Washington have expressed growing anxiety over each other's AI capabilities amid a global race to develop advanced technologies.

The two nations are grappling with how to regulate sophisticated AI models that could enhance military power, facilitate cyberattacks on critical infrastructure, and disrupt labor markets.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is slated to lead the U.S. delegation for the September talks, which Reuters first reported on Tuesday.

While the identities of other participants from both countries, along with the agenda and location, are still under deliberation as preparations are in their initial stages, the discussions mark the first official U.S.-China dialogue on AI under President Trump.

Concerns over intellectual property are high on the U.S. agenda. Secretary Bessent, when asked about the talks on Fox Business Network, did not directly confirm the meeting but highlighted issues with AI model standards.

"We are finding watermarks of our U.S. large language models on many of the Chinese models, and that that's unacceptable," he stated. "We're going to be looking at that in the coming days or weeks."

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer echoed these sentiments, telling CNBC, "We're taking a very close look at how China is propagating its AI development to make sure that our companies compete ... on a level playing field."

The U.S. has already restricted exports of some advanced AI chips to China but has refrained from blacklisting certain Chinese AI companies, including DeepSeek and CXMT, to avoid escalating tensions.

( Reuters )

Meanwhile, Chinese authorities are considering curbs on overseas access to their most powerful AI models, partly due to concerns about the hacking potential of Anthropic's Mythos.

China is reportedly seeking genuine engagement and technical discussions on AI issues rather than political talks.

Analysts suggest Beijing's priorities for the discussions include Mythos, how the U.S. will manage the release of future advanced frontier models, and potential U.S. restrictions on Chinese open-weight models.

Paul Triolo, a partner at DGA-Albright Stonebridge Group, believes the initial meeting will focus on foundational agreements.

"This is the first meeting; they're unlikely to solve any major problems. I think they will try to agree to some basic terms, like what defines a frontier AI model," he commented.

Several anti-war protesters repeatedly interrupted Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth during his appearance in front of a Senate committee as he demands billions of dollars to support the Trump administration’s escalating war with Iran after a 10th consecutive night of attacks.

“Iranian Americans are against this war of aggression,” one protester shouted out. “Your hands are bloody.”

Another shouted out “Stop bombing our children in Iran and Palestine” and condemned an “illegal” war.

Tuesday’s testimony from Hegseth and Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Dan Caine follows the deaths of at least three American service members within two days, with nearly 100 other troops injured within the last month after the collapse of a fragile ceasefire.

At least 18 American troops have died since the beginning of the war, and more than 400 others have been injured.

Hegseth and Caine last testified to members of Congress about the war in May, around the same time they last delivered a public briefing to the press. They are asking for another $67 billion from Congress to cover mounting costs for the war.

Their appearance also follows the president’s meeting at the White House alongside Lebanese president Joseph Aoun, where Trump told reporters that the U.S. could devastate Iran’s infrastructure in ways that it would take “decades” for Tehran to rebuild.

NASA says it’s planning to fly planes into dangerous wildfire-generated storms this summer to help improve forecasting – and potentially save lives.

Major wildfires across the U.S. West have produced clouds that can shoot choking smoke high into Earth’s atmosphere, generate thousands of fire-causing lightning strikes in a matter of just hours, and even spawn destructive, whirling firenadoes.

These clouds and their impacts complicate firefighting efforts and threaten Americans living near the fire and those thousands of miles away.

Rising smoke is responsible for the clouds, known as pyrocumulonimbus clouds. But exactly how the clouds form remains poorly understood and current predictions are often inadequate, the space agency’s researchers say.

That’s concerning in a warming world that is expected to produce more severe and frequent fires. Human-caused climate change is fueling tinderbox conditions that make fires more likely.

open image in gallery A pyrocumulonimbus cloud is generated by the Orroral Valley bushfire in Australia in January 2020. NASA is hoping to better understand these dangerous clouds by sending planes into fire storms in real-time ( Getty Images )

open image in gallery This graphic image shows how smoke from a wildfire helps moisture in the atmosphere condense into a cloud known as a pyrocumulonimbus ( NASA's Earth Science Project Office )

“Measuring and mapping the dangerous storms as they develop in real-time will help scientists forecast them in the future,” NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory said in a statement on Monday.

The experiment is known as the Smoke and PYRocumulonimbus Experiment, or “INSPYRE,” and led by the Naval Research Laboratory.

The plan is to fly NASA’s ER-2 and WB-57 planes out of Montana to record data on the clouds’ formation.

open image in gallery NASA operates two Airborne Science ER-2 aircraft, seen here, for a wide variety of environmental science, atmospheric sampling and satellite data verification missions ( NASA/Carla Thomas )

open image in gallery A fire whirl – or firenado – shoots into the sky amid the Hog fire in Susanville, California, in July 2020 ( AFP via Getty Images )

There would be at least two 6-8-week flight missions over the western U.S. or Canada.

Each mission will include more than a dozen science flights and the planes will be carrying infrared wildfire trackers developed at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California.

NASA is also planning to deploy radar and remote sensing tech on the ground to observe the clouds in the U.S. West.

Canada has seen an especially active fire season this year, resulting in more than 900 blazes across the nation and sending hazardous smoke into major U.S. cities for days.

open image in gallery White pyrocumulonimbus clouds generated by the 2021 McKay Creek fire in British Columbia are seen in this NASA satellite image ( NASA/Landsat 8 )

There are also fires burning in the Pacific Northwest that have triggered air quality alerts.

Some 1,457,545 acres have burned in large fires this year across America, according to the National Interagency Fire Center.

Still, more fires and smoke are likely on the way. Peak fire season in the U.S. doesn’t begin until August.

News.title: 10 European countries that do not have EES for 2026 holidays
News.content:
