Sports.title: Could the World Cup be back in the US as soon as 2038? Absolutely
Sports.content:
As is often the case, it has been left to Donald Trump to say the quiet bit out loud. “We have to do this again and we have to do it while I’m around, you hear that Gianni?” the US president told Fox News in an interview broadcast in the buildup to the World Cup final.

An American bid for the 2038 World Cup has been the talk of the hotel lobbies populated by administrators from around the world over the past month, who have watched this country’s seemingly limitless appetite for major events and willingness to pay whatever it takes to attend them.

Fifa has been quietly, but actively encouraging a US bid for some time and in a meeting at the Waldorf Astoria on Park Avenue in New York on Saturday it became clearer why.

The Fifa president, Gianni Infantino, told representatives of the governing body’s 211 member associations that its revenue projections for the current four-year cycle has increased from $11bn (£8.2bn) to $15bn, with the vast majority of the growth coming from an explosion in ticketing and hospitality revenue.

A Fifa source disclosed that such has been the demand in the US in particular that ticketing and hospitality sales have gone past $5bn, with that part of the market now worth more than the World Cup’s TV rights for the first time.

“Fifa will want to get back here as quickly as possible,” said a senior figure at one of its hospitality partners.

While ticket sales have exceeded expectations, helped by the dynamic pricing and secondary market resale models that are embedded in US culture, in one crucial respect Fifa left a huge amount of money on the table, another reason it is desperate to return.

In an extraordinary deal, Fox Sports was awarded English-language TV rights in the US by Fifa without a bidding process, a precautionary move by the world governing body to prevent a lawsuit when Qatar 2022 was moved to the winter after the TV contracts had already been signed, creating a direct clash with the US domestic sports season, particularly the NFL and NBA.

With no competitive tension, Fox was given a relative bargain, paying $485m for the 2026 rights, the same as in Qatar, despite the World Cup having an extra 40 matches and taking place on home soil. For context, the NFL’s domestic TV deal is worth $11bn a year, with the NBA bringing in around $7bn.

Fox has capitalised this summer as a result, on the back of bumper viewing, with industry experts predicting it will make more than $1bn from TV adverts, whose volume and value has increased due to the addition of hydration breaks.

Fifa is determined to recoup what many regard as lost income from the US market in future TV rights cycles.

Having watched with frustration as Fox has cashed in, ESPN and NBC are expected to bid for the 2030 tournament, while initial conversations have also taken place with Netflix about them joining in the auction.

View image in fullscreen High prices did not deter fans from packing out stadiums at the World Cup in the US. Photograph: Julio Cortez/AP

Netflix has already signalled its growing interest in football by buying American rights for the Women’s World Cup in 2027 and 2031, the latter being held in the US, and another men’s tournament seven years later would spark another boom.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

No country has hosted the World Cup twice in 12 years, but Fifa’s statutes and recent staging decisions give it the flexibility for this to happen.

By taking the 2030 World Cup to three continents and six countries – Spain, Portugal, Morocco, Argentina, Paraguay and Uruguay – before Saudi Arabia hosts in 2034, a North American bid for 2038 is permitted under Fifa’s confederation rotation policy, along with one from Oceania.

Soccer Australia had wanted to bid for 2034, but after being given less than a month to formally register its interest by Fifa, withdrew its candidacy leaving Saudi Arabia to be selected unopposed, Infantino’s preferred method.

To complicate matters slightly, the North American confederation, Concacaf, is understood to have reservations about another US bid as it wants to give opportunities to other members.

Costa Rica, Jamaica and Mexico have been added to the 2031 Women’s World Cup bid and another joint endeavour could emerge, although unsurprisingly Trump would prefer the US to be sole hosts. “Based on the numbers we will be requesting it again immediately,” he told Fox.

Fifa’s timeline for opening the 2038 process is not yet known, but history suggests it could move quickly to secure the outcome it wants. The sudden opening of the 2034 bidding process in October 2024 took most confederations by surprise with Infantino announcing that Saudi Arabia would be the hosts just 25 days later, a decision ratified by all Fifa members at a bizarre virtual extraordinary general meeting two months later.

Infantino will be re-elected for a fourth full term at next year’s Fifa Congress in Morocco, almost certainly unopposed, and then all eyes will turn to the 2038 contest.

Barring what would be an unprecedented change to the US constitution to permit an additional term, Trump is due to leave office in January 2029, which may quickly become the deadline for Fifa.

Sports.title: Liverpool owner in talks to sell stake to QPR co-owner Amit Bhatia
Sports.content:
Liverpool’s owner is in talks over selling a significant minority stake to a consortium led by the Queens Park Rangers co-owner Amit Bhatia and backed by his father-in-law Lakshmi Mittal, the billionaire Indian steel magnate.

Fenway Sports Group confirmed in a statement to the Financial Times that it had begun negotiations with a group led by Bhatia over a potential share sale that would value Liverpool at about £4.5bn.

“An investment consortium led and managed by Amit Bhatia has expressed interest in making a strategic minority investment in Liverpool Football Club,” the statement said.

FSG paid £300m to take control of Liverpool in 2010 and is poised to secure a spectacular return on its investment. The Boston-based investment group led by John W Henry, who also own the Boston Red Sox and Pittsburgh Penguins, has previously held discussions over a minority sale without reaching agreement, but with the Mittal family managing assets of £16bn there is no doubt the buyers have the resources to execute the transaction.

Industry sources expressed surprise at the purported £4.5bn valuation, which is far higher than recent sales of similar sized Premier League clubs.

Chelsea were bought four years ago by the Todd Boehly/Clearlake Capital group for £2.5bn, although that was a distressed sale because the owner Roman Abramovich was subject to UK government sanctions, and Sir Jim Ratcliffe’s purchase of 25% of Manchester United in 2024 valued the club at £3.9bn.

In an indication of the seriousness of the consortium’s bid for Liverpool Bhatia resigned as a director of QPR on Tuesday after 19 years. The London-born entrepreneur has held numerous leadership roles at QPR since investing in the club in 2007. He said: “QPR has been a deeply important part of my life, and of my family’s life … I step back from my formal responsibilities with pride, gratitude and affection.”

Liverpool are in the US under their new head coach, Andoni Iraola, for a pre-season tour which begins with a game against Sunderland in Nashville on Saturday.

Sports.title: Manchester United supporters groups in uproar over suspension of season tickets
Sports.content:
Manchester United’s official Fans’ Forum, Manchester United Supporters Trust (Must), The 1958 and five other such groups have complained to the club over supporters being “treated as suspects” after some had season tickets suspended as part of a move to stop the illegal reselling of seats.

United last week contacted fans who used six or more devices to access accounts linked to the club or to forward tickets as in their view this suggested the potential buying of seats to resell. Members are only allowed to forward tickets to other members, or sell them back to United.

Those contacted were asked why multiple accounts were accessed, to identify the differing devices they used, and for photo ID to prove their validity. “Following a detailed review of activity across our ticketing and digital platforms, we have identified sustained activity associated with your account, or with accounts that appear to be connected to or controlled by you, which may indicate a breach of the club’s ticketing terms and conditions,” the email from United said.

Fans had their accounts suspended, leading to season tickets being frozen, and were given only three days to appeal, despite United’s terms and conditions stating 14 days as a usual timeframe.

“Professional touting, automated purchasing and those who exploit supporters for financial gain have no place at Manchester United and deserve robust action,” read a joint statement from supporter groups.

“However, that action must be fair, proportionate and transparent. Long-standing supporters who have followed Manchester United for decades, often across multiple generations of the same family, should never feel they are being treated as suspects without clear evidence, due process or a meaningful opportunity to respond to the allegations made against them. The current approach has created a growing perception among supporters of ‘ban first and ask questions later’.

“The Fans’ Forum has rightly called on the club to pause the issuing of further suspensions and to halt any cancellation of Season Tickets while meaningful discussions take place. We support this.”

Reasons given by fans for the use of multiple devices to access club accounts includes being able to act for a group of friends or for elderly family members who struggle to use technology. United’s position is understood to be that no bans or formal sanctions have been applied and that any season tickets that have been revoked will be reissued before the team’s first home game of the season, which is against Ipswich Town on 30 August.

United have applied restrictions to accounts and offered only three days to appeal once a verdict is reached, it is understood, as the club is certain some of these are being used for illegal resale and the normal 14 days would be used to sell tickets on.

Sports.title: ‘The scrutiny is constant’: referee Anthony Taylor retires from football
Sports.content:
Anthony Taylor has announced his retirement from elite refereeing after a distinguished career spanning more than two decades and 831 matches.

One of England’s most accomplished officials, the 47-year-old officiated 668 matches in the professional game in England. He brings the curtain down on his career following his final appointment – the World Cup last-16 game between Portugal and Spain in the US.

Reflecting on his career, Taylor said: “Officiating at the elite level has been an immense privilege, but the pressure is intense and the scrutiny is constant. The time is now right to step aside and look forward to transitioning to the next chapter of my career.

“I want to express my deepest gratitude to my two assistants Gary and Adam, my refereeing colleagues and everyone connected with the game for all their support over the years. Most importantly, I want to thank my family and friends for their unwavering support throughout the immense sacrifices this career has demanded.”

Over 16 Premier League seasons, Taylor took charge of 432 top-flight matches and officiated every major domestic cup final. His honours include the FA Cup finals in 2017 and 2020, the 2015 League Cup final, the 2015 Community Shield and the 2018 Championship playoff final.

Taylor also enjoyed an outstanding international career, spending 14 years on the Fifa international list. During that time, he officiated at two World Cups (2022 and 2026), two European Championships (2020 and 2024) and two Club World Cups (2022 and 2025).

Quick Guide How do I 

Across the 163 international matches of which he took charge Taylor was entrusted with some of world football’s biggest fixtures, including the 2020 Uefa Super Cup, the 2021 Nations League final, the 2022 Club World Cup final, the 2023 Europa League final and the 2024 Champions League semi-final.

Howard Webb, chief refereeing officer at Pro Ref, said: “Anthony has been a fantastic servant to the game over many years, both domestically and on the international stage. He has been repeatedly trusted to officiate in the biggest games including Portugal against Spain in this summer’s World Cup which ultimately capped off an outstanding career.

“He’s consistently demonstrated over a sustained period why he is one of the best and most successful officials that English football has ever produced, but it’s not just his on-field achievements that see him as a role model to many. The professionalism he’s shown and the support for his colleagues and the next generation of officials looking to follow in his footsteps is testament to his character.

“We thank him for his immense contribution to the game and wish him every success in the next chapter of his career.”

Sports.title: ‘The utmost respect for him’: Alex Ferguson pays tribute to Kevin Keegan
Sports.content:
Sir Alex Ferguson has saluted Kevin Keegan for building Newcastle’s “greatest team”. Keegan, who had cancer, died on Monday at the age of 75 and Ferguson has joined the tributes for one of football’s most endearing characters.

Ferguson and Keegan were involved a fierce battle for Premier League supremacy, with Ferguson’s Manchester United pipping Newcastle to the title in 1996. “I had the utmost respect for him,” Ferguson told Track Radio. “We had many duels when he was manager of Newcastle, but the job he did at Newcastle was fantastic. He re-energised that club and he brought that enthusiasm and fanaticism great supporters can give.

“And he also brought three great players to the club – [David] Ginola, [Faustino] Asprilla, Philippe Albert – and added a bit of class to the team. The challenges we had with Newcastle at that time were huge.”

Keegan, frustrated by Ferguson’s comments in the media towards the end of the tense title fight, memorably ranted at the Scot in a television interview. Despite that, Ferguson remained friendly with the former Liverpool and England striker and admired Keegan’s impressive rebuilding job at Newcastle.

The club were in danger of relegation to the third tier when Keegan took over, but he saved them from that fate and then won promotion to the Premier League in 1993. Keegan made Newcastle so dynamic they were referred to as “the entertainers”.

Ferguson believes the title runners-up were the best team in the club’s history. “Kevin carried the love of the game on his sleeve, there’s no question about that, and that carried right on to the fans, to the players,” he said. “That period at Newcastle was of emotion, it was excitement. They brought these great players to the club and they added to it, and it gave Newcastle – I think – their best ever team.”

View image in fullscreen Tributes at St James’ Park for Kevin Keegan, who died on Monday. Photograph: Owen Humphreys/PA

Ferguson said he and Keegan had bumped into each other at a pub near Wentworth golf club a few weeks after that season. They spent the night around a piano with all thoughts of the rivalry forgotten. “The great thing about him, he held no grudges,” Ferguson said. “That was a fantastic quality he had and we had a great night.

“All aside whatever happened in previous weeks, that was soon forgotten. I really respected him for that.”

Sports.title: Spurs break their women’s transfer record to sign Alice Sombath from Lyonnes
Sports.content:
Tottenham have signed the France defender Alice Sombath from Lyonnes for a club record fee. The price paid for the 22-year-old has not been disclosed but the previous club record, paid for Signe Gaupset in January, was reportedly more than £375,000.

“The league is very competitive, every game is a tough game and that’s what I’m most excited about,” said Sombath. “I saw that Spurs had a very good season last year. My qualities can bring something to the team, even though I know they already have a lot.”

Sombath spent six years at Lyonnes, the eight-time European champions, joining the club after she was signed from Paris Saint-Germain in 2020.

She won the Champions League in her second season, featuring twice and being on the bench in the final, and won five league titles and two Coupe de France titles.

Tottenham’s head coach, Martin Ho, said the defender “fits the profile of what we’re building”. She has already shown real maturity in her performances and we believe she has all the qualities to continue developing into a top player within our environment.

“Alice is an aggressive defender who is comfortable in possession, competitive in her duels and has the ambition to keep improving every day. Those characteristics are really important to us and we’re excited to help her take the next step in her career while strengthening the squad.”

Sombath is Spurs’s sixth signing of the summer, after Shekiera Martinez, Kirsty Hanson, Victoria Pelova, Caitlin Dijkstra and Selma Panengstuen.

The club are delighted to have got these deals done early, allowing for a full pre-season, and that Sombath’s recruitment means they have secured the services of their six priority targets.

Tottenham finished fifth in the WSL last season after a disappointing 11th the preceding season. They were four points behind fourth-placed Manchester United, but 19 behind the league winners, Manchester City.

Sports.title: Football Daily | Here are 48 reasons to cherish the World Cup (minus the Geopolitics)
Sports.content:
MISTY, WATER-COLOURED MEMORIES

The Geopolitics World Cup is already fading from view, replaced by a thin July gruel of pre-season friendlies and transfer tales. But there’s still time to cast another look back over the 48-team, 104-game, 308-goal leviathan that has dominated the last six weeks of our lives. Without further ado, here are 48 reasons to cherish this year’s World Cup (minus the Geopolitics).

The very first game between Mexico and South Africa saw three red cards dished out, ITV showing off their studio’s Manhattan backdrop, and a duck anointed as a national hero. Germany looked ominous, putting seven past Curaçao, whose solitary goal sent Telemundo commentators wild. Vozinha and Cape Verde had us wondering about Spain, and the giant keeper’s heroics helped his mum get over to watch him play.

View image in fullscreen One more Vozinha pic for the road. Photograph: Daniel Zuchnik/Getty Images for Fanatics

Another classy veteran, Lionel Messi, banged in six group-stage goals, (briefly) becoming the World Cup’s all-time top scorer. Cristiano Ronaldo was bad, then (briefly) “back”, and then gone again. Scotland fans left a far greater impression on the tournament than their team, making Boston their spiritual home. England put away Croatia with a dazzling display of attacking intent that was not to be repeated, while Anthony Barry expertly channeled a frustrated lower-league manager in his half-time interviews.

It’s probably time for a hydration break, but Mauricio Pochettino just kicked over the Powerade. Poch did a great turn as a middle-aged actor playing a World Cup coach, and the US (briefly) looked like a really good team, before being derailed by something or other, we forget. Fellow co-hosts Canada earned their first-ever World Cup win in style, smashing six past Sunday League’s Qatar, who earned two red cards. Also sent off: discretion’s Miguel Almirón, for covering his mouth while talking – not that it helped Turkey, who crashed out after two games despite taking 1,057 shots on goal.

View image in fullscreen Miguel Almirón makes sure to let the ref see his lips. Photograph: Darren Yamashita/Imagn Images/Reuters

Group E saw Japan being tidy on and off the field, an inconsistent Sweden winning and losing 5-1, and Herve Rénard showing up for some reason. Ecuador’s “touchline dreamboat” Sebastián Beccacece turned heads, while Marcelo Bielsa could only shake his dome sorrowfully as Uruguay fell apart in real time. Riyad Mahrez confused everyone by putting Algeria 3-2 up against Austria, who immediately equalised and doubled the torment for Iran, already denied a dramatic winner against Egypt by VAR.

Time for another hydro-break, brought to you by the sweet elixir of goals. Cape Verde’s Sidny Lopes Cabral delivered the goal and celebration of the tournament against Argentina, who brought extra-time magic of their own thanks to Julián Alvarez. Haiti’s Wilson Isidor and Uzbekistan striker Eldor Shomurodov joined the pantheon of great forgotten World Cup goals, while Egypt’s brilliant breakaway against Argentina was cruelly disallowed. Their manager, combustible hardman Hossam Hassan, responded accordingly.

View image in fullscreen Strike! Photograph: Marco Bello/Reuters

The knockouts brought a sharper edge, with Germany bundled out by ‘housery’s Paraguay and the Dutch denied by a Morocco team who lived up to their billing. Portugal v Croatia was absolute psychodrama, and Belgium looked more likely to fight among themselves than find a way back against Senegal. The Battle of the Azteca was a belter. England players threw their heads at everything, Javier Aguirre delivered the GWC’s best touchline moment, and Harry Kane lost his voice. Brazil’s fragile, vibes-based journey was shattered by Erling Haaland’s merciless precision as Norway rowed on in (almost) perfect unison, with Haaland dominating defences and Social Media Disgraces alike. Neymar, meanwhile, won the Mark Corrigan award for winning in the most minor way possible.

On to the quarter-finals, where Kylian Mbappé dictated the play as France (briefly) looked unstoppable, and Spain conceded a goal (Charles De Ketelaere becoming an eternal pub quiz answer). Breel Embolo’s needless dive was exposed in 4K, England got a little help from on high against Norway, Gabriel Clarke stirred the pot, and Danny Murphy continued the sobering tale of Bob the Cat. The semis can be summed up in two key moments – Lamine Yamal turning Lucas Digne’s brain inside-out, and seven defenders failing to close down Enzo Fernández. Oh, England!

View image in fullscreen Lucas Digne having his blood twisted. Photograph: Franck Fife/AFP/Getty Images

The game of the tournament came in the third-place playoff, a ridiculous knockabout affair won 6-4 by England, with Mbappé stat-padding his way to the Golden Boot. The final was not nearly as much fun, with Wayne Rooney neatly summarising the chaotic half-time show, and Fernández’s bone-headed second yellow card summing up Argentina’s reductive efforts. There’s no bigger moment than the one that wins it all, though, so take a bow, Ferran Torres.

Finally, after a tournament of tedious celebrity-spotting, it was nice to see Javier Bardem and Carlos Alcaraz genuinely celebrating Spain’s success, before Keyne Yamal made the pitch his playground. Ominously, Luis de la Fuente’s red-and-gold army are co-hosts next time, when we may have to rattle off 64 memorable moments. We’ll get to work on that, you can start making your predictions and we’ll do it all again in 2030.

KEVIN KEEGAN (1951-2026)

Tributes have poured in over the last 24 hours to Kevin Keegan after his death at the age of 75. His playing career was remarkable – he remains (and will surely remain for a long time) the only British player to be twice named European Footballer of the Year, he won the title three times with Liverpool (and the European Cup), the Bundesliga with Hamburg and was an England stalwart for a decade. But through TV appearances, adverts, even a top 40 hit, his impact as one of football’s early celebrity breakout stars can’t be measured by medals alone. And that’s before we get to his wild managerial career, remembered mostly – for good or ill – by his blow-up at Alex Ferguson in 1996. “Kevin carried the love of the game on his sleeve, there’s no question about that, and that carried right on to the fans, to the players,” said Ferguson on Tuesday. “That period at Newcastle was of emotion, it was excitement. They brought these great players to the club too and they added to it, and it gave Newcastle – I think – their best ever team.” Amid a deluge of other tributes, Alan Shearer perhaps summed up his feelings most succinctly: “My hero. My manager. My friend. Sleep easy Boss.”

For more on Keegan’s remarkable career as a player and manager, here’s Rob Draper’s wonderful tribute, Richard Williams’s obituary, Louise Taylor on his three eras at Newcastle and his life in pictures.

View image in fullscreen Kevin Keegan runs out at Anfield in August 1971 after signing for Liverpool. Photograph: Liverpool FC/Getty Images

QUOTE OF THE DAY

“As time goes by, you realise there is something much bigger than just a result. For years, this group has represented the team in the best possible way. It teaches that competing isn’t just about winning; it’s about giving your all for the jersey and never giving up. It has been a privilege to be part of a group that always stepped up, competed at the highest level, and defended these colours with pride, humility, and commitment” – despite their showing in the GWC final, Enzo Fernández hypes up Argentina’s performance without fully grasping the meaning of the words “pride” and “humility” as they return home.

View image in fullscreen Photograph: Juan Ignacio Roncoroni/EPA

RECOMMENDED FOLLOWING

Big Website: on BlueSpace, TikBook, Instachat, you name it.

double quotation mark President Trump confused (yesterday’s Football Daily)? Maybe that was down to someone telling him that Spain, who he has relentlessly criticised for not spending enough on defence, actually had the best one of all the GWC participants” – John Myles.

double quotation mark Despite your rather mixed review (yesterday’s Football Daily), I actually thought the GWC was quite good. My main focus was the Golden Boot race. Forget match quality or results. With so many elite scorers doing loads of goals it was quite intriguing to see who would come out on top. And for a wee while one of my countrymen, Elijah Just, had the impertinence to be in the mix with his three goals for New Zealand. Exciting” – Rod de Lisle.

double quotation mark So the third-place game was 90 minutes of pointless action and the final was a shot-for-shot remake of the 2010 version? How fittingly American” – Rowan Sweeney.

If you have any, please send letters to the.boss@theguardian.com. Today’s prizeless letter o’ the day goes to … John Myles. Terms and conditions for our competitions, when we run them, are here.

Sports.title: ‘Reclaim football’: Sepp Blatter joins La Liga chief in call for Gianni Infantino to resign
Sports.content:
The Fifa president, Gianni Infantino, has come in for heavy criticism from his predecessor, Sepp Blatter, and the La Liga president, Javier Tebas, with the pair united in the belief that he should stand down.

As Spain celebrated their World Cup win on Sunday, Tebas accused Infantino of “destroying the football industry” by prioritising the World Cup over national competitions. He claimed “his time is up”. Blatter has called for “fans, players and national associations to reclaim football and bring it back to its roots under new leadership”.

Tebas is particularly opposed to the Fifa president’s enthusiasm for expanding the 2030 tournament to 64 teams from 48. “Increasing the number of national teams makes no sense,” Tebas told Italy’s La Gazzetta dello Sport.

“The football industry is not just the World Cup. Not everything can revolve around the World Cup. It is national competitions that support this sport.

“They [Fifa] are destroying the football industry, which generates tens of thousands of jobs, for an event that lasts 40 days and involves a minority of players. We need fewer national teams and more protection for national football, at all levels. They don’t realise they are making irresponsible decisions.”

Tebas believes Infantino should resign, although he admits he finds it hard to envisage such a scenario. “He has the support of the system, of the federations. There is no opposition candidate, nobody wants to stand just to lose. It is a system rotten at its core.”

Scandal-proof: why Infantino’s Fifa power can’t be touched – video

After 10 years at Fifa’s helm, Infantino is poised to be re‑elected for a fourth term in March, potentially standing unopposed for the third time in a row, but Tebas believed the Swiss was a World Cup win away from being forced out. He argues that had the USA defeated Belgium in their last‑16 game Infantino might been mired in an unrecoverable scandal.

The USA striker Folarin Balogun had a one-match ban suspended by the Fifa disciplinary committee, facilitating his involvement against Belgium. The decision was taken after a phone call made to Infantino by Donald Trump. Infantino said the decision to overturn Balogun’s ban was made independently by its disciplinary committee “based on the applicable regulations and the specific facts”.

Tebas said: “The suspension of the American player’s ban was absolutely serious. They were lucky Belgium eliminated the USA because a case could have arisen that might have cost Infantino his job. Since Belgium won they were able to bury the matter. But these things are just the tip of the iceberg.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Blatter, a controversial figure during his tenure as Fifa president, appears to regard the Balogun case as a tipping point. “The longest World Cup has come to an end with the right champions,” he wrote on X. “But on the way to the final whistle, the tournament lost its credibility. Politics must not be allowed to overshadow the game.”

Tebas feels much the same about hydration breaks and extended half‑time intervals. “Fifa arranges things as it wants, for what it wants, for its own interests, certainly not football,” he said. “So if they need a 27-minute half-time break, they’ll have it.

“Hydration breaks are a lie. We have them in La Liga, but when it’s genuinely hot. The pitches in Dallas, Los Angeles, Atlanta had air conditioning; I had to put a jumper on in the stands. It was a lie, a break for advertising.”

Fifa has been approached for comment.

Sports.title: Premier League rival of Man City could make move for John Stones
Sports.content:
Premier League rival of Man City could make move for John Stones

Chelsea are contemplating a move for free agent John Stones following his Manchester City exit, talkSPORT understands.

The 32-year-old is enjoying some respite after his exploits with England at the World Cup.

3 Stones put himself firmly in the shop window with his performances at the World Cup Credit: Getty

Stones, who started last week’s semi-final defeat to Argentina, is pondering his next move after a trophy-laden decade at the Etihad Stadium.

Chelsea are understood to be interested in bringing the experienced centre-back to Stamford Bridge this summer.

New boss Xabi Alonso has made clear his intention to bolster Chelsea’s defensive options ahead of the new Premier League season.

And the Blues will hope Stones could have a similar impact to former defender Thiago Silva when he arrived at the club in 2020, aged 35 should they formalise their interest in the six-time Premier League winner.

Stones is one of multiple centre-backs Alonso is keeping close tabs on.

The Spaniard is on the lookout for players who can have an immediate impact on the first-team squad.

Chelsea could face competition from Premier League champions Arsenal who themselves have shown an interest in the former Everton and Manchester City defender.

The Gunners could be without first-choice centre-back William Saliba for an extended period after he limped out of France’s World Cup semi-final with Spain with a back injury.

It could see Stones link up once again with Mikel Arteta following their time together at City.

Stones was fundamental for the Three Lions this summer despite being reduced to a bit-part role in his final season under Pep Guardiola.

3 Stones bid farewell to the Etihad at the end of May having being reduced to limited game time in his final season Credit: Getty

3 New Chelsea boss Xabi Alonso is a keen admirer of Stones' qualities Credit: Getty

He was reduced to just 18 appearances across all competitions last season, clocking up just 439 minutes of Premier League action.

Following England’s heroic 3-2 win over Mexico earlier this month, Stones revealed he has been physically ready to play top level matches for some time.

“I’ve been ready to go since earlier in the year,” he said. “I’ve not had the opportunity, which is what it is. I’m frustrated when I don’t play. I want to play."

Meanwhile, Chelsea are continuing talks with Saliba’s international teammate Maxence Lacroix over a move away from Crystal Palace and view that as more of a priority over any potential move for Stones.

Palace chiefs are understood to want around £60million for the Frenchman who replaced Saliba after suffering his injury.

Chelsea’s lavish spending shows no signs of slowing down following the £117million acquisition of Morgan Rogers from Aston Villa and their £45m signing of Marco Palestra from Atalanta.

Sports.title: Morgan Rogers joins Chelsea in record-breaking £117m deal from Aston Villa
Sports.content:
Chelsea have finalised the statement signing of Morgan Rogers from Aston Villa, talkSPORT understands.

The 23-year-old joins the Blues in a £117million deal, making him the most expensive British player in history.



2 Rogers has become the most expensive British player Credit: Getty

Rogers was the leading transfer target at Arsenal, who looked set to sign him ahead of their Premier League title defence.

However, it's Chelsea who have welcomed the England international on a six-year deal, with the option of another 12 months.

The deal was done within 48 hours after talks between Chelsea co-owner Behdad Eghbali and Villa owner Nassef Sawiris with Eghbali playing a significant role in pitching Chelsea to the player.



Meanwhile, Chelsea captain and England right-back Reece James, as well as Rogers' close friend Cole Palmer, were also said to be part of the pitch.

Before providing two assists in seven World Cup appearances this summer, Rogers had an excellent season with Villa.



The attacking midfielder hit 14 goals and 12 assists in 55 outings, and won the Europa League.

His former club Middlesbrough are due to earn 20 per cent of the profit from Villa's sale to Chelsea, which will be in the region of £20m.



Blues building

Rogers joins Marco Palestra as a new signing at Chelsea after the latter joined from Atalanta in a £47m deal.

Geovany Quenda and Emmanuel Emegha have also arrived following their pre-agreed moves from Sporting and Strasbourg respectively.

Chelsea are in ongoing and positive talks with Crystal Palace over a deal for Maxence Lacroix.

2 Rogers has penned his deal in west London Credit: Getty



Palace value the French centre-back, who played at the World Cup this summer, at £55m.

John Stones has also been added to Chelsea's list of targets, with the 32-year-old now a free agent after leaving Manchester City.

Xabi Alonso's side made an approach for Alex Scott and are willing to pay in excess of £60m for him, talkSPORT understands.

However, Bournemouth rebuffed it and made it clear that the 22-year-old, who has rejected a new contract, is not for sale.



Arsenal and Manchester United are also understood to be keen.

Meanwhile, Alejandro Garnacho is expected to leave Chelsea and join Villa on loan in a deal that includes a conditional obligation to buy.

Sports.title: Gianni Infantino and Donald Trump wrote Belgium team talk as Folarin Balogun call angered teammates
Sports.content:
For those who watched Donald Trump lift the Club World Cup trophy with champions Chelsea last summer, it will have come as no surprise to see the never-shy US president in the thick of celebrations with World Cup winners Spain.

As talkSPORT exclusively revealed, Infantino told Trump he had permission to break ceremonial protocol. Trump needed no invitation.

13 Rodri had tried to usher Trump off stage but he instead stood there, seemingly unaware of what to do with himself while Gianni Infantino tried to lead him out of the photo Credit: Getty

He seemed determined to photobomb as Rodri lifted the trophy, even as a sheepish-looking Infantino tried to shepherd him off the podium. Spain chose to edit Trump out of the trophy-lift shot they posted on social media.

Touching the World Cup trophy is normally reserved for winners only, and usually the captain removes it from a plinth as a result. Yet Trump had other ideas. One UEFA insider, speaking anonymously to protect relationships, quipped: “If it was in Gianni’s power to make Trump an honorary World Cup winner he would have done so already.”

Instead, the US president will have to settle for the gift of a limited-edition champions ring, which is valued at over £100,000.

Although Trump took centre-stage at the final, he was conspicuous by his absence during the tournament. Spain’s 1-0 extra-time victory over Argentina was the first game he attended in person due to apparent scheduling conflicts. Yet Trump has always been at the epicentre of the 2026 World Cup, dating back to the draw ceremony in Washington D.C. last December.

It was at the Kennedy Center – briefly renamed after Trump only for a judge to reverse the decision – where Infantino pandered to the world’s most powerful person by presenting him with a trumped-up FIFA Peace Prize. This bizarre move essentially compensated Trump for not winning the 2025 Nobel Peace Prize. White House sources have even told talkSPORT that a request was made to ensure the Peace Prize trophy was bigger than the World Cup one. FIFA declined to comment when approached.

Flash forward to the tournament itself and Trump, along with other senior White House officials, also played a role in relocating Iran from their original training base in Arizona to Tijuana in Mexico. The head of Iran’s football federation, Mehdi Taj, insists FIFA simply accepted his country’s request, but it came against the backdrop of rising tensions due to the ongoing war in Iran, and Trump stating before the tournament it might be better if Amir Ghalenoei’s side didn’t compete at all.

“The Iran national soccer team is welcome to the World Cup, but I really don’t believe it is appropriate that they be there, for their own life and safety,” Trump posted on his Truth Social platform ahead of the tournament.

Then there was the curious case of referee Omar Artan, one of Africa’s most respected officials, who was denied entry to officiate at the tournament despite seemingly having valid paperwork. Andrew Giuliani, the head of the White House task force for the World Cup, told talkSPORT Artan was 'talking to some bad people' but refused to elaborate further.

UEFA then stepped in to offer Artan the Super Cup between Champions League winners Paris Saint-Germain and Europa League champions Aston Villa, which takes place in Salzburg on August 12.

And as if navigating these sensitive and serious issues wasn’t enough, Trump got involved on the football side when he asked Infantino to review US striker Folarin Balogun’s red card against Bosnia-Herzegovina, as exclusively reported on talkSPORT.

13 Infantino has been the butt of jokes at UEFA where they laugh that if it was up to the FIFA boss he'd make Trump an honorary World Cup winner Credit: Getty

13 Balogun was allowed to play against Belgium in the World Cup following Trump's phone call to Infantino that saw his red card suspended Credit: Getty

News of Trump’s phone call to Infantino made front and back pages around the world and set in motion a controversial hearing by FIFA’s disciplinary committee, even though FIFA sources had insisted on July 2 after the USA’s 2-0 victory that there were no grounds for an appeal.

Emirati executive Mohammad Al-Kamali, the chair of FIFA’s disciplinary committee, took the decision to suspend Balogun’s red by a year – given for a foul on new Leeds signing Tarik Muharemovic – making him miraculously eligible to face Belgium in the last 16.

“I was forced to call Gianni and just make a recommendation,” said Trump at a fan event at Trump Tower in New York with Infantino alongside him. “I said ‘Gianni, let the guy in the game!’ No, I didn’t say that [laughter]. I said, ‘Gianni, I’d like to wage a complaint’. And I had no idea what was going to happen.

“But it was so much better the way it worked out because there’s no controversy. They [Belgium] won the game, and our team had all its players… Gianni made yet another of his many good decisions.”

Trump had earlier argued from the Oval Office: “FIFA made the right decision because, number one, it wasn’t a foul. And you want to see a game with your best players. How would you feel if I took [Lionel] Messi out if he ran into somebody? Or we took [Cristiano] Ronaldo out? ‘Ronaldo, you bumped into somebody, so we’re gonna take you out of a game.’ Or Harry Kane? ‘Harry, we’re gonna take you out of the game because you happened to hit somebody a little bit harder [than usual].

“If you would’ve taken him [Balogun] out, I think it really would’ve stained this incredible World Cup. I didn’t tell Gianni what to do. I can’t tell him what to do. And I don’t believe he made the decision.”

13 Trump helped FIFA and Infantino make unwanted headlines when he said he asked for Balogun's red card to be looked into Credit: Getty

FIFA insiders quickly downplayed Trump’s involvement, pointing out his call to Infantino couldn’t have influenced the process because of the independent nature of the disciplinary panel. FIFA sources add it was commonplace throughout the World Cup for Infantino to chat to Trump.

And amongst a growing furore, and ultimately more questions than answers, Infantino clarified his own position.

““FIFA’s judicial bodies are independent,” said the FIFA president. “They operate autonomously, apply the FIFA Disciplinary Code, and decide cases based on the applicable regulations and the specific facts before them. Their independence is essential to the credibility and integrity of football, and this must always be respected.

“Yes, I regularly discuss matters related to the FIFA World Cup with the President of the United States, and on this matter, I did receive a call from President Donald Trump…

“During our conversation, I explained that there was an ongoing legal process involving FIFA’s independent judicial bodies and that the case would be decided in due course by the competent bodies. That is how FIFA’s system works, and it is a principle that I will always uphold.”

And yet Republican senator Ted Cruz painted an entirely different picture when, standing next to a smirking Trump, he credited his boss for suspending Balogun’s punishment.

13 When Romelu Lukaku scored against the USA, he and his Belgium teammates celebrated by mimicking Trump's dad dance as fans around the world were pleased to see USA exit the World Cup after winning so many admirers Credit: Getty

“On behalf of all Americans, thank you for getting rid of that ridiculous red card,” Cruz said. “It was spectacular. There was a reason the FIFA trophy sat here [in the Oval Office] for as long as it did.”

Belgium responded revealing their ‘astonishment’ at the decision and promised to pursue all legal avenues. And it was notable that when Romelu Lukaku scored the fourth goal in their emphatic 4-1 victory over the US in Seattle, several of the team sarcastically celebrated by performing Trump’s trademark dance – swaying from side to side with pumped fists pointing in the air. And Belgium’s social media account captioned the full-time graphic with: "Overturn this."

UEFA also chimed in with a scathing statement arguing the decision to allow Balogun to face Belgium had ‘crossed a red line’. UEFA president Aleksander Ceferin even boycotted the World Cup final over the issue, according to sources familiar with his thinking, and as first revealed by The Times. Senior FIFA sources dispute this, maintaining it was common knowledge Ceferin wouldn’t attend the final before the Balogun fallout, adding he also wasn’t present for the 2023 Women’s World Cup as Spain beat England in Sydney or last summer’s Club World Cup final.

“Sometimes rules are open to interpretation,” UEFA’s statement read. “In this case not. A minimum automatic suspension of one match following a red card is not a discretionary option and does not require the decision of a competent body to be enacted. It is a principle embedded in regulations, which cannot be made subject to exceptions, let alone in the middle of a tournament where several other players have been in the same situation and regularly served their suspension… We express our disbelief at such an unprecedented, incomprehensible and unjustifiable decision.”

FIFA’s disciplinary committee put suspending Balogun’s red card down to ‘discretion’ after invoking Article 27, which gives them the power to ‘fully or partially suspend the implementation of a disciplinary measure… [for] a probationary period of one to four years’. No more specifics were offered up in the vague 13-point 870-word written reasons.

The independence of FIFA’s disciplinary panel is a point of debate given the entire judiciary body is run and funded in-house. Al-Kamali, the sole arbiter for the Balogun hearing, also refused to elaborate on his decision-making process when questioned by BBC Sport ahead of England's quarter-final against Norway in Miami.

Sources have told talkSPORT that Trump made the call to Infantino within 24 hours of Balogun’s sending off and that a coordinated White House team worked with US Soccer to rapidly present a case. This included Giuliani, commerce secretary Howard Lutnick and hedge fund manager Scott Goodwin.

The primary argument made in a memo, put together by US Soccer with help from Trump-affiliated lawyers, was that the excessive use of slow motion and still imagery by VAR significantly misrepresented the incident.

13 Giuliani was grilled in his apperance on talkSPORT by hosts Jim White and Simon Jordan g Credit: talkSPORT

talkSPORT understands Trump was also told by various aides how referee Raphael Claus was accused of issuing irregular cards in 2023 by Botafogo owner John Textor. It prompted him to call Claus ‘a little bit suspect’ despite the fact Brazilian authorities and FIFA found no wrongdoing.

FIFA referees’ chief Pierluigi Collina leapt to Claus’ defence pointing out he is “an experienced and highly respected referee and we maintain full confidence in him as a trusted match official.” However, FIFA buried this statement midway through the Belgium game and declined to comment as to why. talkSPORT was told by two different White House sources that there was no desire for FIFA to undermine Trump.

The facts didn’t stop Giuliani doubling down with further unsubstantiated accusations that Claus’ past could have influenced Balogun’s red.

“The process was improper,” he told talkSPORT. “And when you add the fact that this referee, a few years ago, was akin to a match-fixing investigation for giving out improper red cards. And you add that to the fact that in the 64th minute for a contact foul, VAR should never have been used in slow motion to eject [Balogun]. When you add those two things together, it’s suspicious to say the least.”

With White House officials and US Soccer increasingly confident they could lodge and ultimately win an appeal, talkSPORT can reveal Infantino gave Trump a guarantee he was personally looking into the matter. Infantino had already contacted Emilio García Silvero, FIFA’s chief legal and compliance officer, to discuss options. FIFA sources say it was made clear to Silvero reviewing the Balogun red should be dealt with as a high priority.

And it was soon determined it was legally permissible within FIFA’s rules to open a disciplinary panel. From there, FIFA sources maintain Infantino stepped back to let the process run its course.

Despite repeated requests to FIFA, no explanation beyond ‘discretion’ has been given as to why an appeal was suddenly allowed. And it is unusual, given Giuliani argues VAR failed to follow protocol, and a US soccer memo backs up his position, that FIFA’s disciplinary committee make no mention of this in their published findings. No one within FIFA has confirmed still imagery or slow-motion replays were used incorrectly.

talkSPORT has also learned that some senior figures within US Soccer, who confirm they were ‘engaged in the process’, were initially seeking an expedited hearing at the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS). Yet multiple people familiar with both Infantino and the White House’s thinking argue it would have been embarrassing for all parties for a body outside of FIFA to make the final call, and so close to the game. Legal experts approached by talkSPORT have cast doubt as to whether CAS would have reinstated Balogun for the Belgium game.

Added to the mix were fears that had the US won their last 16 game, Belgium would have also challenged the match result at CAS.

CAS confirmed to talkSPORT they did not receive any formal communication from US Soccer or the RBFA on Balogun’s red card.

You can argue US Soccer were perfectly entitled to feel aggrieved by the sending off. It looked harsh at the time, but the key question remains not whether Balogun’s red was right or wrong, but if there was genuine recourse to appeal it within FIFA’s rules.

13 Through no fault of his own, Balogun had created controversy and went out of his way to clear the air with an unhappy Rudi Garcia, the manager of Belgium Credit: Getty

13 Some USA players - none in the above photo - told talkSPORT that Trump publicly confirming he had spoken to Infantino helped Belgium's team talk Credit: Getty

At face value, Article 27 does suggest carte blanche discretion to suspend red cards, but it is worth noting several other bylaws FIFA contradict this.

Article 9.6 states: “No protests may be made about the referee’s decisions regarding facts connected with play. Such decisions are final and not subject to appeal.”

Article 10.6 adds: “If a player or team official is sent off as a result of a direct or indirect red card [second caution], they will automatically be suspended from their team’s subsequent match.”

And Article 66.4 probably provides the most clarity of all: “A sending off automatically incurs suspension from the subsequent match."

The fact Balogun’s red card still stands – it was suspended not rescinded – coupled with a $40,000 fine suggests Al-Kamali, in ruling, did not think the decision was wrong.

FIFA argues it has been transparent in publishing the reasons, but the lack of specifics has led high-profile figures to question Trump’s involvement and flag broader concerns over Infantino’s relationship with the US president. One of the most vocal is the vice-president of US Soccer, Nathan Goldberg Crenier.

“When it comes to Trump’s meddling in the Balogun case, the biggest casualty was soccer’s integrity,” he told the Guardian in a column written in a personal capacity and not necessarily reflecting the views of US Soccer, who did not respond to a request for comment made on Monday.

“Sure, in a narrow sense, US Soccer benefited from having a star player back from suspension. But in a more meaningful sense, US Soccer was also a victim: our players were swept up in a political firestorm before the most important game of their lives, and our biggest chance to showcase American soccer to the world will now forever be tainted by accusations of favouritism at best and corruption at worst, unfairly clouding US Soccer’s credibility and reputation around the world…

13 Infantino has talked up an increase to 64 teams for future World Cups Credit: Getty

“The fact that Infantino has faced little accountability for dragging soccer through the mud reflects a battle for the soul of the sport – about whether its future will be autocratic and hyper-commercialised, rather than a force for good. I say no: soccer leaders must reject Infantino’s egotistical and transactional view of the beautiful game.”

Even disgraced former FIFA president Sepp Blatter had his say, calling Infantino ‘a dictator’. Infantino had originally stood on a platform to ‘clean up’ FIFA from Blatter, something he dubbed “FIFA 2.0” back in 2016.

It is worth noting there are plenty in the game who sympathise with Balogun – caught in the middle of a political tempest days before the biggest game in USMNT history.

USMNT coach Mauricio Pochettino had earnestly tried to deny any pre-match disruption, but there was significant frustration in the camp amongst both players and staff that Balogun, through no fault of his own, had overshadowed the game.

Multiple USMNT players, preferring to remain anonymous to protect relationships, have told talkSPORT that Trump publicly confirming he had spoken to Infantino on July 6 caused more damage in their view than news of the original call itself. This came just a day before the game and was seen as unhelpful because it essentially aided Belgium’s team talk.

Pochettino had initially prepared for the game without his star striker, while the players only learned through social media that Balogun was eligible on July 5. Crystal Palace defender Chris Richards even told talKSPORT he initially questioned whether the news was fake.

To his credit, an apologetic Balogun, who remained ever professional throughout, went out of his way to clear the air with Belgium coach Rudi Garcia. It followed Garcia revealing before the game that he thought the decision to suspend Balogun’s red card was an April Fool’s joke.

“My initial reaction was that I was happy to be back in the team,” Balogun told CBS after the tournament. “But when I started to reflect, I knew it was going to cause a lot of controversy.

13 Infantino has staged the first ever World Cup final half-time show and is unlikely to be challenged when up for re-election in 2027 Credit: Getty

13 Infantino promised FIFA would be unrecognisable from the corrupt organisation people viewed it as when he took over from disgraced Blatter in 2016 - now many think his position is untenable Credit: Getty

13 Cristiano Ronaldo was handed a three-game ban for a red card in 2025, but two matches were suspended allowing him to feature in the first two World Cup group-stage games Credit: Getty

"And I could almost see within my teammates a bit of nerves because it's something that is so unique… It was difficult – there was a lot of outside noise and that's hard to avoid.”

Those close to Infantino dismiss the idea of political interference and paint the Balogun saga as far more magnified in Europe than outside of it. But it’s hard to overlook what appears to be American favouritism.

After all, Balogun became the first player sent off at a World Cup to avoid an immediate ban since Brazil’s Garrincha, who was allowed to play in the 1962 World Cup final after lobbying from the Brazilian government.

There is more recent precedent, too. FIFA took a similar tact with Cristiano Ronaldo when he was sent off for elbowing Ireland’s Dara O'Shea during Portugal's 2-0 qualifying loss in November last year. The 41-year-old was handed a three-game ban, but two matches were suspended allowing the Portugal star to feature in the first two World Cup group-stage games.

FIFA did not provide written reasons, but talkSPORT understands the fact Ronaldo had not received a red card in his other 225 international appearances was factored in. The decision raised its own accusations of favouritism. At the time Simon Jordan told talkSPORT: “We all know what it is: engineering a situation where they want a very marketable asset to be in the tournament.”

The problem is that suspending any ban, especially without detailed reasons or admitting error, sets a dangerous precedent. And when Jarrel Quansah was sent off against Mexico in England’s 3-2 win at the Azteca on July 6, the Bayer Leverkusen defender got a two-match ban with no appeal. It was Quansah’s first red for his country, albeit after a handful of caps, but also just his second career sending off in 121 domestic games.

talkSPORT understands that FIFA and Infantino now believe the Balogun issue has blown over, but the reality is the fall out, including potential RBFA action, could continue well beyond the World Cup.

As talkSPORT revealed, there are growing calls from within UEFA to find a candidate to rival Infantino at March’s FIFA presidential election in 2027. Germany is currently the most high-profile federation yet to endorse him. Spain and Norway are two other FIFA members believed to be considering their options.

Infantino has the luxury of more than 200 letters backing his re-election from FIFA’s 211 members. This suggests a landslide victory although some, like the English FA, sent their endorsement before the World Cup. There is nothing stopping support being transferred to another candidate between now and the November 18 deadline for someone else to stand.

It would be a seismic shock if Infantino isn’t confirmed as FIFA president again, especially given neither UEFA president Ceferin or European Football Clubs chief and PSG president Nasser Al-Khelaifi has an appetite to go head-to-head against him. Yet it is possible UEFA still put forward a rival, if only to spark genuine debate. Legia Warsaw owner Dariusz Mioduski is one name who has been mooted by some senior federation officials.

13 Infantino is mocked mercilessly by fans and has had calls for him to resign throughout the World Cup but he views this as part of the job Credit: Getty

Ultimately, Infantino knows how to win votes, and Europe only has 55 of the 211 available anyway. Plus, the overriding message from the FIFA president is that the 2026 World Cup has ‘exceeded all expectations’ – something many of his backers agree wholeheartedly with.

The proposed expansion of the World Cup from 48 to 64 teams also plays well in Africa and Asia, where Infantino has already locked down the vote. And Cape Verde’s incredible run, including taking defending champions Argentina to extra time in the last 32, can be used as a powerful example for including even more teams at the tournament.

Infantino can also point to sold out stadiums in America, Canada and Mexico. Figures released by FIFA show the average 2026 World Cup attendance at 65,351 per match, with stadiums 99.7 per cent full. And commercial partners, understandably, are all said to be thrilled by the tournament.

With this in mind, standing next to Trump in New York, Infantino felt confident declaring FIFA the ‘official happiness provider to humanity’ before the US president interjected with, ‘Unless your team loses!’ The pair looked like a double act who finish each other’s sentences, although one prominent UEFA official told talkSPORT it appeared more like, “Trump speaking with his ventriloquist ‘Gianni’”.

"The American dream, Mr. President, came to reality," said Infantino as he lavished praise on Trump. "We united the world. You don't need people to compliment you, Mr. President, but this World Cup would not have been such an incredible success without you.

“This has not just been – and is not just – the greatest World Cup of all time. It is the greatest human, social and cultural event that mankind has ever witnessed.”

Detractors will continue to flag the inflated ticket prices, the lack of jeopardy at the end of the group stage and the fact almost every hydration break – clearly just ad-breaks in disguise – were booed by fans.

Infantino seems unperturbed by criticism. He views it as part of the job and, like Trump, can always term it ‘fake news’. It means Infantino likely won’t worry about those who accuse him of running FIFA like a head of state or even lose sleep if a rival does materialise at the next election.

His White House relationship will again pay dividends when America co-hosts the 2031 Women’s World Cup alongside Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica, and there could yet be a further Club World Cup, or even another men’s World Cup on US soil. Trump even joked Infantino should ditch Canada and Mexico and co-host the next World Cup with China.

Of course, a crazy idea like this won’t happen – but it begs the question from critics if Infantino is willing to stand up to Trump or other world leaders. There is a broader debate to be had as to whether being a successful FIFA president actually requires a politician, which no-doubt Infantino would argue, or if FIFA under him has instead simply invited political interference that now muddies decision-making.

And in light of Balogun’s suspended ban, the irony is not lost on many UEFA insiders that it was Infantino, back in 2019, who visited the White House and handed Trump a red card of his own to brandish at will. Seven years on, and it’s hard for Infantino to escape accusations that Trump held all the cards at this World Cup.

Sports.title: Hull City owner promises four new signings this week as he reveals Premier League transfer strategy
Sports.content:
Hull City owner promises four new signings this week as he reveals Premier League transfer strategy

Hull City are set to ramp up their pursuit of new signings as they prepare for life back in the Premier League.

The Tigers were victorious in the Championship play-off final in May to secure a place in the top flight for the first time since 2017.



4 Hull City edged past Middlesbrough 1-0 to secure promotion to the Premier League Credit: Getty

The 2026/27 Premier League fixtures released last month did little to curb the excitement with Manchester United up first for Sergej Jakirovic’s side at the MKM Stadium on Saturday, August 22 – live on talkSPORT.

Hull know they have a huge task on their hands in maintaining their Premier League status, however, owner Acun Ilicali is confident his club can ruffle the feathers of the big boys next season.

With six weeks remaining of the summer transfer window, Hull have only managed to bring in goalkeeper Jack Butland from Rangers.



But fear not Hull supporters, it appears that a summer transfer splurge is on the way.

A busy week ahead

“Think about us like a volcano. It’s boiling right now and it’s going to erupt,” Illicali told talkSPORT.



“At the moment we are preparing a good squad. I’m very, very happy because the targets we have, 80 per cent progress is good.

“We have to make a new team very sensibly I think with ten or 12 players we’re going to bring in. Of course, I cannot pronounce the names!



“I can see that we’re in very good shape. We’re closing deals and three or four new players will come.

“I'm very excited for the Manchester United game.”

One of the names Ilicali is hoping to tie up in the coming days is highly-rated Olympiakos goalkeeper Konstantinos Tzolakis.

4 Ilicali is relishing the visit of Manchester United on the opening weekend Credit: Getty

4 Tzolakis played a key role in Olympiakos' UEFA Conference League triumph in 2024 Credit: Getty



The Greece international is ready to try his hand in the Premier League and Ilicali has kept tabs on the shot-stopper since one particular European performance.

“Yes, we are expecting (to sign for Hull),” Ilicali said.

“He is very talented and an important goalkeeper. He’s very young, 23, and he has the responsibility of a big club like Olympiakos.

“He’s the guy who saved three penalties in the Conference League against Fenerbahce.

“He made us lose our dream of getting the cup but I’m happy that he will probably be together with us.



“I hope in two or three days we can finalise it but in football you never know anything until it’s done.

4 Hull boss Sergej Jakirovic is looking to add a cluster of new faces to his squad this summer Credit: Shutterstock Editorial

Hull's transfer strategy explained

Ilicali knows Hull have the opportunity to add ready-made Premier League stars to their squad this summer.

A year ago, the mixture of young hungry talent and experienced Championship stars including Oli McBurnie helped fire them to the promised land.



But 12 months on, Hull have slightly more pulling power. However, Ilicali believes the correct balance will help Hull reach their season objectives.

“You cannot go one way and have all ex-Premier League players or no Premier League players and just new names,” he explained.

“I will bring four or five experienced Premier League players this week.

“Our advantage is that the players can’t play for Manchester United and Chelsea but they are very, very good.



“They can play at Manchester United in the future so what I tell them is instead of waiting, come here (Hull). This is the best club in the world, for me.

“Then if you prove yourself at the top level you will go to Manchester United.

“There’s so many big talents in Europe now and this time we are waiting for the best ones.”

Sports.title: How new-look Aston Villa could line up for 2026/27 season after £170million exits
Sports.content:
How new-look Aston Villa could line up for 2026/27 season after £170million exits

Unai Emery has worked miracles since he arrived at Aston Villa, but a looming squad rebuild could be his toughest challenge yet.

The Villans knew a number of major sales would be required this summer to avoid falling foul of UEFA's financial restrictions.



9 Rogers' exit has brought clear skies to Villa's financial picture Credit: Getty

Those gloomy skies now appear to have mostly parted following the £117million departure of Morgan Rogers to Chelsea, which will make him the most expensive British player of all-time.

Given Rogers was signed for an initial £8m from Middlesbrough in January 2024, the England international represents arguably Villa's greatest bit of business in history.

Rogers isn't the only big name to wave farewell to Villa Park this summer, with midfield ace Youri Tielemans joining Manchester United for £35m while Lucas Digne is bound for European champions Paris Saint-Germain for £8m.



The £9m sale of Lewis Dobbin to Southampton has also helped Villa's financial picture.

In total, the four departures will generate nearly £170m in funds.

More exits could yet follow, with Hull City in talks to sign winger Leon Bailey.



Given the swathe of departures coupled with Jadon Sancho, Douglas Luiz and Harvey Elliott all returning to their parent clubs after their respective loan spells ended, it leaves Villa and Emery needing some fresh faces through the door.

There's also the added complication of Amadou Onana sustaining an ACL injury during Belgium's round of 16 win over the United States at the World Cup, which means he is not expected to return until 2027.



So, how will Emery's Villa line up for the new season?

Here, talkSPORT.com predicts who the Spaniard will lean on the most as they look to juggle a Premier League and Champions League campaign once more.

9 Onana's injury leaves Villa light in midfield Credit: Getty

Goalkeeper

There isn't any question over who is Villa's first choice between the sticks.

Emiliano Martinez has been Villa's undisputed No. 1 and will be just that once again, even if Juventus tried to prise him away from Villa Park.



The Italian giants made their interest well known but a move was shot down by Villa's director of football operations Damian Vidagany, who told 365 Scores: "The goalkeeper's future is settled, he is staying with us, and we have no intention of letting him go this summer."

Defenders

Villa's defence has largely remained the same throughout Emery's tenure.

Matty Cash is Villa's first choice right-back, although he may soon have competition for the spot from Emerson Royal.

The former Spurs defender is of interest to Villa, although the club is struggling to agree a fee with Flamengo.



9 Cash has made nearly 230 appearances for Villa since he joined in 2020 Credit: Getty

Pau Torres and Ezri Konsa's partnership in central defence doesn't look like being broken in the immediate future, although the Spaniard has revealed he plans to leave at the end of his contract in two years' time and return to boyhood club Villarreal.

The main intrigue here is at left-back, which was predominantly occupied by Digne.

Ian Maatsen is the logical replacement given he is already on Villa's books and started 25 games across all competitions last term compared to Digne's 31 starts.



Villa look set to replenish their left-back stocks with former Brighton defender Pervis Estupinan, but he appears unlikely, at least for now, to slot right in to the starting line-up.

Midfield

Tielemans' departure has left a gaping hole in the heart of Villa's midfield, which has since been exacerbated by Onana's ACL injury.

Luckily for Villa, Boubacar Kamara has returned from a torn PCL, which he sustained in January.

9 Kamara has endured ACL and PCL injuries since he joined Villa Credit: Getty



When fit, Kamara is one of the first names on the team sheet and that doesn't look like changing any time soon.

A defensive midfielder by trade, the fact Kamara has taken the No. 8 shirt vacated by Tielemans could be a clue the Frenchman is set to enjoy more of a ball-playing role.

The real intrigue is who will line up next to Kamara in the middle.

Joao Gomes, a recent £35m acquisition from Wolves, is the likely choice.

The Brazilian is an all-action midfielder, although his specialty lies with his defensive work.



Last season for Wolves, Gomes won 226 duels, the second-most among Premier League midfielders, with only Elliot Anderson boasting more.

9 Gomes was linked with a move to Atletico Madrid, but Villa ultimately won the race for his signature Credit: Getty

Gomes also made the third-most tackles (107), behind James Garner (120) and Joao Palhinha (110), who Villa are hoping to sign on loan.

With Kamara's potential new role in mind, Gomes could act as Emery's midfield pitbull.



Although the central midfield places might not be up for grabs, there's question marks over who will be stationed on the left.

Emiliano Buendia was Emery's main man for the position last season and produced arguably the best form of his career, culminating with a sensational goal in the Europa League final.

However, at age 29 and not exactly blessed with blistering pace, Buendia is not the long-term answer for Villa in the position.

Villa were interested in West Ham's Crysencio Summerville as well as Paris Saint-Germain youngster Ibrahim Mbaye.



9 Villa were credited with an interest in Summerville Credit: Getty

Although it looks like Alejandro Garnacho is the winger who will come through the door, as Villa have agreed a loan deal with an obligation to buy the Chelsea forward.

Summerville, meanwhile, looks set to join Al Hilal after the Saudi club gazumped Roma, with Villa no longer in the picture.

However, Mbaye is only 18 and has been tipped to become a serious star, meaning Villa may need to make a move for him now or else risk missing out for good.



Keeping in mind that this exercise is only a prediction, Garnacho appears to tick the most boxes, especially when it comes to the finances involved and adding some much-needed pace into the line-up, a quality Emery craves.

With Garnacho's mooted arrival, that leaves Villa skipper John McGinn free to retain his spot on the right side of midfield.

9 McGinn is the heart and soul of Villa, having been at the club since 2018 Credit: Getty

As for the attacking midfield position, club record signing Johan Manzambi slots in as Morgan Rogers' replacement.



Following a standout season with Freiburg, Manzambi continued the momentum with a breakout World Cup for Switzerland.

At 20, Manzambi is capable of playing all types of central midfield roles and was even used as a second striker for Freiburg on multiple occasions.

Striker

Ollie Watkins is Villa's main man up front and that does not look like changing just yet.

The 30-year-old has netted double figures for Villa in every Premier League season since he joined.



In fact, Watkins has scored 15 or more goals in the last four league campaigns.

9 Watkins is just nine goals shy of joining the Premier League's 100 club Credit: Getty

Yet Watkins could find himself with additional competition as Villa were also offered Chelsea striker Nicolas Jackson, who is valued at £65m.

Emery previously worked with Jackson at Villarreal and remains an admirer of the forward, who spent last season on loan at Bayern Munich.



With Watkins' contract running through to June 2028, Villa may be tempted to begin a succession plan sooner than later.

Sports.title: New World Cup format would be scrapped immediately under fresh 2030 proposals
Sports.content:
New World Cup format would be scrapped immediately under fresh 2030 proposals

World Cup fever spread like wildfire this summer as the largest-ever edition of the tournament brought drama in abundance.

After debutants Cape Verde stunned to reach the knockouts, Donald Trump intervened in a red card suspension and England failed to get over the line yet again, Spain claimed the international crown.

4 Spain won the first 48-team World Cup this summer Credit: Getty

For the first time in its history, the World Cup involved 48 competing nations as part of an expansion from the usual 32-team format.

However, as things stand, the 2030 World Cup is set to bring a second consecutive increase in participants as 64 countries prepare to join in the competition's centenary celebrations.

Alejandro Dominguez, the president of the South American football governing body CONMEBOL, has all but confirmed a record number of teams will qualify.

The increase would divide opinion among football fans, from casuals to enthusiasts, but FIFA president Gianni Infantino has already hinted at its outcome in a bid to organise a tournament 'for the whole world'.

We have another 1,418 days to go until the 2030 World Cup begins, but it's worth looking at the logistics and potential optics of what will be the grandest display of world football.

When is the 2030 World Cup?

According to information posted by FIFA in March, the World Cup will kick off on Saturday, June 8.

Across this day and the next, a centenary celebration ceremony is set to take place alongside the opening home matches for all of Uruguay, Argentina and Paraguay as part of the 100-year festivities.

Uruguay beat Argentina 4-2 in the inaugural World Cup in 1930, and the CONMEBOL headquarters are based in Luque, Paraguay.

These matches will come before the official opening ceremony and matches, which is when Morocco, Portugal and Spain take on their host duties.

Sunday, July 21 is the scheduled day for the final but with a little over four years until the World Cup starts, these dates could change.

4 Estadio Centenario looks set to host the opening match in 2030 Credit: Getty

How would the 2030 World Cup groups work?

The 2026 edition included a round of 32 for the first time following an expansion of competing nations, with the top two in each of the 12 groups advancing into the knockout stages.

Another eight teams were able to qualify as the best-ranked third place sides.

But this format would be scrapped immediately under the new proposals.

There will likely be 16 groups of four teams in 2030, meaning there is no need for any best-ranked teams who finish in third.

Only the top two teams in each group would reach the knockout stages as they will amount to 32.

Any more would not work for a knockout format - and it is likely goal difference would have to be reintroduced as a tie-breaker (over head-to-head) to avoid a large number of dead rubber matches in gameweek three.

4 Infantino has talked up an increase to 64 teams for 2030 Credit: Getty

Who will qualify for the 2030 World Cup?

Morocco, Portugal and Spain have already qualified as co-hosts, and Uruguay, Argentina and Paraguay are also in as centenary match co-hosts.

That means 58 nations will have to go through the usual qualification process via the six confederations.

AFC (Asia), CAF (Africa), CONCACAF (North, Central America and the Caribbean), CONMEBOL (South America), OFC (Oceania) and UEFA (Europe) teams will compete for these spots.

UEFA had the largest allocation of the 48 teams this summer with 16, which is a third in total, and they would likely earn another four to five teams at a 64-nation tournament.

It means Wales, Republic of Ireland and Northern Ireland, who missed out for 2026, would have better chances of qualifying.

How many players will be at the 2030 World Cup?

Each nation named 26-man squads this summer, so there were 1,248 available players.

4 Morocco, Portugal and Spain are the host nations for the centenary edition Credit: Getty

However, with 64 teams, this would increase to a whopping 1,664 - barring any changes to squad sizes.

Add coaching staff, officials and fans to this number, and there could be some logistical issues to overcome beforehand.

Teams will be allocated training bases across the host nations, which is where they will call home for the duration of the tournament.

Hotels and other accommodation will also need to be organised to deal with the sheer number of personnel travelling from across the world.

Where will the 2030 World Cup matches be played?

The Uruguay, Argentina and Paraguay capitals Montevideo, Buenos Aires and Asuncion are hosting the centenary matches.

There will then be 17 different host cities across Morocco, Portugal and Spain, with six, two and nine allocated to each respectively.

2030 World Cup stadiums and capacities Uruguay: Estadio Centenario, Montevideo - 63,000 (projected) Argentina: Estadio Monumental, Buenos Aires - 100,000 (after expansion) Paraguay: Estadio Osvaldo Dominguez Dibb, Asuncion - 46,000 (projected) Morocco: Adrar Stadium, Agadir - 46,000 (projected)

Hassan II Stadium, Casablanca - 115,000 (after construction)

Fez Stadium, Fez - 55,800 (after expansion)

Marrakesh Stadium, Marrakesh - 45,860 (projected)

Prince Moulay Abdellah Stadium, Rabat - 69,500 (after construction)

Ibn Battouta Stadium, Tangier - 92,000 (planned) Portugal: Estadio da Luz, Lisbon - 68,100

Estadio Jose Alvalade, Lisbon - 52,095

Estadio do Dragao, Porto - 50,033 Spain: Camp Nou, Barcelona - 105,000 (after expansion)

RCDE Stadium, Barcelona - 40,500

Estadio de San Mames, Bilbao - 53,331

Estadio de Gran Canaria, Las Palmas - 44,500 (after expansion)

Bernabeu, Madrid - 83,186

Estadio Metropolitano, Madrid - 70,692

Estadio de Anoeta, San Sebastian - 42,300

Estadio de La Cartuja, Seville - 70,000

Nou Mestalla, Valencia - 70,044

Estadio de Balaidos, Vigo - 44,000 (projected)

Estadio Nueva Romareda - 43,110

Hassan II Stadium is set to be the largest stadium in terms of capacity with 115,000 once its construction near Casablanca is completed, which is expected to be in late 2028.

Barcelona's iconic home at Camp Nou will boast 105,000 once its expansion is fully complete next year, and Real Madrid's Bernabeu will accommodate 83,186.
