In late February, Infantino expressed his support for Mexico continuing as a co-host of the World Cup, despite the outbreak of violence on Feb. 22 after Jalisco New Generation Cartel leader Nemesio “El Mencho” Oseguera was fatally shot in an army operation in Jalisco.

None of the 13 matches played in Mexico was disrupted by security concerns, leading Martínez-Celis to say that “we can say that Mexico was indeed ready to host” the World Cup.

“The best indicator for us is that today the world is talking about how well the matches were organized in Mexico,” the FIFA official told EFE in Mexico City.

He also said that Jalisco — where the violence in late February was concentrated — proved itself to be a worthy World Cup host. Four matches were played in Guadalajara, the state capital.

Martínez-Celis said that the federal government’s security cabinet, which was responsible for executing Mexico’s World Cup security plan, did an “excellent job.” Security Minister Omar García Harfuch said last week that Mexico had demonstrated its “capacity to organize global events with professionalism, hospitality and close coordination between the three levels of government.”

“The organization of the tournament strengthened Mexico’s image around the world and confirmed that the institutions of the Mexican state have the capacities needed to plan and carry out large-scale security arrangements in a coordinated and effective way,” he said.

Martínez-Celis said that “the World Cup for Mexico was an issue of national security and an issue of national pride.” He highlighted that the opening ceremony and match of the tournament in Mexico City went off well despite “additional pressure” from things such as transport concerns and protests.

Turning his focus to a World Cup tragedy, Martínez-Celis acknowledged the deaths of four people in Mexico City in a crowd crush during celebrations following Mexico’s June 30 win over Ecuador. He described the deaths as “terrible” and said that FIFA would review and analyze what happened.

Despite that calamity, the FIFA official made it clear that soccer’s international governing body considered the World Cup in Mexico a success. Most Mexican fans — who bonded over an optimistic (but ultimately unfulfilled) dream that El Tri could go all the way in 2026 — would probably agree, although the vast majority of them were unable to afford a ticket to watch a match live.

With reports from EFE

World.title: Feds and Jalisco state are joining forces to tackle water contamination in greater Guadalajara
World.content:
The federal and Jalisco state governments are embarking on a joint effort to clean up the region’s rivers, improve wastewater treatment and fix the water distribution system in a long-awaited effort to end the water pollution crisis affecting millions of residents in the Guadalajara metropolitan area.

With federal technical support, the project will rehabilitate the antiquated Chapala aqueduct in Guadalajara, clean up the Lerma-Santiago river basin, increase enforcement against industrial polluters and increase investment under the National Water Plan.

At President Sheinbaum’s morning press conference Thursday, head of the National Water Commission (Conagua) Efraín Morales confirmed federal collaboration with Jalisco’s government to address the water quality crisis.

“We are doing our part from the Federation to provide technical support so that the project is a real solution to the problems experienced in the city of Guadalajara as well as its metropolitan area,” Morales said.

Morales attributed Jalisco’s water issues to the deterioration of the original Chapala aqueduct, which has long lacked adequate maintenance.

The Chapala-Guadalajara aqueduct carries water from Lake Chapala — the main source of supply for the Guadalajara metropolitan zone (ZMG) — to the city. The original pipeline is in a critical state, with leaks, internal corrosion and loss of capacity, which increases the risk of failures and leads to sediments and contaminants in the water that reaches the network.

Simultaneous with the pipeline rehabilitation will be an increased cleanup effort for the region’s rivers. Mexico’s Environment Ministry (Semarnat) said that the ZMG’s water issues are also linked to industrial contamination, with discharges from industries polluting the Lerma River.

“Industrial discharge is crucial as that’s where heavy metals and truly toxic products come from, and Lerma is one of the rivers presenting such a problem,” Semarnat Minister Alicia Bárcena said.

She added that companies thought to be responsible for discharging industrial waste have been identified and that inspections are underway that could lead to penalizing any proven to have violated environmental regulations.

She also explained that the federal government is implementing the 2024–2030 National Water Plan, a 20-billion-peso (US $1.15 billion) initiative that includes river cleanup programs and new wastewater treatment plants in the Atoyac, Lerma–Santiago and Tula river basins, Mexico’s most polluted rivers.

Although the federal government pledged technical support for the river cleanup efforts, experts argue that addressing Guadalajara’s water crisis will also require a stronger local strategy.

With reports from Zona Franca

World.title: Is iceberg lettuce from Mexico safe to eat?
World.content:
Updated July 21, 2026:

Yes, at least according to available evidence.

So far, authorities in Mexico and the United States say there is no confirmed evidence that iceberg lettuce sourced in central Mexico was contaminated with Cyclospora cayetanensis, the parasite responsible for a multi-state outbreak of Cyclospora infections in the U.S. that is widely known for its unpleasant side effect of “explosive diarrhea.”

On July 21, Mexico’s Ministry of Health (SS) confirmed three cases of cyclosporiasis in Mexico, but described the cases as “usual” and ruled out a domestic outbreak.

The news development comes after a series of conflicting findings in the investigation, including the U.S. Food and Drug Administration’s (FDA) reversal on July 19th of a positive test result for the Cyclospora parasite, obtained from lettuce sourced from Taylor Farms in Guanajuato.

The false positive was revealed after the agency’s laboratory specialists reviewed the sample again and concluded that the initial result was incorrect.

Taylor Farms de Mexico echoed the FDA’s statement and acknowledged its correction. “To be clear, at this moment, FDA has not identified a single positive product test result for Cyclospora,” the company said.

Still, Taylor Farms maintains its voluntary recall of all iceberg lettuce produced in central Mexico, which was served at Taco Bell restaurants in Indiana, Kentucky, Michigan, Ohio and West Virginia. Taco Bell also reported that it recalled lettuce sourced from Taylor Farms de Mexico starting on July 17. The products compromised are as follows:

Marketside-brand product available at Walmart described as “Iceberg Salad 12-oz or 24-oz” and “Shredded Lettuce 8-oz or 16-oz” with Best if Used By dates of 7/18/2026 to 8/3/2026 and July 18th to Aug 3rd 2026

Speaking at Tuesday’s presidential press conference, Health Minister David Kershenobich addressed the FDA’s correction and insisted that so far, there is no conclusive evidence of contaminated produce in Mexico.

Nonetheless, he said Mexican authorities have gone to Guanajuato to take samples and conduct their own research in collaboration with the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

In addition, the Mexican Ministries of Health and Agriculture activated an inter-institutional technical group led by the Federal Commission for Protection against Sanitary Risks (Cofepris) and the General Directorate of Epidemiology (DGE) to collaborate with the U.S. in the investigation of the outbreak.

From the outset, the Mexican government clarified that the reference to the country of origin was a traceability measure, not conclusive proof that the contamination had occurred within Mexican territory.

Authorities in Mexico said they will continue working in coordination with the U.S. to determine the source of the outbreak and protect the population of both countries.

With reports from Bloomberg and El País

World.title: Nuevo León leads all Mexican states in announced investments so far this year
World.content:
Nuevo León ranks No. 1 in investment expectations this year, accumulating 12% of all investment announcements recorded by Mexico’s Finance Ministry through June.

The northern state received pledges for US $5.58 billion of the cumulative US $46.96 billion committed to Mexico through the first six months of 2026.

The official data recognizes Nuevo León as the state with the highest expectations, followed by Chihuahua, Sinaloa, Hidalgo and México state.

According to information from the state and federal governments, the projects announced in Nuevo León will include the creation of 6,120 new jobs, primarily in advanced manufacturing, electromobility, technology, logistics, energy and innovation.

While acknowledging that the results reflect the joint effort of the state and federal governments, the business sector and universities, Nuevo León Economy Minister Betsabé Rocha Nieto said they also demonstrate the reputation the state enjoys.

“There is no doubt about the strength and confidence of national and international companies in Nuevo León as a primary destination to develop new productive projects,” she said.

Every new project “represents more opportunities for development, quality jobs and heightened welfare for Nuevo León families,” she said.

Recently, the national statistics institute INEGI reported that Nuevo León had also received the most investment in construction projects over the previous 20-month period.

In last week’s investment update, the Finance Ministry revealed that manufacturing remained the top recipient of announced investments during the first six months of the year.

Pharmaceutical companies — among them, Laboratorios Kener, Liomont, Bayer and Grupo Neolpharma — were among the leading investors, while automotive companies, as well as logistics and infrastructure companies, were also well represented.

Investment expectations in Mexico’s automotive sector surpassed US $2 billion, heavily focused on electromobility, supply chain integration and regional production.

In early June, e-commerce and financial services platform Mercado Libre announced an investment of US $4.6 billion with a particular focus on logistics, development and technological innovation.

As for infrastructure investments, Vinci Airports provided US $800 million to modernize and expand the network of airports managed by Grupo Aeroportuario del Centro Norte.

With reports from El Economista, MVS Noticias and Mexico Business News

World.title: 6 celebrities who you might not realize are (kind of) Mexican
World.content:
What does it mean to be Mexican? It’s a complicated question — since not only are there more than 130 million native-born citizens, but a Mexican diaspora numbering over 40 million around the globe — making it nearly an impossible task to come up with a completely satisfying definition.

One thing is clear: Mexico is a very warm country, especially when it comes to welcoming those who embrace it with love. There’s even a popular saying that captures this idea: “Los Mexicanos nacemos donde se nos pega la gana,” which means that a Mexican can be born wherever they choose.

The nation is also a melting pot, having welcomed significant populations of Italians, Germans, Lebanese, Argentinians, Venezuelans, Japanese and Koreans into the country as immigrants since the late 19th century. President Claudia Sheinbaum comes from a family of European Jews who settled in Mexico, for example, and the many examples like this make the question of Mexican identity even more nuanced.

If we consider Mexican identity not only in the traditional sense (native-born citizens), but also more inclusively to include those with Mexican roots or heritage, there are more international Mexican celebrities than you might think. In fact, a few of the names on this list even surprised us.

Alan Cleland

A professional surfer who competed in the 2024 Paris Olympic Games and won gold at the 2023 International Surfing Association (ISA) World Surfing Games, Alan has been making his mark in extreme sports. But with sandy blonde hair and a surfboard on him at all times, the average person may think he’s just another Californian who grew up near the beach.

Born to a Mexican mother and an American ex-pro surfer father in Boca de Pascuales, Colima, Alan learned to surf before he even learned to speak English. He later moved to San Diego to further develop his surfing skills and began competing in the World Surf League when he was only 13.

After he won gold in 2023, there was even a video of him carrying the Mexican flag and chanting “Viva Mexico” as any proud Mexican would in the same position. He completed the 2025 season ranked 19th in the World Surf League (WSL) tour.

Wee Man

Best known for his role in the “Jackass” movie franchise, Wee Man has made a name for himself by performing stunts on film that the average viewer should never try at home. In addition, he’s a pro skateboarder and was a host on the Fox Sports Net television show “54321.” Despite his impressive resume, his background is more diverse than most people would assume.

Wee Man’s legal name is Jason Shannon Acuña, and he is of Mexican and German descent. He’s spoken openly in the past about growing up eating tacos and menudo. The “Jackass” actor, idolized for getting into cages with bulls, bungee jumping and funny pranks, also has an entrepreneurial side, having been a long-time investor in the popular Mexican-American franchise Chronic Tacos.

Kat Von D

A well-known public figure in her niche, Kat Von D may look like the reincarnation of Amy Winehouse, yet is actually a Mexican-born tattoo artist from Nuevo León.

She’s most recognized for her work on the TLC reality show “LA Ink.” On the show, she set the record for the most tattoos done in 24 hours at 400 and was named to the Guinness Book of World Records for that milestone — a record that has since been surpassed.

In addition, Von D has also released a makeup collection with Sephora in 2008, released two studio albums and written two New York Times bestselling books.

Anthony Quinn

If you’re a fan of old movies and love trivia, Anthony Quinn could be defined as a legend of Hollywood. In the 1950s, he cleaned up at the Oscars — winning two Best Supporting Actor awards, one in 1952 for “Viva Zapata!” and another in 1956 for “Lust for Life.” What many U.S. audiences didn’t know at the time, however, was that he was also Mexican.

His legal name was Manuel Antonio Rodolfo Quinn Oaxaca. What’s also intriguing is the fact that he was born in Chihuahua at the midpoint of the Mexican Revolution in 1915. It’s said his father was Irish and his mother was from Mexico, yet in his biography, “The Original Sin: A Self-Portrait,” he claimed his Irish father was just a story made up by Hollywood publicists. In other words, he was as proud to be Mexican as they come. That alone deserves to be celebrated as much as his Oscars.

Hubertus von Hohenlohe-Langenburg

Most people know a famous Mexican soccer player or boxer, but what about one who’s a well-known skier? Hubertus Hohenlohe-Langenburg is a pioneer in niche sports in Mexico, having competed in six Winter Olympics as an alpine skier and founded the Mexican Ski Federation in 1981.

His family story is also one that could be turned into a scripted television series. Hohenlohe is a descendant of German royalty, being the son of Prince Alfonso of Hohenlohe-Langenburg and Princess Ira von Fürstenberg. He was born in Mexico City, moved to Spain and then eventually settled in Austria.

In addition, Hohenlohe is a photographer and businessman and was even a pop singer who went by the stage names Andy Himalaya and Royal Disaster.

Lupita Nyong’o

Having won an Oscar for Best Supporting Actress in the film “12 Years a Slave” in 2014, Lupita Nyong’o has gone on to be one of Hollywood’s brightest stars, appearing in “Black Panther” and “Star Wars: The Force Awakens.” But the most intriguing thing about her is her cultural background. Not only does she hold U.S. and Kenyan citizenship, but she also carries Mexican citizenship.

Her father is a Kenyan politician who was teaching in Mexico City when she was born. Although she grew up in Kenya and later came over to the United States to study at Yale University, she has always maintained that she is Kenyan-Mexican.

So who else should have been mentioned on our list? Let us know in the comments below.

Ian Ostroff is an indie author, journalist, and copywriter from Montreal, Canada. You can find his work in various outlets, including Map Happy and The Suburban. When he’s not writing, you can find Ian at the gym, a café, or anywhere within Mexico visiting family and friends.

World.title: Zacatecas AG: Multihomicide of 10, including officials, may be linked to extortion and collusion
World.content:
The murders of 10 men whose bodies were found in three different municipalities in the state of Zacatecas on Saturday could be linked to extortion and collusion between criminals and public officials, the Zacatecas attorney general said Sunday.

The bodies — including that of Ignacio Castrejón Valdez, a former mayor of Sombrerete, Zacatecas — were found in the municipalities of Morelos, Pánuco and Saín Alto, all located north of Zacatecas City. Five of the bodies were found hanging from a bridge in Pánuco.

Among the other victims were Fidel Alvarado de la Torre, an official with the Fresnillo municipal government, and Andrés Vázquez Gurrola, an ex-councilor in the municipality of Canatlán, Durango.

In a video message on Sunday, Zacatecas Attorney General Cristian Paul Camacho said that “various pieces of evidence have been collected, which indicate that the main lines of investigation involve possible acts of extortion and collusion by public officials.”

“This investigation must be carried out in a very exhaustive and very professional way,” he said, adding that a financial probe could be part of it.

Camacho said that authorities had obtained video footage that allowed them to establish the vehicles that were used in “the criminal events” — i.e., those used to dump the bodies in public places.

“It is necessary to inform that at this time a search warrant is being executed at a property in the municipality of Fresnillo, where it has been determined at least two of the victims were there before they were killed,” he said.

“… At a different place, a vehicle related to the events was seized.”

Camacho said that eight of the victims were from Zacatecas and two were from the neighboring state of Durango.

“Among the victims is the ex-mayor of Sombrerete, Ignacio Castrejón Valdez, and two officials from the municipality of Fresnillo. One of them worked as the director of social development and one was a Civil Protection member,” he said.

Referring to ex-municipal councilor Andrés Vázquez Gurrola, Camacho said that another victim was a lawyer and former police officer from Durango. Six others were businessmen in various fields including agriculture, entertainment and construction. One of the businessmen owned a bar.

Camacho said that eight of the victims were strangled to death, while two others, including Alvarado, the social development director in Fresnillo, were shot. He said that bullet casings recovered by authorities were being subjected to an “exhaustive analysis” in order to establish whether perpetrators of the murders had used the same weapons in other crimes.

According to the attorney general, four of the victims stopped communicating with their families last Thursday, while five ceased communication last Friday. The other victim ceased contact with his family on Saturday.

Camacho said that the Zacatecas Attorney General’s Office didn’t receive any reports that the victims had been abducted.

Citing the results of toxicology tests, Camacho said that five of the victims, including the two municipal officials from Fresnillo, had recently consumed drugs.

In the same video message, Rodrigo Reyes Mugüerza, general secretary of the Zacatecas government, said that it had been a “weekend of uncertainty … fear and concern” for residents of the northern state.

Homicides declined by more than 60% annually in Zacatecas in the first six months of 2026, according to government data, but Reyes said that “days like Saturday … remind us that the process of pacification is a complex and continuous process.”

He said that state authorities were carrying out an operation aimed at detaining those responsible for the murders and were committed to “minimizing the possibility of these events being repeated.”

“From the state government, we once again confirm our commitment to peace, to security and above all to solidarity with all the people of Zacatecas,” Reyes said.

At a press conference on Monday, Governor David Monreal Ávila conveyed his condolences to the victims’ families and declared that there will be no impunity for the murders.

“Far from intimidating us, expressions of barbarity like those of last Saturday force us to redouble efforts. They oblige us not to let our guard down, not to take a backward step or fear groups that violate peace,” he said.

The Morena party governor said that his government is supported by the federal government, and stressed that the state of Zacatecas has sufficient technology, equipment and trained security personnel.

“We’ll put all this capacity in play to shed light on the events of Saturday and, above all, to guarantee that they are not repeated and to ensure that whoever committed this atrocity receives the appropriate punishment,” Monreal said.

With reports from Aristegui Noticias, Reforma, El Financiero and El Sol de Zacatecas

World.title: WEG Q2 Preview: Analysts See an 8% Profit Dip
World.content:
Brazil · Business

Key Facts —Net revenue estimate. Analysts project net revenue around R$ 9.97 billion (US$ 1.96 billion), a roughly 3% decline from a year earlier. —Net income forecast. Bradesco BBI sees net income falling 8% year-on-year to approximately R$ 1.47 billion (US$ 289 million). —Margin pressure. The EBITDA margin is expected to hover near 21%, squeezed by currency effects and factory expansion spending. —Release timing. WEG typically publishes second-quarter results in late July or early August, putting the report days away. —Share price context. Bank of America and Citi hold neutral ratings with target prices near R$ 50 (US$ 9.84), implying modest upside.

WEG, the Brazilian multinational that manufactures electric motors, generators, and transformers, is expected to report weaker second-quarter results within the next two weeks, according to estimates compiled from major financial institutions.

WEG manufactures electric motors and industrial equipment for global markets.

What WEG Makes and Why It Matters

WEG is one of Latin America’s largest industrial groups, producing everything from industrial electric motors and power transformers to automotive alternators and home-appliance components. Its equipment drives factory floors, wind turbines, transmission grids, and household appliances across more than 135 countries.

For Brazil’s export story, an electric motor maker carries outsized weight. WEG converts domestic engineering into high-value manufactured goods sold abroad, making it a bellwether for the country’s industrial competitiveness and a direct beneficiary—or victim—of currency swings.

The Numbers: What Analysts Are Previewing

Bradesco BBI forecasts net revenue of R$ 9.97 billion (US$ 1.96 billion), down roughly 3% from the same quarter in 2025. Safra and Citi publish similar top-line estimates, while BTG Pactual’s consensus sits slightly lower at R$ 9.8 billion (US$ 1.93 billion).

Net income is expected to land near R$ 1.47 billion (US$ 289 million), an 8% year-on-year decline. EBITDA should reach about R$ 2.1 billion (US$ 413 million), implying a margin around 21%, a touch below last year’s level.

Why WEG’s Results Are Under Pressure

A stronger Brazilian real is the main headwind. The exchange rate has hovered near R$ 5.05 per US dollar, reducing the local-currency value of revenue earned abroad by an estimated 3% to 5%.

WEG generates a large share of its sales outside Brazil, so a firmer real directly compresses reported top-line figures.

Costs tied to transformer factory expansion in Brazil are also eating into margins. While the new capacity should support future revenue growth, the near-term drag is showing up in analyst spreadsheets.

Slower domestic demand for industrial equipment adds a third layer of caution.

The Bigger Picture: WEG’s Role in a Shifting Economy

WEG’s performance often mirrors broader trends in Latin America’s largest economy. When the real strengthens, Brazilian exporters across the board see their overseas earnings shrink when converted back to local currency, and WEG is no exception.

The company’s transformer expansion is a strategic bet on long-term electrification demand, both in Brazil and abroad. For foreign investors, this kind of capital expenditure signals confidence in future orders, even if it temporarily weighs on profitability and keeps the stock in a holding pattern.

What It Means for Expats and Investors

For expats and foreign investors holding Brazilian assets, a weaker quarterly report from a blue-chip industrial name like WEG can reinforce caution about the country’s near-term growth story. Currency volatility remains a double-edged sword: a stronger real helps your purchasing power locally but can hurt the companies in your portfolio that depend on exports.

Analysts at Safra and Itaú BBA note that as transformer capacity comes online and if currency pressures ease, revenue growth could reaccelerate in the second half of 2026. That potential recovery makes the current dip worth watching for those considering entry points into Brazilian industrials.

What Comes Next for Investors

WEG has not yet confirmed the exact publication date, but the company historically releases second-quarter figures between July 30 and early August. That puts the report roughly ten days away from the current date of July 21, 2026.

Despite the cautious preview, some analysts see a progressive recovery later in the year. Bank of America and Citi maintain neutral ratings with target prices near R$ 50 (US$ 9.84), implying modest upside from current levels.

The market will be listening closely for any update on transformer orders and export demand during the earnings call.

Frequently Asked Questions

What does WEG manufacture?

WEG produces electric motors, generators, power transformers, automotive components such as alternators and starters, and motors for home appliances and HVAC systems. The company sells to more than 135 countries and is a key player in industrial electrification.

Why are WEG’s Q2 2026 earnings expected to decline?

Analysts point to a stronger Brazilian real reducing export revenue, costs tied to transformer factory expansion, and softer domestic demand for industrial equipment. The exchange rate near R$ 5.05 per US dollar has trimmed the local-currency value of overseas sales by an estimated 3% to 5%.

When will WEG publish its second-quarter 2026 results?

WEG has not confirmed the exact date, but based on historical patterns the report is expected between late July and early August 2026. Investors typically receive the full earnings release and a conference call with management shortly after publication.

World.title: Argentina’s Milei in Brazil for Trade, Not Lula Talks
World.content:
Brazil · Politics

Key Facts —Primary event Milei will headline a campaign rally for presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro in São Paulo on July 25. —Blocked visit A Supreme Court justice barred Milei from visiting former President Jair Bolsonaro, who remains under house arrest in Brasília. —No Lula meeting The agenda includes no bilateral talks with President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva or his ministers. —Trade mission Milei frames the trip as part of an outward-looking strategy to attract commerce and investment to Argentina. —Regional tour The Brazil stop precedes visits to Peru, Colombia, and Ecuador to meet conservative allies.

Javier Milei touches down in São Paulo on July 25 for what his team calls an investment and trade outreach mission, though the official agenda revolves around a single campaign rally for a key political ally.

Argentine President Javier Milei is a libertarian economist leading South America's second-largest economy.

A Campaign Stop With a Commercial Pitch

The Argentine president will headline an event backing Senator Flávio Bolsonaro of the Liberal Party (PL), who is mounting a bid to unseat President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in next year’s general election.

Milei’s advisers insist the trip is not purely political. They describe it as one leg of an outward-looking tour designed to unlock more commerce and investment for Argentina’s struggling economy.

The rally is contingent on Flávio Bolsonaro’s formal anointment as the PL candidate at the party convention, a step that is scheduled for July 25 and would clear the way for the high-profile endorsement.

For foreign observers, the fusion of a campaign event with a trade mission reflects Milei’s unconventional diplomatic style, one that often blurs the line between statecraft and ideological alliance-building.

Why Javier Milei Is Betting on Brazil

Brazil remains Argentina’s largest trading partner, absorbing roughly 15 percent of its exports, from wheat and automobiles to natural gas.

Milei wants to deepen those commercial channels and has signaled he will use every foreign stop to pitch Argentina as a deregulated, investor-friendly destination.

Argentina’s economy has long relied on Brazilian demand for its manufactured goods and agricultural products, a relationship that becomes even more critical during periods of domestic recession.

By framing the São Paulo stop as a trade mission, Milei aims to reassure Brazilian business leaders that political drama will not derail the deep commercial interdependence between the two neighbors.

Mercosur Tensions Simmer in the Background

The trip highlights the awkward state of the Mercosur trade bloc, which also includes Uruguay and Paraguay. Milei has criticized the group’s protectionist rules and, as our reporting has shown, has repeatedly threatened to exit the bloc if necessary to pursue a free trade agreement with the United States.

Brazilian officials note that no Mercosur summit or formal negotiation session is scheduled during the visit, leaving the bloc’s reform debate for another day.

Mercosur has struggled for years to finalize a long-awaited trade agreement with the European Union, and Milei’s skepticism toward the bloc adds a new layer of uncertainty for investors watching the region.

For expats and companies operating across South America, any move to weaken Mercosur could reshape supply chains, customs procedures, and the ease of moving goods and personnel between member countries.

The Blocked Bolsonaro Visit and What Comes Next

As The Rio Times previously reported, Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes rejected Milei’s request to visit former President Jair Bolsonaro, who is confined to his Brasília home and barred from receiving political visitors.

The court ruling, issued on July 18, specifically prohibits visits of a “political-electoral nature” to the former president, who is already restricted to receiving only family, doctors, lawyers, and healthcare staff.

Milei had publicly stated his intention to greet Jair Bolsonaro personally, making the judicial block a symbolic setback that underscores the legal constraints surrounding Brazil’s former leader.

After São Paulo, Milei travels to Lima for Keiko Fujimori’s inauguration on July 28, then to Colombia in early August for Abelardo de la Espriella’s event, and finally to Ecuador to meet President Daniel Noboa, reinforcing his strategy of aligning with conservative leaders across the region.

What This Means for Expats and Investors

For foreign residents and investors in Argentina and Brazil, Milei’s trip signals both opportunity and political risk. His pro-market rhetoric may open doors for deregulation and foreign capital, but the absence of formal government-to-government talks leaves bilateral policy uncertain.

Brazilian companies with Argentine subsidiaries, and vice versa, should watch for any post-visit shifts in trade facilitation or regulatory tone, even if no agreements are signed this week.

The political polarization on display—Milei campaigning for Lula’s rival while ignoring Brasília—could also affect the mood in cross-border business forums and investor conferences in the months ahead.

The Broader Regional Picture

Milei’s multi-country tour reflects a deliberate effort to build a network of like-minded conservative leaders at a time when left-leaning governments still hold sway in several major Latin American economies.

By visiting Peru, Colombia, and Ecuador immediately after Brazil, Milei is stitching together a coalition that could influence regional policy debates on trade, security, and the future of multilateral blocs like Mercosur and the Pacific Alliance.

For tourists and short-term visitors, the political maneuvering is unlikely to disrupt travel plans, but those doing business across borders should monitor whether the ideological alignment translates into concrete bilateral deals down the line.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Javier Milei meeting President Lula during this trip?

No. The agenda contains no bilateral meeting with President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva or any Brazilian government minister. The visit is focused entirely on the campaign rally for Flávio Bolsonaro and Milei’s broader investment outreach.

Why was Milei barred from visiting Jair Bolsonaro?

A Brazilian Supreme Court ruling, issued by Justice Alexandre de Moraes on July 18, prohibits visits of a political-electoral nature to the former president. Jair Bolsonaro remains under house arrest in Brasília and is only allowed to receive family members, doctors, lawyers, and healthcare staff.

What is the main trade goal of Milei’s Brazil stop?

Milei aims to attract Brazilian investment and strengthen commercial ties by promoting Argentina as a deregulated, investor-friendly market. However, no formal trade talks or Mercosur negotiation sessions are scheduled during this visit, making the commercial pitch largely rhetorical for now.

World.title: French Firm Ships 1M Barrels of Venezuelan Crude Under US Waiver
World.content:
Venezuela · Business

Key Facts —Second cargo volume. Approximately 1 million barrels of Merey 16 heavy crude. —First cargo. 500,000 barrels shipped in June 2026. —US authorization. Operates under OFAC General License 50A, issued February 18, 2026. —Venezuelan partner. Joint operator with state-owned PDVSA in the Urdaneta Oeste field. —Production share. Maurel & Prom holds a 40% working interest, yielding roughly 9,000 barrels per day.

Maurel & Prom, the Paris-based oil explorer, is loading a second cargo of roughly 1 million barrels of Venezuelan crude at the end of July 2026, a small logistical event that signals a tectonic shift in Washington’s sanctions architecture.

Tankers transport unrefined petroleum from production sites to refineries around the world.

A Quiet Tanker, a Loud Message

The vessel is scheduled to lift Merey 16 heavy crude from Venezuela’s TAECJAA terminal, following a smaller 500,000-barrel shipment the company completed in June.

For a mid-sized European producer, moving two cargoes in as many months would normally be routine business, but in the context of Venezuela’s long-isolated oil sector, it represents a dramatic reopening.

The Licence That Let Maurel & Prom Back In

What makes this possible is a single document: General License 50A, issued by the U.S. Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) on February 18, 2026.

GL 50A authorizes Maurel & Prom to resume oil operations and financial transactions with PDVSA, Venezuela’s state oil company, without fear of American secondary sanctions.

How the Sanctions Framework on Venezuelan Crude Works

For years, U.S. sanctions walled off Venezuela’s oil industry from the global financial system, threatening penalties on any foreign firm that did business with PDVSA.

A general license is essentially a written permission slip from OFAC that carves out an exception, allowing specific companies or activities that would otherwise be illegal under the sanctions regime.

GL 50A is not a blanket repeal of Venezuela sanctions; it is a targeted, conditional authorization that lets named European operators lift crude, process payments, and repatriate profits for a defined period.

The license reflects a broader recalibration after U.S. forces detained and removed President Nicolás Maduro in January 2026, a geopolitical earthquake that prompted Washington to ease energy restrictions.

Who Gets a Seat at the Table

Maurel & Prom is not alone. Spanish major Repsol and Italian giant ENI have also sought or received U.S. licenses to export Venezuelan oil, creating a selective club of European operators.

The company works through its 80%-owned unit M&P Iberoamerica, which holds a 40% working interest in the Urdaneta Oeste field alongside PDVSA.

Gross production at the field sits around 22,500 barrels of oil per day, translating to roughly 9,000 barrels daily on Maurel & Prom’s net share.

The destination of the second cargo remains undisclosed, though the crude type and the company’s European base point toward refineries across the Atlantic.

The Bigger Picture: Venezuela’s Oil Reopening

The Urdaneta Oeste field, located in western Venezuela, is one of the country’s mature oil assets that had seen years of underinvestment and production declines during the sanctions era.

Merey 16, the heavy crude grade being lifted, is a staple of Venezuela’s export basket and requires specialized refineries, typically found on the U.S. Gulf Coast or in Europe, to process it into fuels.

The relaxation of energy sanctions in February 2026 marked the most significant U.S. policy shift since restrictions were tightened in 2019, effectively ending a near-total embargo on Venezuelan crude exports.

Originally, a six-month easing of restrictions announced in October 2023 was conditional on progress toward fair elections and the release of political prisoners, but Maduro’s ousting in January 2026 effectively superseded those conditions.

What It Means for Expats and Investors

For foreign investors and expatriates watching Latin America, the resumption of Venezuelan crude flows signals that the country’s vast oil reserves—the world’s largest—are slowly becoming accessible again after years of paralysis.

However, the selective nature of the licenses means that only a handful of pre-approved European firms currently benefit, leaving the broader investment landscape in Venezuela highly restricted and politically sensitive.

The presence of established European operators like Repsol, ENI, and Maurel & Prom suggests that energy-sector normalization is proceeding cautiously, with Washington retaining tight control over who can engage with PDVSA.

Expats in Venezuela should note that while the oil sector is showing tentative signs of life, the broader economic and security environment remains complex, and the political transition following Maduro’s removal is still unfolding.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is OFAC General License 50A?

It is a U.S. Treasury authorization issued in February 2026 that allows Maurel & Prom to resume oil operations and transactions with Venezuela’s PDVSA without violating American sanctions. The license is targeted and conditional, applying only to specific activities for a defined period rather than lifting sanctions entirely.

Why did the U.S. ease sanctions on Venezuelan oil?

The policy shift followed the U.S. detention and removal of President Nicolás Maduro in January 2026, which prompted Washington to recalibrate its sanctions posture toward the energy sector. The easing allows select European firms to re-engage with PDVSA under strict oversight.

What type of crude is Maurel & Prom lifting?

The company is exporting Merey 16, a heavy crude grade commonly produced in Venezuela and typically destined for refineries configured to process denser oil. Merey 16 is one of Venezuela’s benchmark export blends and requires specialized refining capacity.

World.title: Brazil Authorizes Armed Forces for 2026 Election
World.content:
Brazil · Politics

Key Facts —Legal framework. The operation falls under the Guarantee of Voting and Result Verification (GVA), grounded in the Electoral Code and Complementary Law No. 97/1999. —Who requested it. Seven Regional Electoral Courts (TREs) requested support: Acre, Amapá, Amazonas, Mato Grosso, Mato Grosso do Sul, Rio de Janeiro, and Roraima. —Approval chain. The Superior Electoral Court (TSE) must approve each state request before it reaches the Presidency for final authorization and Defence Ministry planning. —Troop numbers. No specific troop count has been disclosed; exact figures and assignments will be defined after TSE approval of the state requisitions. —Past precedent. In 2018, 513 municipalities across 11 states received military support; in 2022, that number rose to 568 municipalities.

President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva authorized the deployment of Brazil’s armed forces to guarantee voting security, logistics, and result verification during the 2026 general elections, according to a decree published Tuesday in the Official Journal of the Union.

The Brazilian armed forces are the unified military organization responsible for defending the country.

What a GVA Order Means

The operation is framed under the Guarantee of Voting and Result Verification, known by its Portuguese acronym GVA. It is a strictly electoral mechanism, distinct from the broader public-security instrument called Guarantee of Law and Order, or GLO, which was not cited in the July 21 decree.

Under a GVA mission, soldiers may protect polling stations, escort ballot boxes, and provide transport in areas of difficult access. They may not interfere with the act of voting itself, question voters, or remain inside the voting room unless explicitly requested by the presiding poll worker.

This distinction matters because a GLO deployment temporarily places military personnel in a policing role on the streets, a far more sensitive intervention in daily civilian life. The GVA framework keeps the armed forces tightly bound to electoral logistics, reinforcing their function as a neutral guarantor of the voting process rather than an enforcer of public order.

Who Can Request the Armed Forces

Only a state’s Regional Electoral Court, or TRE, can formally ask the Superior Electoral Court (TSE) for military support. The TSE, Brazil’s highest electoral authority, reviews each request to confirm it meets the legal threshold of exceptional logistical difficulty or a concrete risk to electoral normality.

Once the TSE approves a petition, it forwards the dossier to the Presidency. The president then signs a decree authorizing the Defence Ministry to plan and execute the mission.

No deployment can occur without completing this three-step chain.

This layered approval process is designed to prevent unilateral use of the military in elections. For foreign observers and investors, it represents an institutional check that keeps the armed forces under civilian electoral authority at every stage, from the local TRE up to the presidency.

The Seven States and Their Requests

Seven TREs submitted requests by June 2026: Acre, Amapá, Amazonas, Mato Grosso, Mato Grosso do Sul, Rio de Janeiro, and Roraima. The requests focus on municipalities with limited road access, strategically vulnerable areas in the Amazon basin, and parts of the Rio de Janeiro metropolitan region.

Rio de Janeiro’s petition specifically cited territorial control by criminal organizations as a justification. The other six states emphasized logistical hurdles in remote communities, continuing a pattern seen in earlier election cycles.

For readers unfamiliar with Brazil’s geography, Acre, Amapá, Amazonas, and Roraima form a large portion of the country’s northern frontier, where river transport and small aircraft are often the only ways to reach isolated voting stations. Mato Grosso and Mato Grosso do Sul, in the center-west, contain vast agricultural expanses with similarly challenging infrastructure.

Precedent from Earlier Elections

Brazil has deployed the armed forces for election support in every recent general vote. In 2018, military personnel operated in 513 municipalities across 11 states.

In 2022, the footprint expanded to 568 municipalities.

The 2026 authorization is narrower so far, limited to seven states, with the final number of municipalities still pending TSE approval. The Defence Ministry has confirmed that operational planning draws directly on the 2022 experience and will follow the same TSE requisition model.

The shrinking geographic scope may reflect improved civilian logistics capacity in some regions, but it also underscores a more targeted approach. Rather than a blanket presence, the armed forces are being directed only where local electoral courts have formally demonstrated a genuine need.

What It Means for Expats and Investors

Foreign residents and investors often worry that a military presence signals instability. In Brazil’s electoral context, however, the GVA deployment is a routine, legally bounded operation that has accompanied every recent presidential vote.

The explicit exclusion of a GLO order in the decree should reassure markets that the armed forces are not being repositioned as domestic security actors during the election period. The mission remains logistical and protective, centered on ballot boxes and isolated polling stations rather than urban policing.

For expats living in the seven named states, the practical impact is likely to be visible but limited: military vehicles near voting locations, soldiers assisting with transport in remote areas, and a generally heightened institutional presence on election days. Voting itself remains a civilian-run process.

What Happens Next

The TSE will now examine each state request in detail, verifying the specific municipalities and the nature of the logistical or security challenge cited. Only after this technical review will the court forward approved dossiers to the Presidency.

Once the final authorization reaches the Defence Ministry, planners will assign troop numbers, define transport routes, and coordinate with local electoral officials. The first round of voting is scheduled for October 4, 2026, with a potential runoff on October 25, giving commanders roughly two and a half months to complete preparations.

Observers will be watching closely to see whether the final municipality count approaches the 500-plus level of the last two elections or stays closer to the current seven-state footprint. That number will signal how broadly Brazil’s electoral authorities perceive a need for military logistics support in 2026.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the difference between a GVA and a GLO operation?

A GVA is an electoral mission focused on protecting polling stations and transporting voting materials. It operates strictly under the Electoral Code and TSE supervision. A GLO is a broader constitutional mechanism for public-security emergencies, granting soldiers temporary police powers in civilian areas, and was not invoked in the 2026 election decree.

Can soldiers enter a polling station in Brazil?

Soldiers may only enter a polling station if the presiding poll worker formally requests their presence. They cannot patrol inside the voting room or interact with voters on their own initiative. This rule preserves the civilian character of the voting act and prevents any perception of military influence over voters.

How many troops will be deployed for the 2026 election?

No troop number has been announced yet. The Defence Ministry will define the exact personnel count and assignments after the TSE approves each state's request and the Presidency issues the final authorization. Based on past cycles, the figure will depend on how many municipalities are ultimately included in the approved requisitions.

World.title: Brazil’s Nubank, Itaú Lead Latin America AI Bank Ranking
World.content:
Latin America · Business

Key Facts —Who ranks them. Evident Insights, an independent research firm, published the 2026 Evident AI Index for Banks – LATAM. —The method. It scores the 20 largest banks on 60-plus indicators across Talent, Innovation, Leadership, and Transparency using only public data. —The top four. All four are Brazilian: Nubank, Itaú Unibanco, Banco Bradesco, and Banco do Brasil. —Investment reality. Over 70% of Latin American financial entities are already investing in artificial intelligence. —What is still rare. Only 8% of large LATAM banks have advanced generative AI in production.

When a ranking names the region’s smartest banks in artificial intelligence, the method matters more than the medal. The 2026 Evident AI Index for Banks – LATAM, published by independent research firm Evident Insights, scores the 20 largest banks across four pillars using only publicly available data, then hands the top two spots to Brazilian heavyweights Nubank and Itaú Unibanco.

Digital banking platforms in Latin America offer financial services through mobile apps and websites.

How Evident Insights Actually Scores the Banks

Evident Insights builds its index from millions of public data points: patents, research papers, earnings-call transcripts, and strategy documents. No bank fills out a questionnaire, and no one pays to be included.

The firm evaluates each bank on 60-plus indicators grouped into four pillars: Talent (who they hire and how they train), Innovation (patents and research output), Leadership (what executives say on the record), and Transparency (how openly they disclose their AI work). The result is a single maturity score that rewards substance over press releases.

What Nubank's Artificial Intelligence Work Changes for a Customer

Nubank, the São Paulo-based digital bank with over 100 million customers across Brazil, Mexico, and Colombia, now runs a proprietary model called NuFormer for real-time credit decisions. In practice, that means a freelancer in Mexico City who applies for a Nu credit card gets an approval or decline in seconds, not days, based on data patterns a traditional scorecard would miss.

The bank says nearly 100% of its employees use AI tools daily, and it is building what it calls a “bank native to AI.” For an ordinary user, that translates to fewer generic chatbot loops and more cases where the app already knows why you are calling before you finish typing.

Itaú Unibanco: 500 Use Cases, One App

Itaú Unibanco, Latin America’s largest bank by assets, has deployed over 500 internal artificial intelligence use cases. The ones customers actually feel are embedded in everyday channels: Pix payments initiated via WhatsApp, investment recommendations inside the Itaú app, and fraud checks that run silently behind a card swipe.

The bank’s focus is scaling AI across both customer-facing products and back-office productivity. For a small-business owner in São Paulo, that means faster loan pre-approvals and fewer documents to upload, because the system already pulls and verifies tax and invoice data from public and private registries.

Why Brazil Sweeps the Board

Brazilian banks account for 35% of the 20 institutions in the index but produced 49% of all AI use cases with reported outcomes over the past two years. The country’s mature instant-payment rails (Pix), high smartphone penetration, and a regulatory sandbox at the Central Bank of Brazil give its lenders a head start that peers in Mexico, Chile, or Colombia have yet to match.

Globally, about 85% of financial AI use cases still sit in back-office tasks: data processing, compliance screening, operational optimization. In early 2026, roughly 30% of new global use cases shifted toward agentic AI, autonomous systems that can act without a human clicking “approve.” Latin America’s leaders are watching that shift closely, but for now the customer-facing wins are concentrated in credit and payments.

The Investment Landscape: Big Spending, Early Stages

More than 70% of Latin American financial entities are already investing in artificial intelligence, and 61% of executives confirm they are increasing that investment. The returns are coming quickly: 77% of firms reported a positive return on investment within the first year of a generative AI project.

Yet the gap between intention and production remains wide. Only 8% of large Latin American banks have advanced generative AI in production, while 58% have not started any generative AI project at all.

For expat investors and fintech entrepreneurs, this signals a market still rich with opportunity but demanding patience and local partnerships.

What This Means for Expats, Investors, and Tourists

For a foreigner living in or moving to Latin America, a bank’s AI maturity directly shapes daily financial life. Faster credit approvals mean a newly arrived professional in Mexico City can get a local credit card without a years-long local credit history, because Nubank’s NuFormer model reads alternative data patterns.

For investors, the Brazilian sweep of the top four spots is a signal of where scalable fintech returns are most likely. The combination of Pix, a forward-leaning central bank, and fierce competition among digital-first and legacy lenders creates a laboratory for AI-driven products that often reach consumers before similar tools appear in Europe or the United States.

Tourists benefit more subtly. AI-powered fraud detection running behind every card swipe means fewer blocked transactions and fewer embarrassing declines at a Rio de Janeiro restaurant.

Itaú’s WhatsApp-based Pix payments also let visitors pay instantly without downloading a local banking app, a quiet convenience built on machine-learning infrastructure.

Frequently Asked Questions

Which Latin American bank ranks first for artificial intelligence in 2026?

Nubank ranks first in the 2026 Evident AI Index for Banks – LATAM, followed by Itaú Unibanco in second place. The index, compiled by independent research firm Evident Insights, evaluates the 20 largest banks in the region using more than 60 publicly available indicators across talent, innovation, leadership, and transparency.

What does Nubank use artificial intelligence for?

Nubank uses its proprietary NuFormer model for credit scoring and loan decisions in Brazil and Mexico, and has integrated AI tools across nearly all employee workflows. The bank describes its strategy as building a "bank native to AI," meaning artificial intelligence is embedded in customer-facing features like instant credit approvals as well as internal operations.

Why are Brazilian banks ahead in AI adoption?

Brazil benefits from a large digital-banking market, the Pix instant-payment system, a supportive regulatory sandbox at the Central Bank of Brazil, and heavy investment in AI talent and patents. These factors give Brazilian lenders a structural advantage that peers in Mexico, Chile, or Colombia have not yet replicated, which is why all four top spots in the 2026 Evident AI Index belong to Brazilian institutions.

World.title: Argentina Moves to End Fixed Book Prices, Cut Library Funds
World.content:
Argentina · Life & Culture

Key Facts —Uniform price law. Law 25.542, enacted in 2001, mandates all retailers in Argentina sell the same book at the same price. —Current push. In July 2026, the Milei government renewed a legislative effort to fully repeal the uniform book price. —Price impact. Supporters argue repeal will lower consumer prices; opponents warn of predatory discounts by large chains. —Library funding. The proposal also eliminates a special fund for popular libraries, removing their tax exemptions and subsidies. —Industry scale. Argentina's publishing ecosystem includes hundreds of small bookshops that rely on price stability to compete.

In Argentina, a renewed government push to abolish the fixed price of books is redrawing the line between market freedom and cultural protection, promising cheaper paperbacks for readers while threatening the neighborhood bookshops that have weathered decades of economic turmoil.

Argentina’s publishing industry produces and sells books across a vast Spanish-speaking market.

What the Uniform Price Actually Does

Since November 2001, Law 25.542 has required every bookshop, supermarket, and online platform in Argentina to sell a new title at the same public price set by the publisher. The rule was designed to stop large retailers from slashing prices in a way small independents could never match.

For a reader buying a novel in Buenos Aires, this meant the cost was identical whether purchased from a tiny Palermo bookshop or a giant chain. Supporters call the system a shield for bibliodiversidad, the rich variety of small publishers and niche titles that might otherwise vanish.

The Government's Case for Deregulation

Minister of Deregulation Federico Sturzenegger argues that scrapping the fixed price will unleash commercial freedom and drive down costs for consumers. The proposal, re-introduced in July 2026, would let supermarkets and online platforms discount bestsellers, potentially cutting the price of a new release by 20% or more.

A reader who now pays R$ 25,000 (US$4.92) for a mass-market paperback could see that figure drop if retailers compete on price. The government frames the repeal as a simple pro-consumer reform that ends a 23-year restriction on how businesses set their own prices.

What a Small Bookshop Stands to Lose

Independent bookshops in Argentina operate on thin margins and cannot absorb the deep discounts a large chain or e-commerce giant can offer. Industry leaders warn that without the uniform price, a handful of big players will undercut everyone else on bestsellers, then raise prices on backlist titles once the competition is gone.

The Fundación del Libro, which organizes the Buenos Aires Book Fair, says the repeal would collapse the value chain that links authors, small publishers, distributors, and neighborhood stores. A bookseller in Córdoba or Rosario would face the same squeeze, forced to match a price set by a retailer with a national logistics network.

Beyond the Bookshop: Libraries and a Cultural Ecosystem in Argentina

The deregulation package goes further than book pricing. It proposes dissolving the special fund for Bibliotecas Populares, the popular libraries that offer free reading access in small towns, by removing their postal franchises, tax exemptions, and maintenance subsidies.

The plan also deletes a decades-old requirement that most imported books be translated into Spanish, a change that could flood the market with cheaper foreign editions. For a reader, the full picture is a trade-off: possibly lower prices on some titles today, against a thinner network of bookshops and libraries tomorrow.

A Long Road to Reform: Background and Legal Wrangling

The uniform price law was born from crisis, enacted in November 2001 just before Argentina’s economy collapsed, and formally promulgated in January 2002. For over two decades it has been the bedrock of a publishing ecosystem that survived hyperinflation, currency controls, and repeated recessions.

The current push is not the government’s first attempt. A sprawling omnibus bill sent to Congress in December 2023 included the repeal, and a subsequent Decree of Necessity and Urgency (DNU) tried to bypass lawmakers, only to face legal challenges that blocked full implementation.

The July 2026 anteproyecto represents a fresh legislative route, signaling that deregulation remains a core priority for the Milei administration.

What This Means for Expats, Investors, and Tourists in Argentina

For foreign residents and visitors who buy books in Argentina, a repeal could mean cheaper bestsellers at large retailers and airport shops, at least in the short term. English-language imports and translated editions might also become more widely available if the translation requirement disappears.

However, the cultural landscape that makes neighborhoods like Palermo or San Telmo attractive could shift if independent bookshops close. Investors eyeing Argentina’s retail or publishing sectors should watch for a potential consolidation wave, where large players gain market share and small competitors vanish, reshaping a US$300 million-plus industry that has long been defined by its diversity.

Frequently Asked Questions

How would the repeal change the price I pay for a book in Argentina?

A new release could become cheaper at large retailers and online platforms that choose to discount, but prices at small bookshops may stay the same or rise if they lose volume. The uniform price law currently applies to both print and digital editions, so e-book prices could also diverge between sellers for the first time in over two decades.

Why do independent bookshops oppose ending the fixed price?

They argue that without price protection, big chains will sell bestsellers at a loss to attract customers, driving small stores out of business and reducing the diversity of available titles. Once competition thins, those large retailers could raise prices on backlist and niche books, leaving readers with fewer choices and weaker local literary culture.

Does the proposal affect digital books in Argentina?

Yes, the uniform price law currently covers digital editions as well, and its repeal would allow retailers to set different prices for e-books and print copies. This could lead to aggressive discounting on e-books by large platforms, further pressuring physical bookshops that cannot match digital price cuts.

World.title: Sustainable Aviation Fuel: Brazil Bets on Its Sugarcane
World.content:
Brazil · Business

Key Facts —Mandate start. A 1% sustainable aviation fuel blend is required in Brazil from 2027, rising to 10% by 2037. —Feedstock advantage. Sugarcane ethanol gives Brazil a unique Alcohol-to-Jet pathway that the US and Europe cannot yet match at scale. —Investment pipeline. Announced SAF projects exceed R$50 billion (US$9.8 billion), with the full program projected to unlock R$260 billion (US$51.2 billion) through 2037. —Current production. Only Petrobras’s Duque de Caxias refinery is co-processing tiny volumes of SAF today, using a 1.2% corn oil blend. —Passenger reality. No commercial plant will produce meaningful SAF volumes before 2027, and dedicated large-scale output waits until after 2029.

Brazil is pouring billions of dollars into sustainable aviation fuel, betting that its sprawling sugarcane fields and soybean harvests can turn the country into a global supplier long before most of its competitors. The legal architecture is now in place, but the gap between announced projects and fuel flowing into aircraft tanks remains wide.

Brazil produces sustainable aviation fuel from sugarcane to cut aviation's carbon emissions.

The Combustível do Futuro Law Sets a Slow-Burn Mandate

President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva signed the Combustível do Futuro (Future Fuel) Law on October 8, 2024, creating the National Sustainable Aviation Fuel Program, known as ProBioQAV.

It requires airlines operating in Brazil to cut emissions by blending 1% sustainable aviation fuel from 2027, a figure that climbs to 10% by 2037, generating an estimated demand of 1.2 billion liters annually.

The mandate is less aggressive than Europe’s ReFuelEU Aviation regulation, which started at 2% in 2025 and targets 6% by 2030.

Brazilian officials project the framework will unlock R$260 billion (US$51.2 billion) in total investment through 2037, with development banks BNDES and FINEP pledging up to US$1 billion in financing.

Sustainable Aviation Fuel: What Exists Today, What Is Only Announced

Right now, only one Brazilian refinery produces any sustainable aviation fuel at all. Petrobras’s Duque de Caxias plant (Reduc) in Rio de Janeiro state co-processes a 1.2% blend of corn oil, yielding roughly 600,000 liters per year, a negligible volume in commercial aviation terms.

Everything else remains on drawing boards or in early construction. Brasil BioFuels (BBF) is commissioning a HEFA-technology plant in Manaus, deep in the Amazon, designed to process soy, palm, and corn oil into 250,000 cubic meters of fuel annually, with output expected between 2025 and 2026.

Raízen, a joint venture between Shell and Cosan, targets 2027 for its Alcohol-to-Jet (ATJ) plant in Piracicaba, São Paulo, though the company has acknowledged unresolved technology challenges.

Energis8, another ATJ project relying on sugarcane ethanol, has announced a far more ambitious 1-billion-liter-per-year capacity but does not expect operations before 2031. Petrobras plans a dedicated ATJ unit at its Paulínia refinery after 2029, and a larger HEFA and ATJ complex at Itaboraí with a potential capacity exceeding one billion liters annually.

Acelen, which operates the Mataripe refinery in Bahia, is aiming for 2027 with a 500,000-cubic-meter HVO and SAF plant using soy, corn, and macaúba palm oil.

GEO Biogás and Copersucar are testing a biogas-to-SAF pathway in Paraná, producing just 750 liters per day at a commercial-scale demonstration unit that started in 2025.

Why Sugarcane Gives Brazil a Genuine Head Start

Brazil’s structural advantage lies in its mature ethanol infrastructure. The country produces over 30 billion liters of sugarcane ethanol annually, providing a ready feedstock for the Alcohol-to-Jet pathway that the United States and Europe cannot replicate at comparable scale.

The US relies primarily on soybean oil and corn oil for the HEFA process, while Europe depends heavily on used cooking oil and animal fats because of limited agricultural land for energy crops. Brazil can deploy both HEFA and ATJ, diversifying its feedstock base across soybean oil, corn oil, used cooking oil, and biomethane.

By 2050, industry projections suggest Brazil could produce up to 9 billion liters of sustainable aviation fuel per year, potentially covering 35% of global demand.

Yet building a plant typically takes five to seven years from initiation to startup, and even optimistic estimates assume four years for facilities already in the pipeline, meaning passengers will not board a flight powered substantially by Brazilian SAF this decade.

What It Means for Expats, Investors, and the Global Market

For foreign investors, Brazil’s sustainable aviation fuel push represents a long-term industrial play anchored in a legal mandate that guarantees demand, even if that demand starts small.

The involvement of global players like Shell (through Raízen) and Mubadala Capital, which has a US$13.5 billion biofuels program, signals that international capital views Brazil’s feedstock advantage as a durable asset rather than a short-term speculation.

Expats living in Brazil are unlikely to notice any immediate change at the pump or in airfare prices, since the initial 1% blend will be absorbed into existing fuel supply chains with minimal cost impact.

However, the construction of major plants in cities like Manaus, Piracicaba, and Itaboraí will create skilled jobs and ancillary service opportunities in engineering, logistics, and agribusiness over the next decade.

When a Passenger Might Actually Fly on It

The 2027 mandate will likely be met through a combination of imported sustainable aviation fuel and small domestic batches from early movers like BBF and Raízen, assuming their timelines hold.

A passenger flying from São Paulo or Rio de Janeiro in 2028 might travel on a jet burning a 1% blend, an improvement so marginal it will be imperceptible in terms of emissions reduction or ticket cost.

Meaningful volumes that could dent aviation’s carbon footprint will not arrive until the 2030s, when Petrobras’s larger plants, Energis8, and other second-wave projects reach full capacity.

Until then, Brazil’s sustainable aviation fuel story is one of industrial policy with a long time horizon, built on a genuine feedstock advantage but still waiting for steel to meet soil.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Combustível do Futuro law?

It is a Brazilian law enacted in October 2024 that mandates a 1% sustainable aviation fuel blend from 2027, rising to 10% by 2037, and creates the ProBioQAV program to promote research and commercialization. The law also provides tax benefits and economic incentives designed to unlock an estimated R$260 billion (US$51.2 billion) in total investment through 2037.

Which Brazilian companies are leading SAF production?

Petrobras, Brasil BioFuels (BBF), Raízen, Energis8, and Acelen have announced major plants. Only Petrobras’s Duque de Caxias refinery is producing small volumes today. Raízen is a joint venture between Shell and Cosan, while Acelen operates the Mataripe refinery in Bahia, highlighting the mix of state-owned and private capital driving the sector.

When will Brazilian airlines actually use SAF on passenger flights?

Airlines will begin blending 1% SAF from 2027 under the legal mandate, but substantial domestic production volumes are not expected until after 2029, with large-scale output arriving in the 2030s. In the near term, Brazil may need to import sustainable aviation fuel to meet the initial mandate while domestic plants ramp up construction.

World.title: Mexican Singer Lila Downs Wins Top World Music Prize in Spain
World.content:
Mexico · Life & Culture

Key Facts —Award: Premio La Mar de Músicas 2026, presented July 20 in Cartagena, Spain. —Festival: Part of the 31st edition of La Mar de Músicas, running July 17–25, 2026. —Venue: Auditorio Paco Martín, overlooking Cartagena's bay and Roman theater. —Presenter: Cartagena Mayor Noelia Arroyo handed Downs the sculpture. —Previous winners: Rubén Blades, Susana Baca, Omara Portuondo, and Youssou N'Dour.

Lila Downs, the Grammy-winning singer whose voice bridges the ancient hills of Oaxaca and the jazz clubs of New York, received the Premio La Mar de Músicas on Monday night in Cartagena, Spain.

The Guelaguetza is an annual celebration of Oaxacan indigenous dance, music, and community sharing.
