A Voice Born in the Mixtec Highlands

Lila Downs was born in Tlaxiaco, a market town nestled in Oaxaca’s Mixtec region, to a Mixtec mother and a Scottish-American father. That dual heritage became the engine of a singular career—one that treats borders not as walls but as invitations.

For three decades, she has woven indigenous Mexican folk melodies with jazz, blues, and soul, singing in Spanish, English, Mixtec, and Zapotec. Her music carries the weight of migration, the pride of pre-Hispanic roots, and the restless energy of a woman who grew up between two countries.

Downs spent parts of her childhood in California and Minnesota before returning to Mexico as a teenager, an experience that deepened her connection to her indigenous identity. She later studied anthropology and voice, blending academic rigor with the raw storytelling traditions of Oaxaca’s markets and ceremonies.

The Premio La Mar de Músicas and Its Mission

The Premio La Mar de Músicas is the flagship honor of Cartagena’s international world-music festival, now in its 31st edition. Organized by the city council, the award recognizes artists who build cultural bridges between countries and musical traditions.

Cartagena Mayor Noelia Arroyo presented the trophy—a sculpture by local artist Fernando Sáenz de Elorrieta—at the Auditorio Paco Martín. The open-air venue sits inside Parque Torres, with views sweeping across the bay and the city’s famed Roman theater.

The festival itself has grown into one of Europe’s most respected gatherings for global music, held each July in this historic Mediterranean port city. For foreign visitors and expats living in Spain, it offers a rare chance to see world-class artists in an intimate, ancient setting far from the crowded summer circuits of Barcelona or Madrid.

How Lila Downs Marked the Evening

Downs took the stage and reflected on the festival’s name with a line that rippled through the audience: “La Mar de Músicas, a great concept, because we come from the sea and will always return to the sea.” She then paid tribute to Paco Martín, the festival’s late founder, calling him “a brave person who loved music.”

Journalist and poet Lara López delivered the evening’s tribute speech, highlighting Downs’ defense of women’s and indigenous rights and her work promoting original languages through song. After the ceremony, Downs performed a full concert alongside Portuguese singer Carminho, Mexican singer-songwriter Silvana Estrada, and Andalusian artist El Nieto Manuel.

The audience stood and danced throughout her performance, which featured representative songs from her career. For Downs, the moment was both a celebration and a reflection on the power of music to carry memory across oceans and generations.

A Festival That Gathers the World

La Mar de Músicas has long been a Mediterranean lighthouse for global sounds. The award’s previous recipients read like a roll call of world-music royalty: Malian legend Salif Keita, Peruvian icon Susana Baca, Cuban maestro Eliades Ochoa, Panamanian superstar Rubén Blades, and Senegalese giant Youssou N’Dour.

The 2026 edition runs through July 25, filling Cartagena’s plazas and stages with artists from across Latin America, Africa, and Europe. For Downs, the honor lands in a year that reaffirms her place as one of the Americas’ most vital musical storytellers.

Other past winners include Oumou Sangaré, Omara Portuondo, Gino Paoli, Cheick Lô, Pablo Milanés, Totó la Momposina, Jorge Drexler, and Toquinho, who received the prize in 2025. The list underscores the festival’s commitment to honoring artists who transcend borders and genres.

What It Means for Expats and Investors

For the international community following Latin American culture from abroad, Downs’ recognition signals the growing global appetite for artists who blend indigenous traditions with contemporary sounds. Her music resonates far beyond Mexico, drawing listeners in the United States, Europe, and across Latin America.

Cartagena itself is increasingly on the radar of expats and investors looking beyond Spain’s larger cities. Events like La Mar de Músicas boost the city’s cultural profile and property market, making it an attractive destination for those seeking a Mediterranean lifestyle with deep historical roots.

For tourists planning summer travel, the festival offers a compelling reason to visit Cartagena in July. The combination of Roman ruins, seaside venues, and world-class music creates an experience that is both culturally rich and refreshingly uncrowded compared to Spain’s better-known coastal destinations.

What Happens Next for Lila Downs

The award adds to a career already decorated with one Grammy and six Latin Grammy Awards. It also arrives at a moment when Downs continues to tour internationally, bringing her message of cultural fusion and indigenous pride to new audiences.

While no new album has been announced immediately following the award, the recognition is likely to fuel further collaborations with artists across the Spanish-speaking world. For fans and followers of Latin American music, Downs remains an artist to watch closely in the months ahead.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is Lila Downs?

Lila Downs is a Mexican-American singer-songwriter born in Tlaxiaco, Oaxaca, known for fusing Mexican folk and indigenous music with jazz, blues, and soul. She has won one Grammy and six Latin Grammy Awards over a three-decade career, singing in Spanish, English, Mixtec, and Zapotec.

What is the Premio La Mar de Músicas?

It is an award given by the La Mar de Músicas festival in Cartagena, Spain, honoring artists who build cultural bridges between countries and musical traditions. Past winners include Susana Baca, Rubén Blades, Youssou N'Dour, and Salif Keita.

Where did Lila Downs receive the award?

She received it at the Auditorio Paco Martín in Parque Torres, Cartagena, an open-air venue overlooking the city's bay and Roman theater. Cartagena Mayor Noelia Arroyo presented the sculpture on July 20, 2026, during the festival's 31st edition.

World.title: Costa Rica’s Public Health Waiting Lists Hit 1.4 million, Audit Finds
World.content:
A newly surfaced internal audit at the Caja Costarricense de Seguro Social (CCSS) has intensified scrutiny of Costa Rica’s public healthcare system, and it has now drawn a formal demand for answers from the Legislative Assembly. Deputy Ángela Aguilar Vargas, of the Partido Liberación Nacional, has written to CCSS executive president Mónica Taylor Hernández requesting a detailed explanation of the findings and of the corrective measures the institution intends to take.

The document at the center of the dispute is the internal audit advisory cataloged as AS-ASALUD-0057-2026, dated June 3, 2026, which compiled the principal findings of a series of audits conducted between 2022 and 2025. According to that report, as of March 2026 the Caja carried 1,440,547 registered cases on its waiting lists.

That headline figure is easily misread by anyone accustomed to comparing it against a national health service abroad, so it warrants a careful reading: it is the combined total of three separate lists rather than a count of 1.44 million distinct individuals. A single insured person waiting for a specialist appointment, a diagnostic procedure and an operation can appear on all three at once, and official reporting uses the words “patients” and “cases” interchangeably.

The three lists break down as follows in the audit’s most recent snapshot. Roughly 204,622 people were awaiting surgery, some 362,356 were waiting for a specialty outpatient consultation, and the largest category by far, medical procedures, accounted for about 873,572 pending cases. The procedures list is where the backlog has grown most sharply, and it is the category that most distorts the topline number for readers who assume “waiting list” means “waiting for an operation.”

The audit’s central conclusion is not simply that the lists are long but that they are growing despite a dedicated plan to shrink them. Comparing December 2024 with March 2026, the report found the combined lists rose from 1,094,093 to 1,440,547 cases, an accumulated increase of 346,454 people, or 31.7 percent, over that roughly fifteen-month span. The auditors traced the persistent backlog to a shortage of medical specialists and nursing staff, the underuse of operating theatres, deficiencies in how the institution manages its own data, and problems of coordination across the hospital network.

Those failures are measured against a specific commitment. In May 2023 the CCSS board of directors approved what it called a roadmap to advance the management of waiting lists and of specialized health personnel, and it declared the matter an institutional emergency. The current audit concludes that the roadmap’s targets were not met, attributing to the administration a direct responsibility for the lack of effective results and pointing to weaknesses in the planning, execution and follow-up of the measures adopted.

It is on that basis that Aguilar has pressed the executive presidency for answers. In her letter she posed four questions: what corrective and complementary actions the administration will implement in response to the audit’s observations; what immediate steps it will take to relieve the bottleneck in specialized outpatient consultation; how it will ensure administrative accountability so that the shortcomings identified are not repeated; and which specific actions have already been set in motion on the audit’s recommendations, together with any preliminary results.

The deputy framed the stakes in human terms, stating in a translated remark that the deterioration shows the 2023 roadmap measures went unfulfilled, with serious consequences for users who face delays that harm their quality of life and allow their conditions to worsen.

The CCSS has publicly acknowledged the scale of the problem in recent months. Taylor has described the waiting lists as extremely difficult to reduce in the short term and has pointed to a strategy of strengthening emergency services to decongest hospitals, while the board earlier this year approved a new multi-year plan intended to distribute resources more evenly across the system. At the time of writing, the executive presidency had not issued a public response to Aguilar’s specific letter.

For the roughly five million people insured through the Caja, including foreign residents, retirees and residency applicants who pay monthly contributions and depend on the system for their care, the audit is less a single alarming statistic than a measure of how long the wait for specialist attention, diagnostics and surgery has become, and of whether the institution’s repeated promises to fix it are producing results.

World.title: Brandon Nakashima Wins First UTS Tournament in South America
World.content:
Brandon Nakashima claimed the title at the Ultimate Tennis Showdown’s first tournament in South America, defeating 17-year-old Brazilian Guto Miguel in a tightly contested final at Rio de Janeiro’s Maracanãzinho arena. The American completed a remarkable turnaround by beating Miguel 3-0 on Saturday, July 18, with quarter scores of 15-14, 17-14 and 15-13. Although the score appeared one-sided under the UTS system, all three quarters were decided by three points or fewer.

Nakashima earned $368,800 for winning UTS Rio, which was also his first appearance in the alternative tennis competition. “It was a great couple of days here,” Nakashima said after the final. “I really enjoyed my first experience here in Brazil and first UTS experience.” His path to the championship was far from straightforward. Nakashima opened the tournament with a 3-1 victory over top seed Francisco Cerúndolo before losing 3-2 to Miguel in Sudden Death during the round-robin stage.

The loss left Nakashima relying on quarter and point differentials to reach the semifinals as the fourth qualifier. Once there, he produced one of his best performances of the tournament, recovering from the loss of the opening quarter to defeat Nick Kyrgios 3-1. Nakashima won the final three quarters against Kyrgios by scores of 20-10, 17-12 and 20-10, ending the Australian’s bid for his first UTS title.

Miguel provided the tournament’s biggest surprise. The Brazilian teenager defeated Kyrgios, Nakashima and Cerúndolo during his run to the final, winning all three matches in Sudden Death. Miguel entered the event as a late replacement for Ugo Humbert but quickly became one of the central figures of the three-day competition.

He began by stunning Kyrgios 3-2, winning the first two quarters before surviving the Australian’s comeback. Miguel then defeated Nakashima by the same score and overcame Cerúndolo 3-2 in the semifinals after losing the opening quarter 23-11. Miguel had already enjoyed a breakthrough season after becoming the first Brazilian-born player to win the boys’ singles title at Roland Garros.

His victories over three established professionals in Rio offered another indication of his potential, even though Nakashima’s consistency proved too much in the final. Brazilian fans had initially expected João Fonseca to lead the home challenge. Fonseca defeated Tallon Griekspoor 3-1 in his UTS debut but was eliminated after Kyrgios swept him 3-0 in only 37 minutes.

Fonseca, Kyrgios and several other players finished the round-robin stage with one victory, leaving quarter and point differentials to determine the four semifinalists. Fonseca later defeated Corentin Moutet 3-1 in a classification match to finish sixth. Cerúndolo also recovered from an opening defeat, beating Cameron Norrie 3-0 to qualify for the semifinals. The Argentine eventually finished third after his Sudden Death loss to Miguel.

UTS Rio was held from July 16 through July 18 on an indoor hard court at the 11,000-seat Maracanãzinho. It marked the tour’s first appearance in South America and the second event of its 2026 season after an April tournament in Nîmes, France. The distinction is important: UTS had already staged an event in Latin America when Guadalajara, Mexico, hosted a tournament in 2025. Rio was the competition’s first stop on the South American continent.

Created by coach Patrick Mouratoglou, UTS replaces traditional games and sets with eight-minute quarters. The first player to win three quarters takes the match, while a 2-2 tie leads to Sudden Death, where a player must win two consecutive points. Players receive only one serve, fans may make noise during points and each competitor can use a bonus card that makes the next point worth three.

Rio also introduced a single eight-player round-robin table, with each player facing two opponents before the top four advanced to the semifinals. The event ultimately produced two significant results for UTS: a debut title for Nakashima and a breakthrough week for one of Brazil’s most promising teenagers.

World.title: Costa Rica Clears Legal Path for Recope to Move Beyond Petroleum
World.content:
Costa Rica’s Legislative Assembly has approved a reform that frees the state fuel company to work with energy sources other than oil for the first time, though drivers should not expect any immediate change in what they pay at the pump. Lawmakers gave final approval on July 16, to the Law to Promote the Energy Transition in the Fuel Sector, passing it in second debate with 54 votes in favor, none against and three legislators absent.

The bill had cleared its first debate two days earlier, capping an effort that had stalled repeatedly in the Assembly over more than a decade. It now goes to the executive branch for the president’s signature and publication before it can take effect. The reform rewrites the 1981 law governing the Refinadora Costarricense de Petróleo, or Recope, which until now was limited by statute to refining, transporting and selling petroleum and its derivatives.

Under the new framework, Recope keeps every one of those responsibilities but gains authority to research, acquire, import, export, process, store, transport and sell wholesale fuels derived from sources other than oil, with biofuels and green hydrogen named specifically. The law also brings natural gas within the company’s reach and broadens the mandate of the public services regulator, the Autoridad Reguladora de los Servicios Públicos, to cover the supply of gas, green hydrogen, biofuels, asphalts and naphthas.

Officials have stressed the limits of what the vote accomplishes. The measure works as a legal foundation rather than a finished project, and before Recope can enter any of these new markets it must present the Ministry of Environment and Energy, which sets national energy policy, with technical and operational studies showing that each step is warranted and consistent with that policy.

In the short term the law changes neither fuel prices nor the products available at service stations, and it does not mean green hydrogen or biofuels will go on sale anytime soon. To keep the reform from becoming a backdoor for fossil fuels, the text specifies that any Recope involvement in natural gas cannot be used to delay, replace or scale back investment in renewable energy.

Supporters frame the change as a matter of both economics and energy security. Costa Rica imports nearly all of the oil it burns, which leaves household budgets, business costs and public finances exposed to global price swings the country cannot control. That vulnerability stands in sharp contrast to the electricity sector, which drew 98.6 percent of its power from renewable sources in 2025, according to the Instituto Costarricense de Electricidad, after a two-year dip caused by drought. Even so, roughly 70 percent of the total energy the country consumes, transport fuel included, still comes from imported oil and gas, and that is the gap the reform is meant to begin closing.

The near-term consequence for drivers is a separate initiative that the new law reinforces but does not itself enact: the introduction of ethanol-blended gasoline. That plan, developed by the Ministry of Environment and Energy together with Recope, the services regulator and the University of Costa Rica, centers on an E10 blend, 10 percent ethanol mixed with 90 percent conventional fuel, the same standard sold across much of the United States. The blend would go first into premium gasoline, whose typically newer engines are designed to handle it, and Recope has already run pilot testing in the Pacific region to gauge both performance and public acceptance.

The timeline, however, has slipped. Authorities once aimed to have the blend reaching consumers by 2027, but the Ministry of Environment and Energy acknowledged in late June that the date is no longer assured. Recope must first make a series of purchases to produce the mixture, including sourcing the ethanol itself through an international tender that officials estimate will take about a year, and no firm calendar yet exists. Once the project’s implementing decrees are published, the company is expected to draw up a road map with clearer dates.

World.title: Belize City man sentenced to 6 months for stealing sister-in-law’s phone and unpaid court fines
World.content:
Belize City man sentenced to 6 months for stealing sister-in-law’s phone and unpaid court fines

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 21-year-old Belize City labourer has been sentenced to six months in prison after pleading guilty to stealing his sister-in-law’s cellphone.

Elwin Pitter, of Pitter Street, appeared unrepresented in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Monday and pleaded guilty to one count of theft.

Pitter admitted stealing a black Maxwest Nitro A65 cellphone valued at $295 from his 35-year-old sister-in-law on July 17, 2026. The phone had reportedly been kept inside a bureau drawer in Sandoval’s daughter’s bedroom.

The court sentenced Pitter to three months in prison for the theft. However, he also owed the court $1,000 in outstanding fines, which carried a default sentence of six months.

Pitter asked that the warrants for the unpaid fines be enforced because he was unable to pay the money. The Senior Magistrate ordered that the sentences run concurrently, meaning Pitter will serve the longer six-month term.

Police said Sandoval reported the cellphone missing after another relative allegedly saw Pitter holding a phone matching its description. Pitter was later taken to the Raccoon Street Police Station, where Sandoval identified him as her brother-in-law.

He was subsequently charged with theft and began serving his sentence on Monday.

World.title: Alexander Reynolds denied bail in attempted murder case involving police officer
World.content:
Alexander Reynolds denied bail in attempted murder case involving police officer

By Breaking Belize News Staff: High Court Justice Candace Nanton has denied bail to Belize Defence Force soldier Alexander Fredrick Reynolds, who is accused of shooting and injuring a police officer during a dispute at a repast in Lemonal Village.

Reynolds, 27, is charged with attempted murder, dangerous harm and use of deadly means of harm in connection with the June 22, 2026 shooting of Police Constable Pharon Muslar.

His attorney, Leeroy Banner, argued that Reynolds acted in self-defence and submitted that a proper police investigation would have shown that his client was defending himself during the confrontation.

Justice Nanton, however, noted that Reynolds has two previous convictions and is awaiting trial on two aggravated assault charges. The judge said that although the defence had advanced special reasons for bail, Reynolds’ criminal history and the seriousness of the latest allegations weighed against his release.

Police allege that Muslar was attending a repast when Reynolds pushed him and later fired a shot above his head. A struggle reportedly followed, during which Muslar was shot in the chest and shoulder.

According to the police account, Muslar used a machete to chop Reynolds during the confrontation. Both men were taken to the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital for treatment.

Reynolds was later charged and remanded to the Belize Central Prison. He was informed that he may reapply for bail after the required period has elapsed.

World.title: Ammunition cache and cannabis found hidden in abandoned house
World.content:
Ammunition cache and cannabis found hidden in abandoned house

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Acting on a tip, police in Orange Walk have uncovered a hidden stash of live ammunition and suspected cannabis inside an abandoned house on the Palmar Road, with no one around to answer for it.

According to the Belize Police Department, on Saturday, July 18, 2026, officers of the Orange Walk Quick Response Team, acting upon information received, conducted a search at an abandoned house in the area.

The hiding spot was a simple one. Searching under a yellow sponge, an officer found a transparent plastic containing 27 rounds of 9mm ammunition of assorted brands, along with a black magazine, and a separate plastic containing a green leafy substance suspected to be cannabis.

With no one in the immediate area, the items were retrieved and taken to the Orange Walk Police Station as found property.

At the station, the suspected cannabis was weighed at 93.13 grams. The drugs, the 27 rounds of ammunition, and the magazine were sealed in labelled envelopes and handed over through the chain of custody as found property.

No one has been arrested in connection with the find, and the matter remains under police attention.

The discovery of live 9mm rounds comes at a time of heightened concern over gun violence in the district, where expended 9mm shells featured in the recent drive-by shooting on San Antonio Road. Police have drawn no link between the found ammunition and any incident, but the cache is a reminder of the firearms and rounds circulating beyond legal hands.

Anyone with information on the stash is urged to contact the Orange Walk police or Crime Stoppers anonymously at 922.

World.title: High Court denies Akeem Ferguson bail for second time in attempted murder case
World.content:
High Court denies Akeem Ferguson bail for second time in attempted murder case

By Breaking Belize News Staff: High Court Justice Candace Nanton has denied bail to 30-year-old Akeem Fernando Ferguson for a second time in connection with the attempted murder of Ladyville resident Lionel Nigel Logan.

Ferguson is jointly charged with 21-year-old Brandon Christian Villamil over the April 11, 2026 shooting and stabbing of Logan on Henry Street in Ladyville. Villamil has since been granted bail by the High Court.

During Wednesday’s hearing, Ferguson’s attorney, David McKoy, argued that his client’s criminal record should not automatically prevent him from receiving bail and submitted that the court could impose strict conditions.

Justice Nanton, however, noted Ferguson’s previous convictions, including aggravated assault and a drug offence, and found that no special circumstances had been presented to justify granting bail before the usual statutory period had elapsed.

The judge reportedly stated that Ferguson’s previous conviction for an offence of a similar nature provided grounds for denying bail.

Ferguson was previously denied bail by Justice Nigel Pilgrim in June.

Police allege that Logan was walking on Henry Street on April 11 when he was approached by two men and became involved in an altercation. Logan was allegedly stabbed in the lower back and shot before the attackers fled.

Police said Logan identified Ferguson at the scene and later positively identified him as the person who shot him. Ferguson was detained later that night.

Ferguson and Villamil are scheduled to return to the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on August 24, 2026. Ferguson would have to make any further bail application before the High Court.

World.title: Watchman found dead at construction site he guarded
World.content:
Watchman found dead at construction site he guarded

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Police in the Orange Walk District have opened a death investigation after a watchman was found lifeless at the construction site where he worked in San Jose Nuevo Palmar village, with a post mortem examination expected to determine how he died.

According to the Belize Police Department, information was received by phone at about 10:15 p.m. on Friday, July 17, 2026, of a motionless body at a construction site off the Philip Goldson Highway. Officers responded to the location, a two-floor construction site, where they found the body of a man lying in a sideways position with injuries to his head and body.

The man was identified by a family member as 38-year-old Javier George Ewan, a Belizean watchman of San Jose Palmar Village, who worked as a security guard at the site, located directly in front of his home.

Initial investigations indicate that Ewan was last seen alive that morning, at about 10:00 a.m., when a relative visited him at the site and found him lying down and vomiting, reportedly after drinking the night before. He asked her to bring him food when she returned that night. When she came back at about 10:00 p.m., she entered the building and found him lying motionless on the floor. She immediately ran to a neighbour’s house for help in calling the police.

The scene was processed by scenes of crime personnel, and Ewan was transported to the Northern Regional Hospital, where he was pronounced dead at 12:10 a.m. on Saturday, July 18. His body awaits a post mortem examination, which is expected to establish the cause of death.

Police have not indicated whether foul play is suspected, and the matter remains under investigation. Anyone with information is asked to contact the Orange Walk police.

World.title: Woman choked and beaten at home as children looked on
World.content:
Woman choked and beaten at home as children looked on

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A 32-year-old Orange Walk Town woman endured a terrifying early-morning ordeal at her own home, reporting that her partner dragged her, beat her, and choked her behind a locked door while her two young sons were in the house, and a man is now detained pending charges.

According to the Belize Police Department, the woman, of the San Lorenzo Area, reported that on Saturday, July 18, 2026, at about 1:00 a.m., she was at home with her sons, ages 13 and 6, when her common-law husband arrived under the influence of alcohol and began behaving aggressively toward her.

She told police that when her elder son went outside and she stepped out to check on him, the man locked her out of the house, forcing her to beg to be let back in. When he opened the door, she reported, he grabbed her by her blouse and dragged her inside with both hands.

Fearing for her life and her children’s safety, she tried to leave with both boys. According to her report, the man followed, seized her arm, and flung her onto the verandah, where she fell to the floor. He then struck her several times about the head, forced her back inside, locked the door, and began choking her, causing her pain.

She managed to call the police, and the man was detained at the scene and escorted to the station.

Police recorded a statement from the woman, who requested court action. She was issued medico-legal forms, and a doctor certified her injuries as harm. A 32-year-old labourer of Trial Farm Village remains detained pending charges of harm. As he has not yet been formally charged, his identity is being withheld.

If you or someone you know is experiencing violence at home, help is available. You are encouraged to reach out to the police or a trusted support service. No one should face abuse alone, and children should never have to witness it.

World.title: Licensed gun holder charged with possession of firearm while under the influence
World.content:
Licensed gun holder charged with possession of firearm while under the influence

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A licensed firearm holder is before the court after police found him armed, injured and smelling of alcohol on the streets of Orange Walk Town over the weekend.

Police report that on Sunday, July 19, at about 11:00 p.m., officers on mobile patrol received information of an armed man with bloodstained clothing walking on Guadalupe Street. On arrival, officers observed a man in a white shirt and khaki three-quarter pants limping toward San Antonio Road with blood on his face and clothing, and with what appeared to be a gunshot wound and a cut to the right side of his forehead.

A search of the man turned up a black 9mm pistol loaded with nine live rounds, while a cross-body bag he was carrying contained a second magazine with three more rounds. The man produced a valid gun license and identified himself as Carlos Alfredo Castellanos, 38, according to initial police reports, a Belizean contractor of Yo Creek Village, Orange Walk District. Officers, however, detected a strong smell of alcohol on his breath, and he was detained for possession of a firearm while under the influence of alcohol before being taken to the Northern Regional Hospital for treatment.

Initial police investigation suggests that earlier the same night, Castellanos was involved in a struggle with other men at a gas station parking lot on the Belize Corozal Road, during which he allegedly fired a shot accidentally, injuring himself, before walking toward Guadalupe Street.

At the hospital, Castellanos agreed to provide a urine specimen, which was sealed as evidence in his presence. The firearm, two magazines and thirteen rounds were likewise sealed. Following his discharge, he was formally arrested and charged on Tuesday, July 21, with possession of a firearm while under the influence of drugs or alcohol. He was cautioned and chose to remain silent.

World.title: Man charged with wounding after knife incident at Nuevo San Juan football field
World.content:
Man charged with wounding after knife incident at Nuevo San Juan football field

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A 24-year-old laborer of Nuevo San Juan Village, Orange Walk District, has been arrested and charged with wounding following a weekend altercation at the village football field.

According to the report made to police, a 40-year-old Belizean laborer, also of Nuevo San Juan, was at the field around 4:40 p.m. on Saturday, July 18, painting it for a game along with other villagers when a man approached within about three feet of him. The man allegedly told him that he would not forget a previous misunderstanding involving the older man’s son, then pulled out a silver knife and advanced toward him.

The man reported that he moved backward and a struggle ensued, during which he managed to grab his attacker and take away the knife. He sustained a cut to his back, a cut to his left hand and a bite to his left underarm. He sought medical attention, and a doctor certified his injuries as wounding.

Initial checks in the village did not locate the suspect. On Monday, July 20, police swore to an information and complaint, obtained a warrant in the first instance, and formally arrested and charged Jorje David Mendez, 24, of Nuevo San Juan Village, with the crime of wounding. He was cautioned and remained silent. The complainant has requested court action.

World.title: ‘Highway robbery’
World.content:
New toll fees affecting motorists using the North-South Highway are expected to take effect at the end of the month.

“HIGHWAY robbery” is how Noel Williams, president of the Kingston Chapter of Jamaica Union of Travellers Association (JUTA) Tours, has described the impending toll road rate increases, which transport operators fear could impact their operations. The increases prompted more calls on Monday for the Government to step in.

JUTA representatives, in collaboration with Jamaica Cooperative Automobile & Limousine (JCAL) Tours Limited and other transport organisations, gathered at the Jamaica Pegasus hotel in New Kingston for a meeting on Monday, hoping to get an audience with representatives of the Ministry of Transport and the Toll Authority of Jamaica to share pressing concerns.

But despite being invited, according to Williams, there were no representatives from either group.

Williams told the Jamaica Observer that their no-show was a clear indication of the scant regard which they have for transport operators.

“We are saying to the Government and the Toll Authority, that we cannot any longer absorb this toll increase, because we are of the opinion that this is the most expensive toll anywhere in the world,” Williams said, expressing that many operators already find it difficult to pay fees for certain categories of vehicles on the toll and cannot manage any upward adjustment at this time.

The new toll fees, to affect motorists using the North-South Highway, are expected to take effect at the end of the month.

The Government has published the proposed new rates with a capped toll of $2,610 each way for Class 1 vehicles. Operators of Class 2 vehicles would pay $5,220 one way, while the proposed toll for Class 3 vehicles, including larger trucks, is $7,830.

Williams recommended that the move be put on pause for a year, to allow for consultation among stakeholders.

“I think this is highway robbery by the Toll Authority, and the Government sits there completely complacent and they do nothing about it. With that said, we are asking the Government to have dialogue with the Toll Authority. We are having a serious issue already with what we are paying for one coaster bus to go from Kingston to St Ann and back. One round trip [now] costs bus operators $15,000. We will be asked to pay $15,680 when the new rate is introduced. If we are to do that, then we have to keep on passing on these increases to the passengers, who already have been complaining about what we are charging now,” he said.

The president said that numerous letters have been written to policymakers, but they have never responded.

He specifically referred to some representatives of the Toll Authority as being very disrespectful.

“We sent letters to the Toll Authority about another bus we have in the system, which is the new type of Hiace bus. It has a longer front than the older one, and hence when these buses go to the toll, they have to pay the same money as what the coaster pays,” he said.

“And when you question it, they are telling you that it’s because of the length of the bus. Nothing is put in place to accommodate the service that we provide in terms of transportation. And also the toll road barely has any lights. With all of this, we have to be paying so much money…

“We are definitely calling on the Government to sit and have a look at the situation and to renegotiate the contract so as to benefit the Jamaican people. A lot more people would use the toll as well, if it was much cheaper, but these people are just thinking about collecting money… they’re not thinking about us.“

Williams lamented that those operators who opt to take the alternative route from Kingston to St Ann cannot do so because those roads are deplorable. He appealed to the Government to have these alternative routes fixed.

“Right now, I believe it is a breach of people’s constitutional rights because they have been literally forced to use the toll, which is costly. The original roads are there, but they are not comfortable for people to drive on.

Meanwhile, Lorraine “Oscar” Finnikin, president of the All Voice Taxi Association, was among transport association heads present at the meeting.

He told the Observer that he attended to show solidarity with the JUTA president.

“They have tried their best over the years to not pass on the cost to their passengers but as it is now, they don’t have any choice,” he said.

“There are a lot of overhead expenses facing the public passenger vehicle sector. One is the cost of gas due to the situation in the Middle East, then there are overall expenses through maintenance, operational costs and service parts. With the increase in the toll fees, it has reached a stage where it is just too much for the sector to bear anymore.”

In a statement last Thursday, Minister of Transport Daryl Vaz acknowledged the concerns expressed by motorists, but explained that the concerning toll rates were yet another example of the former People’s National Party Administration entering into a less than favourable toll deal, which does not yield any tangible advantages for the Jamaican populace.

Vaz said the toll agreement binds current and future governments to its terms, but said the Government was moving to have discussions towards arriving at a more favourable and affordable toll cost for Jamaicans.

“However, the binding agreement entered by the former administration has put us in a position where the concessionaire has to agree to whatever we suggest in order for it to be implemented,” Vaz said.

He also said suggestions that Government pay off the toll operators in an effort to discontinue the unsustainable rise in rates, were impractical.

The Concession Agreement for the North-South Highway (Caymanas to Ocho Rios) was executed in June 2012 under a 50-year Build-Finance-Operate-Transfer arrangement.

World.title: Sweltering heat threatens egg industry
World.content:
President of the Jamaica Egg Farmers Association Mark Campbell on his egg farm in Trelawny on Monday. (Photo: Horace Hines)

FALMOUTH, Trelawny — President of the Jamaica Egg Farmers Association (JEFA) Mark Campbell is urging members to protect their flock from an ongoing heatwave that is taking a toll on the industry, even as it recovers from the double whammy of hurricanes Beryl and Melissa.

Speaking with reporters on his farm in Trelawny Monday afternoon, Campbell noted that prolonged high temperatures have been especially hard on farmers along the island’s south coast, where laying hens have died from heat stress. He said farmers have reported losses of hundreds of birds, representing millions of dollars in replacement costs, plus income lost from reduced egg production.

“This year, 2026, the egg industry has come under sweltering heat, and a number of farmers, particularly those on the south side of the island — St Elizabeth, and Clarendon — they have suffered heavy losses. One farmer over there told me that he has lost over 700 chickens because of the heat that is on the land. And another farmer on the same south side of the island lost over 600 chickens. Now, those two figures run into millions of dollars just in the cost to purchase these chickens. And then the opportunity that has been lost is significant,” said Campbell, who is also operator of Campbell’s Egg Farm Limited in Trelawny.

He explained that laying hens perform best at temperatures between 60 and 70 degrees Fahrenheit and become increasingly vulnerable as temperatures approach about 106 degrees Fahrenheit, which is their body temperature.

The JEFA president is recommending that farmers install irrigation systems or lawn sprinklers on the roofs of bird houses to help reduce temperatures during the hottest part of the day, between 10:00 am and 2:00 pm.

“The heat that radiates off these roofs and goes down to the chickens is what really hurts them. Once the temperature comes up to the body temperature of the chicken, the bird is going to die,” he explained.

Campbell pointed out that while temperature-controlled poultry houses provide greater protection, many local producers may not be able to afford them. To compensate, he encouraged farmers constructing new poultry houses to incorporate adequate roof height and insulation.

Other advice provided by the JEFA president involve feeding birds during cooler hours of the morning, adjusting lighting schedules to encourage earlier feeding, and providing vitamin supplements to help maintain feed intake.

“We have to start looking at how we are going to prepare for periods of elevated heat because laying birds cannot deal with heat at all,” he urged.

Campbell said chickens experiencing heat stress often reduce their feed intake, resulting in lower egg production. He added that production losses could range from 50 to 70 per cent if birds remain exposed to excessive heat. He said farmers in cooler, mountainous areas have not reported similar levels of losses because of lower temperatures and stronger winds.

Despite the challenges being faced by some farmers, Campbell cautiously said he does not expect any scarcity of eggs this year as replacement birds are entering production.

“I hate to make forecasts about production because so many I have made in the past have been wrong. But this is the period between now and the end of the year where a significant number of new birds are going in the field, and if the farmers pay attention to good practices, I do not see a shortage because of the heat at the moment,” he said.

World.title: Supporting acts, fireworks fuel A Taste of Sumfest
World.content:
A section of the Sumfest crowd at Plantation Cove in St Ann.(Photo: Garfield Robinson)

Although thousands of patrons from across Jamaica and the Diaspora travelled to Plantation Cove in St Ann to witness the highly anticipated reunion of dancehall rivals Vybz Kartel and Mavado on the same stage at A Taste of Sumfest, the night’s supporting acts proved they were more than capable of delivering memorable moments of their own.

From explosive pyrotechnics and dazzling fireworks to energetic choreography and crowd-pleasing performances, the annual Reggae Sumfest warm-up event transformed Plantation Cove into a pulsating celebration of dancehall culture long before the night’s main attraction.

The night’s entertainment included music from selectors Code Red Sound, C Note Sound, DJ Mac and Baba, Boom Boom, DJ Ashile, DJ Tom & Reavers, and Ricky Platinum, who kept the energy high with a carefully curated mix of dancehall anthems that had patrons dancing from the early hours of the evening.

One of the standout performances came from Ayetian, whose appearance was especially significant as it followed his impressive seven Caribbean Music Awards nominations. Clearly determined to celebrate the milestone with fans, the artiste delivered an energetic set featuring crowd favourites Wah Yo Deh Pon, Tip, and Balance, with the audience enthusiastically singing along to every word.

Recording artiste Marcy Chin also commanded the stage with a bold and unapologetic performance that reaffirmed her place among dancehall’s elite. Addressing critics who questioned her repeated appearances at Sumfest, Chin declared that, “Sumfest is my home,” before reminding patrons that, “It nuh tek bwoy fi do music,” earning loud cheers for her statement celebrating women’s place in the male-dominated genre.

Dressed in a striking red velvet, long-sleeved monokini emblazoned with her name on the sleeves, sheer fishnet stockings, and thigh-high boots, Chin captivated audiences from the moment she stepped onstage. She was joined by a dancer from France and a male performer during Gimme More, creating one of the night’s most visually engaging performances. She also drew laughter and applause after delivering a cheeky freestyle playfully addressing long-standing rumours linking her romantically to Downsound Entertainment CEO Joe Bogdanovich.

Dancehall artiste Shawn Storm was equally well received, earning several pull-ups for his hit Itch Scratch, originally released in December 2025. The humorous track, which marked a departure from his usual catalogue centred on women and relationships, has grown into a fan favourite, with patrons repeatedly demanding rewinds.

He also performed songs including Empire and My Life, while encouraging fans to continue representing Gaza, reaffirming his unwavering loyalty to the movement that has defined much of his career.

Shauna Controlla, Youngwildapache, and Jamal each maintained the night’s momentum, delivering energetic sets that kept patrons engaged.

Veteran deejay Harry Toddler delivered one of the night’s most emotional moments as he paid tribute to late reggae artiste Fantan Mojah, who died on July 14 at age 49. The heartfelt tribute prompted patrons to observe a moment of silence, creating a touching contrast to the night’s otherwise high-octane energy. It marked the first of two tributes to the late singer during the event.

Another memorable appearance came from cultural icon Queen Ifrica, who explained why she was included on a show centred on Gaza founder Vybz Kartel.

Reflecting on the height of the infamous Gully-Gaza rivalry, she reminded the audience of the role she played in promoting peace.

“Me a the bravest fi stand up inna the middle of the war and tell dem fi look out fi the children, and we still a dweet in 2026,” she said, drawing loud applause from sections of the crowd.

The event attracted visitors from several countries, many of whom described the experience as unlike anything they had witnessed before.

“I flew from Toronto just for Sumfest, and every performer gave us a reason to dance. The energy, the music, the fireworks — it wasn’t just a concert; it was a celebration of who we are,” one patron told the Jamaica Observer.

First-time visitor Marcus Bennett from London, England, said the event exceeded his expectations.

“I’ve watched dancehall online for years, but nothing compares to seeing it in Jamaica. The passion of the performers and the connection they have with the crowd is incredible. This culture is alive, authentic and unforgettable,” he added.

World.title: World Cup champs Spain get heroes’ welcome home
World.content:
Spain fans pack Cibeles Square in Madrid on July 20, 2026, as they await the arrival of Spain’s players one day after the national football team won their second FIFA World Cup title with a 1-0 victory against Argentina. Spain’s World Cup winners come back home to a heroes’ welcome in Madrid where a reported one million fans showed up to greet them after a night of raucous celebrations across the country. (Photo: AFP)

MADRID, Spain (AFP) — New World Cup champions Spain began their celebration parade on an open-top bus through the streets of Madrid on Monday, early evening.

Local authorities told AFP that a jubilant crowd of over a million people turned out to celebrate.

The players, some shirtless, others holding drinks, set off on their procession under a blazing sun, along the main arteries in the city centre where a sea of fans in red and yellow were waiting, with the destination Cibeles square.

After flying back from the United States to Madrid, the players were received by King Felipe VI and the royal family, and then Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, before kicking off the parade.

Players passed around the gleaming World Cup trophy and waved to a sea of delighted Spain fans in red and yellow, the day after defeating Argentina 1-0 in extra-time in New Jersey.

Ferran Torres’s strike in extra-time was enough to bring Spain their second World Cup, following a first victory in 2010.

“You have shown your grit, your resilience and your courage, always backed by your technical skill, your control and command of the game, combining head and heart,” the king told La Roja’s stars, who were dressed in suits but changed to more casual clothing for their parade on a hot summer’s day.

“Kings of the world” ran the words on the front of their vehicle, with fans chanting “champions” to their heroes.

Spain captain Rodri held the World Cup trophy aloft at the top of the stairs as he descended from the Iberia plane that flew the team home after clinching their second star.

Later at Moncloa, Rodri said this was the crowning achievement of his career.

“I’ve always said it, winning with your country is the most beautiful thing there is, above all a World Cup,” he said.

“This generation grew up watching [Iker] Casillas and [Andres] Iniesta lift the cup and that we can do it today is the biggest thing you can do in football.”

Many younger supporters were not yet born when Iniesta’s extra-time goal against the Netherlands secured Spain’s first World Cup in South Africa 16 years ago.

Match-winner Torres joked he was “flying, literally” after the team returned from the United States after beating Argentina in New Jersey.

“I’m very happy to see how excited all of the children are… [and] to have the parade and celebrate with all of the Spaniards,” he said.

Spain’s World Cup winners bus parade started at Moncloa before heading towards Cibeles square, where hordes of fans had reserved their spots hours in advance.

A ceremony involving the players and a concert will then be held at the square, the traditional gathering point for celebrations by the Spanish national team and its supporters. Over 120,000 people were estimated to be waiting there.

Spain’s women’s side won the World Cup in 2023, meaning for the first time a country has both trophies at the same time.

In 2030, Spain will defend their crown on home soil, as one of the World Cup hosts along with Portugal and Morocco.

“It’s two for two,” said Prime Minister Sanchez, of Spain’s record in World Cup finals. “Why not dream of a third in 2030, especially with Spain as hosts?”

The Spanish press was running out of superlatives to describe its heroes after they overcame favourites France in the semi-finals before downing Argentina.

“The kings of all-time!” wrote Marca, celebrating a “second star that will now be stitched onto the Spanish jersey after yet another masterclass in collective play”.

Argentina, despite the presence of all-time great Lionel Messi, failed to create clear chances against Spain’s well-organised and more positive side in the final.

Messi had a sensational World Cup but drifted through the final like a ghost, shedding tears at the end.

“The pain is immense, and it’s going to be hard for this wound to heal,” Messi wrote on Instagram.

In Madrid, tears also flowed on Monday night, but they were tears of joy.

World.title: A host of concerns
World.content:
An architectural design of the National Stadium redevelopment project unveiled by the Sports Ministry in 2025.

DESPITE FIFA expressing concerns about Jamaica’s readiness to host matches at the Women’s World Cup in 2031, Jamaica Football Federation (JFF) President Michael Ricketts says he’s confident the country will secure hosting rights, with an official announcement expected in November.

Last October, Jamaica joined the USA, Mexico, and Costa Rica in launching a joint bid to host the 2031 tournament, which would mark the first time a FIFA World Cup would be staged across four countries.

A FIFA delegation visited the island in February, inspecting facilities including the National Stadium and meeting with representatives of the Jamaica Football Federation and the Government. Hosts were initially expected to be confirmed at the FIFA Congress in Canada in April, but the world governing body postponed the announcement until November 23.

Despite the delay, Sports Minister Olivia Grange told Parliament last month that Jamaica had been selected as one of the hosts, although FIFA has yet to officially confirm the successful bid.

FIFA Consultant and Women’s Football Division Advisor Jose Andres Portabella told the Jamaica Observer that while FIFA is enthusiastic about Jamaica hosting matches, there is no guarantee the country will be selected.

“I couldn’t be more excited about the possibility of the World Cup coming to Jamaica in 2031,” he said. “FIFA wants to see football all over the world. Next year, the 2027 FIFA Women’s World Cup will be held in Brazil, which shows the first time ever that the World Cup goes to South America. It’s going to be a fantastic performance by players, by fans, incredible stadiums, so why not Jamaica in 2031 with the US, and Mexico, and Costa Rica?”

“There’s a lot of work to be done, let’s be clear. We have had a delegation that’s come here to visit already [so] you (Jamaica) know what you need to do. The infrastructure is a key component of hosting the Women’s World Cup so we’re hopeful, we’re excited, and we’re looking forward to seeing what Jamaica does to bring this tournament to the island.”

It’s understood that USA and Mexico are almost guaranteed to host the tournament given their established infrastructure, some of which was on display during the recently concluded FIFA Men’s World Cup. Costa Rica is also reportedly well positioned, having hosted FIFA youth tournaments including the Under-20 Women’s World Cup in 2022.

Jamaica has never hosted a FIFA tournament but it has staged several Concacaf competitions, most notably the 2019 Concacaf Gold Cup, becoming the first Caribbean nation to do so.

Although the country faces a nervous four-month wait for the Women’s World Cup decision, Ricketts told the

Observer he’s optimistic Jamaica will host matches after seeing the level of work and commitment that has gone into the bid.

“When the FIFA team came here we had intense discussions with the contractors who would be doing the renovation and the refurbishing of the National Stadium, and they would have done a presentation which, based on the body language from the FIFA reps, we’re pretty satisfied and pretty confident that we will be in a position to host the Women’s World Cup in 2031,” he said.

“Minister Grange did make an announcement in Parliament. She was pretty confident and so am I, and I want to believe that we will be one of the four countries that will be hosting the 2031 Women’s World Cup.”

The redevelopment of the National Stadium, which is intended to meet FIFA standards, is expected to begin in July or August 2027, with United Kingdom-based Ryder Architecture and global consulting firm CAA Icon currently completing the detailed design phase, after the feasibility study and concept design.

Last summer Grange said the redevelopment would be completed in 2029. However, during World Athletics President Seb Coe’s visit to Jamaica in January she said she could not provide a completion date, although she was “conscious that we have to be finished by a particular time”.

Ricketts says FIFA would still allow Jamaica to host the World Cup even if the National Stadium’s full upgrade isn’t completed by 2031.

“I would want to think that even if — and I’m hoping that it doesn’t happen — the stadium is not completely refurbished we still would be in a position to host,” he said. “Of course our stadium is, maybe, archaic but when you look at some other stadiums around Concacaf, it is still not the worst. And I would think if we can’t get it fully refurbished and we can do minor repairs and minor adjustments, we still would be in a position to host the World Cup.

“It’s unfortunate that we really do not have options like some countries do but this is our main stadium — and, of course, it’s probably the only stadium that could really host a World Cup game — but it’s not that bad. And I don’t think FIFA would come down [hard, even though] they would not be totally happy if the stadium was not refurbished and ready, because they were given some kind of a guarantee from the contractors.

“It’s out of the hands of the JFF and out of the hands of even Concacaf but the Government has given an indication. And, having had discussions with the contractors who did a presentation to the FIFA group in the presence of the IPL [Independence Park Limited] personnel, persons representing Minister Grange’s office, the JFF and Concacaf… we are pretty confident that we will host this major tournament — probably the biggest thing ever to happen in local football, maybe in local sport.”

World.title: More Than Practice: Why Your Wedding Rehearsal Matters
World.content:
More than a run-through, the wedding rehearsal is a chance to gather loved ones and savour the moments before “I do.”

When couples think about wedding planning they often focus on the venue, flowers, menu, music, and décor. The wedding rehearsal, however, is sometimes treated as an optional extra or simply another item to check off the list. In reality, it is one of the most meaningful moments of the entire wedding journey.

A wedding rehearsal is about much more than practising how to walk down the aisle. It is an opportunity to slow down, gather the people who matter most, and prepare emotionally and practically for one of life’s biggest milestones.

For many couples the rehearsal is the first time everything begins to feel real. The ceremony space is set, family and friends have arrived, and suddenly the months — or even years — of planning come together. It becomes a quiet pause before the excitement of the wedding day. As you stand where you will exchange your vows, the reality often sinks in: Tomorrow, you begin a brand-new chapter together as husband and wife.

It is also a rare opportunity to spend quality time with your closest family members and wedding party before the celebrations become a whirlwind. Wedding days move incredibly quickly. From hair and make-up appointments to photography, greeting guests, speeches, dancing, and countless other moments, couples often find they have very little uninterrupted time with the people they love most.

The rehearsal creates a more intimate setting in which conversations are unhurried, laughter comes naturally, and emotions can be shared without the pressure of a full schedule. Parents offer words of wisdom, siblings share stories, lifelong friends toast the journey ahead, and everyone has the chance to simply be present together before the festivities begin.

Beyond the emotional value, a rehearsal is essential for ensuring your ceremony runs smoothly.

Every member of the wedding party should know exactly where to be, when to move, and where to stand. From the procession order to the recessional, everyone should understand their role. This eliminates uncertainty and helps avoid awkward pauses, confusion, or unnecessary delays during the ceremony.

The rehearsal also allows everyone to become familiar with the venue. Questions such as where parents will be seated, how the bridal party will enter, where the officiant will stand, how bouquets will be handed off, and where readers or musicians will be positioned can all be answered ahead of time.

For couples who are nervous about speaking in front of a crowd, rehearsing provides confidence. Walking through the ceremony once beforehand helps reduce anxiety because the setting already feels familiar. Instead of wondering what comes next, you can focus on the moment itself.

Your wedding planner and officiant also benefit from the rehearsal. It gives them the opportunity to coordinate timing, fine-tune logistics, answer last-minute questions, and identify any adjustments before guests arrive. A small issue discovered during rehearsal is far easier to resolve than one encountered during the ceremony.

One of the simplest pieces of advice I give every wedding party is this: Please pay attention during the rehearsal.

It may seem obvious, but conversations, mobile phones, and side discussions can easily distract everyone. The more focused the group is during those 30 to 60 minutes, the more relaxed and seamless the ceremony will feel the following day. Listen carefully, ask questions if you’re unsure, and remember where you’re meant to stand and when you’re meant to move. Those few moments of attention make an enormous difference.

If you’re planning a destination wedding, rehearsals become even more valuable. Many guests and members of the wedding party may be unfamiliar with the venue, so walking through the ceremony helps everyone feel comfortable and confident in the space.

When the wedding day finally arrives, you’ll be grateful you took the time to rehearse. Everyone knows where to go, transitions happen naturally, and the ceremony flows effortlessly. Instead of worrying about logistics, you can focus on what truly matters — looking into the eyes of the person you’re about to marry and embracing one of the most unforgettable moments of your life.

A wedding rehearsal is not simply a practice session. It is the bridge between planning a wedding and beginning a marriage — a chance to reflect, connect, prepare, and fully appreciate the incredible journey that starts the very next day.
