World.title: Iran war delays upgrades to Queensland’s Triple Zero phone system
World.content:
A project to upgrade Queensland's Triple Zero (000) phone system has been delayed until next year, with the closure of the Strait of Hormuz being a contributing factor.

The Queensland Ambulance Service has been leading the project, called Triple Zero (000) Telephony Refresh, that was launched in March 2024.

The high-priority upgrades were due to be completed this December.

A QAS spokesperson said it is "currently scheduled for completion by the end of March 2027" due to "third-party service provider delays".

The ABC understands that parts for the upgrade had been delayed due to the war in Iran and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

QAS received a Triple Zero every 24 seconds in the first three months of 2026. (ABC News: Glen Armstrong)

"Current Triple Zero operations will not be impacted by the project's extension," the spokesperson said in a statement to the ABC.

The $12.7 million project aims to refresh the technology infrastructure to support more than one million emergency calls received every year from across the state.

Across Australia, emergency calls initially go to a nominated emergency call service operator, which is currently Telstra.

From there, the call centre operator, run by the telco, asks if the emergency relates to ambulance, fire or police before transferring the call to the relevant state-based emergency service.

The upgrades are set to offer better support to medical dispatchers. (ABC News: Chris Gillette)

In the last financial year, QAS continued to experience growth in demand for services.

In the first three months of this year, QAS received a Triple Zero call every 24 seconds.

The latest performance data showed almost 95 per cent of Triple Zero calls were answered in 10 seconds in 2025/26.

The upgrades would modernise the call delivery system to ensure emergency calls are answered on a more reliable and contemporary platform that offers better support to medical dispatchers.

The QAS spokesperson said the project was "focused on delivering an improved platform for frontline staff to continue providing world-class care to the communities we serve".

'Closely monitored' project status

Last October, Queensland's government Digital Projects Dashboard marked the project with an "amber" status for "closely monitored".

A QAS spokesperson says current Triple Zero operations have not be impacted by the delays. (ABC News: Chris Gillette)

"The project is reporting amber due to finance as the cost estimates of proposed solutions are higher-than-anticipated," the dashboard said.

"The project team is working with governance to confirm system scope and functionality requirements.

"It is worth noting that the potential solutions are expected to deliver greater overall value than initially planned," it said.

It returned to a "green" status, indicating it was "on track," in November.

A QAS spokesperson told the ABC in July the project's "approved expenditure of $12.74 million is on track".

A spokesperson for Ambulance Services Minister Tim Nicholls say the upgrades would enhance service capabilities. (ABC News: William Murray)

A spokesperson for Ambulance Services Minister Tim Nicholls said the "essential project" had been "a long-time coming" since the Public Safety Business Agency was disbanded in 2021.

"This upgrade to our lifesaving Triple Zero services is just one of the ways the Crisafulli Government is enhancing and growing the Queensland Ambulance Service capabilities," the spokesperson said in a statement to the ABC.

They noted earlier this year the state government opened an $8.31 million QAS Clinical Hub at Kedron in Brisbane.

The hub provides secondary triage and health navigation for people after they've called Triple Zero.

World.title: JackJumpers coach shares advice on how to win over Tasmanians
World.content:
Visibility will be key for incoming Tasmania Devils coach Ken Hinkley, according to the man who led the state to National Basketball League glory in 2024.

JackJumpers coach Scott Roth has implored Hinkley to hit the road, listen to the locals and find out what Tasmania means to the people who call it home when he commences the role from November.

"This state is big and people want to see you," Roth said.

"They want to see you in the coffee shops, they want to see you in the gas station, they want to see you going through the supermarket or wherever.

" You've gotta be out there pressing the flesh. "

US-import Scott Roth coached the JackJumpers in their first NBL season. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Roth, who hails from Ohio and arrived in Tasmania in 2021 to coach the JackJumpers in their first NBL season, believes his willingness to travel to all corners of the state earned him the trust of the Tasmanian public.

He also believes Tasmanians will be able to easily identify with "Camperdown Ken" who comes from country Victoria.

"It's about checking your ego at the door," Roth advised.

" Most people are casual and easygoing. They don't like flash and dash, they like normal. It's a working-class environment. "

Scott Roth says his willingness to travel to all corners of the state earned him the trust of the Tasmanian public. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

So highly regarded is Roth for what he has achieved in Tasmania in just five years, he says he was contacted by hopeful Devils coaching candidates, looking to tap into the Tasmanian psyche.

"I talked to quite a few people who reached out to me about interviewing for the job and what they were looking for here and just trying to pick my brain," Roth said.

"I'm available, obviously, and my phone number got out, so a few people called and asked what's going on down there?

" How can I get this job? "

The Devils will build a playing list from scratch before entering the AFL in 2028. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

'Humble' recruits needed, Roth says

Hinkley will officially commence his five-year stint with the Devils in November.

He will help oversee the formation of a playing list, and assist in picking key support staff ahead of the Devils' AFL entry in 2028.

A number of players he coached at Port Adelaide will be out of contract at the end of next year, including defender Miles Bergman and star forward Mitch Georgiades.

Port Adelaide chief executive Matthew Richardson said he had no fears of a Hinkley-led raid on his club, and backed his players to re-sign.

"We congratulated Ken yesterday. Now he's an opposition coach, so we move forward," Mr Richardson said.

" We back our environment and the culture we're creating. "

Hinkley has been billed as an ambassador, charged with coaching a football team and uniting a state. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

Roth says his JackJumpers teams have been built in the image of the Tasmanian people, and the state's new AFL club should also recruit accordingly.

"It's a working-class state, so you need workers. You need humble. You don't want guys flying around in bars and doing crazy things," Roth said.

"I find that's what works here … The more humble a player you can get, with a high character, the better off you'll be."

Ken Hinkley is a former Port Adelaide coach. (ABC News: Owain Stia-James)

Devils 'nailed it' with Hinkley appointment

The football world has overwhelmingly endorsed Tasmania's decision to appoint Hinkley, over high-profile contenders John Longmire and Nathan Buckley.

Ken Hinkley announced as inaugural Tasmania Devils coach The former Port Adelaide coach is formally announced as the inaugural coach of the Tasmania Devils.

Melbourne captain Max Gawn told Triple M he would "definitely" play for Ken Hinkley, and that the Devils had "nailed it".

On Channel 7's The Agenda Setters program, Kane Cornes, who played two seasons under Hinkley, said: "He gets you feeling like you want to run through a brick wall for him".

"If you're a parent of one of these 17 or 18-year-olds who are going to go down to Tassie on this adventure, you should feel like your son is in really safe hands," Cornes said.

Geelong Brownlow medallist Jimmy Bartel echoed those sentiments on Channel 9's Footy Furnace.

"He can coach the footy 'dorks' and coach the footy rogues as well, and bring it all together," he said.

Iconic Tasmanian footballer and member of the AFL's Team of the Century, Royce Hart, said the Devils had selected the best candidate for the job.

"He was the best-qualified person who could coach Tasmania. They've done a good job, but the proof will be in the pudding.

"He came from Geelong, more or less a Tasmanian-type town, went to the Gold Coast and then did well at Port [Adelaide]."

Hinkley will officially commence his five-year stint with the Devils in November. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Hart, who holds "legend" status in the Australian football hall of fame, said Hinkley would feel at home in Tasmania.

"Well, you've only got to breathe in the air," Hart said.

World.title: Woman's family wrongly told she was dead in hospital identity error
World.content:
Michelle Buckley vividly remembers the moment she was told she was supposed to be dead.

It was a Saturday night in May, and the 54-year-old had been making pizzas at home when her former partner received a message.

"He said: 'Oh my God. You're never going to believe what it says,'" Ms Buckley said.

"He brought his computer over, and there was a message from my brother's girlfriend saying, 'I'm really sorry to hear that Michelle's passed away'.

"I just felt like time stood still. I couldn't believe what I was hearing."

Minutes later, Ms Buckley's phone rang. It was her family.

They were shocked when she answered.

"I could hear them crying … My poor older aunty and my cousins, everybody had been notified," Ms Buckley said.

" I can't tell you what it's like. It's so surreal to be told that you're dead. "

Ms Buckley would quickly learn that Queensland Police, at the behest of Victoria Police, had knocked on her brother's door and had told him his sister was dead.

From there, word spread rapidly.

Ms Buckley said the ordeal had left her family shaken and traumatised, especially after the death of her parents a couple of years earlier.

"I feel ashamed and guilty, in a weird way, that my family went through this," Ms Buckley said.

"My aunt had to go and stay with my cousins for a week or so because she was so upset."

That same night, Ms Buckley contacted Victoria Police to inform them that she was, in fact, not dead and also to understand how the mistake had been made.

She was stunned when she learnt the body of a woman had been found in Melbourne's west, with patient documents from Werribee Mercy Hospital identifying her as Michelle Buckley.

The health record mix-up

Ms Buckley called Werribee Mercy Hospital twice the following day for an explanation. She was told nobody could speak to her and that she needed to contact police.

It would be another 10 days before she finally heard back.

"I was just beside myself, I thought 'Please, just tell me what happened,'" Ms Buckley said.

Werribee Mercy Hospital says it's investigating the incident. (ABC News: Margaret Paul)

Ms Buckley's anxiety only intensified when she checked her medical information on online portal My Health Record and realised the deceased woman's medical history had been mixed in with her own.

Ms Buckley's health record, seen by the ABC, showed various hospital appointments and medical tests belonging to the other woman, dating back months.

To make matters worse, Ms Buckley had also been undergoing medical treatment.

"I thought, 'Oh my God, I've had so many tests and scans, and some of them the same as this other person,'" Ms Buckley said.

"I thought, 'Have I been given the right results?'"

Ms Buckley has never received treatment from Werribee Mercy Hospital, despite living in Werribee, but has previously received a referral.

She considers herself fortunate that she did not attend the hospital while her medical history had been combined with the other woman's.

In an email sent two weeks after she first contacted the hospital, a Mercy Health representative confirmed the misidentification to Ms Buckley.

"You would have learnt from police that another consumer with a very similar name has been managed wrongly under your own name," the email said. "This resulted in your Mercy file having new entries added that were not related to yourself."

Hospital admits it was aware of mistaken identity

Last month, Ms Buckley sat down for an open disclosure meeting with a representative from Mercy Health to discuss her case.

Open disclosure is a formal discussion between healthcare providers and a patient, or their family, that occurs when a patient has experienced harm while receiving care.

Do you know more about this story or others like it? Contact Leanne Wong at wong.leanne@abc.net.au

at If your information is sensitive, you can also reach her at leanne_wong12@proton.me

During the meeting, the hospital representative admitted to Ms Buckley that the other woman had, on four occasions prior to her death, informed staff that her personal details were incorrect, but that no action was taken.

The deceased woman had been in contact with Werribee Mercy Hospital and Mercy's community team for about six months, and had been misidentified from the very start.

Her name and date of birth were said to have been similar to Ms Buckley's.

She had been homeless.

"I'm devastated for the woman who's passed away," Ms Buckley said.

"I hope she was treated in the right way. I don't know if they were using my records."

A spokesperson for Victoria Police told the ABC the deceased was later identified as a 55-year-old woman, one year older than Ms Buckley.

Her body had been found by passers-by outside a Tarneit residence on May 13, and her death was not being treated as suspicious.

"The woman was initially misidentified by police as a 54-year-old Werribee woman as a result of documents located in possession of the deceased woman," a police spokesperson said.

"A notification was made to the Werribee woman's family before she was found to be alive and well."

'Never seen a case like this before'

Ms Buckley has since hired law firm Slater and Gordon to investigate not only how the misidentification initially occurred, but how it was able to continue for so long.

Public liability lawyer Kieren McKenzie said the focus would be on understanding the full scale of the alleged privacy breach, a process which could take months.

"The simple fact is, I've never seen a case like this before," Mr McKenzie said.

"I know Slater and Gordon certainly haven't seen a case like this before.

"It's so rare and so novel that it's almost as if, in terms of investigating this claim, we'll have to do things differently and do almost a bespoke investigation."

Lawyer Kieren McKenzie says his client's ordeal highlights the importance of rigorous processes around personal data. (ABC News: Richard Sydenham)

Mr McKenzie said the case, which he described as being akin to a "Hollywood script", highlighted the importance of ensuring personal information was looked after with care and respect.

"More than just something that has been written down on paper, what's happened here shows the actual human impact of how things like this can go wrong, and how they can affect people such as Michelle," Mr McKenzie said.

Hospital and police apologise for mistake

In a statement to the ABC, a spokesperson for Mercy Health apologised for the "mistaken identification", but did not address questions about what measures the hospital took to verify patient identities, or why the deceased woman's details weren't updated when she allegedly raised concerns.

"We are deeply sorry to the patients and family involved and to everyone affected. Every patient has the right to expect that their identity and health information are managed safely and accurately," the spokesperson said. "We are undertaking a thorough review to understand how this occurred and to identify any improvements needed to strengthen our patient identification processes and ensure that it does not occur again. "As the review of this matter is ongoing, we are unable to provide further detail at this time."

Ms Buckley has received a formal apology from Victoria Police for the "distress caused" to her by the misidentification and incorrect death notification, but she is also critical of the force's verification processes.

Two months later, Ms Buckley is still untangling her medical records, spending hours on the phone with Services Australia.

"There are still some things I don't know if they're hers or mine," Ms Buckley said.

"It's still really hard to get my head around what's happened. But I'd like to make sure it doesn't happen to anyone else."

World.title: AI company plan to tap into irrigation system disappears after ABC question
World.content:
An artificial intelligence company says it plans to use irrigation water for one of its proposed Tasmanian AI data centres, but the state-owned irrigation company says that's not its purpose.

Firmus Technologies is building an AI factory in the Launceston suburb of St Leonards and has proposed two more, one in Bell Bay in the state's north and another in Wesley Vale in the north-west.

The company has submitted a development application to Latrobe Council for its Wesley Vale proposal, but the council is waiting for more information from Firmus before releasing the application to the public.

AI factories contain data centre infrastructure, advanced cooling systems and graphics processing units which generate AI tokens — the currency of AI needed for tools such as ChatGPT.

Firmus has been attempting to quell community concerns over its Tasmanian plans.

Co-CEOs of Firmus Technologies Tim Rosenfield and Oliver Curtis (right). (ABC News: Morgan Timms)

On the weekend, the company announced community drop-in sessions for its proposed Wesley Vale AI facility, and posted answers to "frequently asked questions" on its website.

It accidentally included a section about water usage.

"Not likely to use Tas Water for this site. They do not have [a] connection to this site," the FAQ section stated.

"We will likely use Tas Irrigation, but we do not want to highlight this yet, as they are yet to agree to supply us, as we fall outside their normal customer base [agriculture] and they need legal approval to supply us.

"[The] majority of our water use for cooling will come from rainwater capture from roof."

After the ABC contacted Firmus, the section was removed.

Firmus's FAQ page with a note on irrigation water, which was later removed. (Firmus)

'No undertaking to Firmus'

Tasmanian Irrigation is a state-owned company that provides water to farmers around the state.

"Tasmanian Irrigation has given no undertaking to Firmus," a spokesperson said.

"Our legislative framework is set up to enable the supply of water for agriculture and for hydrogen production.

"Any application for water from industries outside of this would require consideration by the Tasmanian government and engagement with the community, including our customers."

Firmus wants to build an AI factory on part of the old paper mill site at Mill Park in Wesley Vale. (ABC News: Mackenzie Heard)

Firmus told the ABC it had not intended to make the information public.

"We have updated our Wesley Vale FAQs on our website to correct some internal information that was inadvertently published," they said.

" We are focused on providing the Tasmanian community with clear and accurate information. "

The company said it had not yet made a formal request to Tasmanian Irrigation.

"Rainwater harvesting and on-site storage are proposed as the primary water solution for the facility and have been designed to meet the project's operational requirements," a spokesperson said.

"Discussions regarding any supplementary water sources are separate to that primary strategy and relate to resilience and contingency planning.

"Initial cooling water requirements are expected to be fulfilled through use of water cart if Tasmanian Irrigation connection is not available prior."

Firmus has begun construction at its St Leonards site, and has submitted a development application for its other two Tasmanian proposals. (ABC News: Morgan Timms)

The Firmus website states it only needs a very limited amount of water for its AI factories, as cooling is only required on days where the temperature reaches 26 degrees Celsius.

The company says the Wesley Vale facility, running at its full capacity of 52 megawatts, would use the same amount of water per year as a "restaurant".

Firmus co-CEOs Oliver Curtis (centre) and Tim Rosenfield met with Premier Jeremy Rockliff (left) at the data centre's research and development site in Launceston. (Supplied: Tasmanian government)

Irrigation water for farming, TasFarmers says

Neil Grose, chief operating officer of peak farming body TasFarmers, said it would be "highly unusual" for Tasmanian Irrigation to supply water to a data centre.

Are wheels falling off AI boom? Overshadowing the tumult that is global politics has been a financial boom beyond almost anything witnessed before.

"Irrigation water is for irrigating farmland," he said.

"It would concern us that Firmus are planning to use, and are talking about using irrigation water, without going through the proper channels first and talking to people, but most importantly, talking to farmers."

Mr Grose said farmers needed to be confident of their water supply, including in dry seasons.

" Having the demands of a data factory is something very, very different from what that scheme's designed for and what the farmers in that area would be expecting. "

The only instance of Tasmanian Irrigation agreeing to supply water to a non-agricultural user, Mr Grose said, was the proposed Tamar Scheme, which would support both farmers and hydrogen developments in northern Tasmania.

"That's been very carefully planned, it's gone through legislation, industry and farmers alike have been consulted and agree there is a joint interest in the Tamar Scheme — that hasn't happened with Wesley Vale."

He said TasFarmers was open to speaking with Firmus.

"If they're prepared to provide new infrastructure and invest in new infrastructure, then that's a conversation worth having, but I'm not sure they've started that conversation," Mr Grose said.

World.title: Victorian teachers are going on strike again — here's what you need to know
World.content:
Victorian state school teachers and educators are going ahead with their second major strike on Thursday, after union members voted to reject the government's latest pay offer.

It follows a 24-hour strike in March which saw about 35,000 educators and supporters marching through Melbourne's CBD to state parliament.

The union had initially thought its prolonged industrial dispute was over after it reached an in-principle agreement with the state government in May but its members went against its advice and threw out the proposal.

So, why was the deal voted done? What will a strike mean for families?

And how has the government responded?

What happened to the pay offer?

Negotiations on a new enterprise bargaining agreement for Victorian principals, teachers and support stalled well over a year ago.

Initially, the Australian Education Union (AEU) was fighting for a 35 per cent rise over three years for all members, arguing they were paid far less than those in other states.

After no progress was made in talks with the government, union members voted to hold their first statewide 24-hour strike in 13 years in March, effectively shutting down schools and bringing traffic to a standstill as an estimated 35,000 people rallied in Melbourne's CBD.

In May, the union announced it had reached an in-principle agreement that would see teachers receive a pay rise of between 28 and 32 per cent over four years, depending on their role and an increase in student-free days.

But a month later, unexpectedly, the offer was put to the union members for a vote and they rejected it citing excessive workloads, a lack of adequate funding for schools and a failure to offer a decent pay rise to support staff.

Teachers went against the union's advice and rejected the government's pay offer in June. (ABC News: Stephanie Ferrier)

Negotiations resumed and the government made a new offer last week to try to head off the second strike.

This time it included support staff in a 28 per cent pay rise over 4 years and a halving of the number of compulsory meetings educators must attend.

More than 50,000 members voted on that proposal over the weekend, and that was again rejected.

Why was the latest offer voted down?

The union said just with over 51 per cent of its members opposed the new offer.

AEU Victoria Branch president Justin Mullaly said teachers wanted a three-year deal and more action to alleviate teachers' workloads.

"You've got a state government that wants to call Victoria the education state but can't actually back that up with the resources that school staff need to delver the quality education that our children deserve," he said.

"Our members have had enough of it, they've had a gutful and they want our schools funded properly they also want the terms and conditions that they need in order to thrive."

AUE president Justin Mullaly says members have had enough. (ABC News)

Mr Mullaly said there continued to be a staff shortage in state schools but the government had not done anything meaningful to fix it.

"Our members are carrying the weight of all the excessive workload.

"[The government has] got to do better, they've got to do more, they've got to step up."

What does this mean for classes?

There will be major statewide disruptions, with the strike again effectively shutting down state schools tomorrow.

Some schools are telling parents they will not have enough staff to run classes or provide supervision.

Others may be offering limited supervision for students.

The strike will shut down Victorian state schools. (ABC News: Billy Draper)

"Students in Year 11 and 12 are asked to stay home, and to use the time for independent work that sill support their learning," one high school advised.

"Some teachers may choose to provide guidance on what work should be completed on this day, however teachers taking industrial action cannot be required to provide work to students."

Union members once again are expected to rally in Melbourne's CBD, this time meeting in the Bourke Street Mall and marching to Parliament House.

More than 35,000 teachers and supporters took to the streets of Melbourne in March. (ABC News)

What does the government say?

Deputy Premier and Education Minister Ben Carroll said he was disappointed with the outcome of the teacher vote.

"This deal would have made Victorian teachers and education support staff the best paid in the country together with the best conditions," he said.

"Students should be in classrooms and parents shouldn't be left scrambling for childcare or losing a day's pay."

"This was a close vote and my door is always open. I again urge the AEU leadership to call off this strike."

Education Minister Ben Carroll says he's disappointed with the outcome. (ABC News)

Mr Carroll has not provided any detail about the government's next steps.

World.title: Map reveals Australia's 'pharmacy deserts' are not all in the bush
World.content:
Locations of Australia's "pharmacy deserts" have been mapped for the first time, showing fewer services in remote Northern Territory communities and outer-city Melbourne.

The study, published in the Australian Journal of Rural Health, used 2024 data to map the density of Australia's 6,032 community pharmacies per 10,000 people.

It found several areas with no community pharmacies at all, including remote Aboriginal communities in West Arnhem Land and the Tiwi Islands; rural towns south of the Blue Mountains and the coastal region of Jervis Bay.

And it's not just the bush with fewer services.

Areas just outside of big city centres — including outer-city Melbourne and outer-city Perth — recorded community pharmacy density levels below the national average.

Community pharmacies are especially important for older residents as they typically have more complex health needs. (Unsplash: Franki Chamaki)

It was a pattern which surprised the study's lead author Michael Leach, a senior lecturer at Monash University's School of Rural Health.

"This hasn't been looked at before in Australia, so really we didn't know what to find," he said.

"We found that community pharmacy density overall across regional, rural and remote areas was significantly higher than metropolitan areas overall.

" And we found that overall across Australia, community pharmacy density was below the global average. "

Australia's community pharmacy 'deserts'

Based off 2024 data, Dr Leach's study found there was an average of 2.2 community pharmacies for every 10,000 Australians.

This was "well below" the global average of 2.75, he said, which indicated "room for improvement" to make sure all Australians had access to pharmacy services.

Dr Leach said community pharmacies, also known as retail pharmacies, were often the "first port of call for patients" who were unwell, so having easy access to one was in the best interest of the community.

This global average was calculated off 2021 data from 77 countries, a comparison which Dr Leach conceded "wasn't ideal" but was the best available as a benchmark.

The study found "pharmacy deserts" — defined as multiple areas next to each other with few community pharmacies per 10,000 people — in all Australian states and territories.

Areas with fewer than 1.73 community pharmacies per 10,000 people — including Alice Springs and north of Cairns — were classified as "very low community pharmacy density".

Dr Leach said just because some regions had very high community pharmacy density — such as Outback South in rural Queensland — it didn't mean everyone who lived there had equal access to services.

Outback South had 10 pharmacies servicing 17,629 people who lived across 625,222 square kilometres, which meant some people who lived in the region would still need to travel long distances to reach a pharmacy.

Dr Leach said "unsurprisingly" areas with very high community pharmacy densities — more than 2.88 per 10,000 people — included the big city centres of Sydney, Brisbane, Melbourne, Adelaide and Perth.

But the data shows an interesting phenomenon unfolding outside these city centres, including Perth, Sydney and Melbourne.

This is best illustrated looking at a map of Victoria.

While Melbourne City has a very high community pharmacy density, there are multiple areas with very low density just on the outskirts of the city.

"It's possible that there's relatively few community pharmacies in those outer city areas, because potentially people are travelling into the city and then getting their prescriptions filled," Dr Leach explained.

But he noted there needed to be more initiatives to attract and retain pharmacy workers outside big cities, with areas with few or no community pharmacies prioritised in future legislation.

Not all pharmacies created equal

Mark Naunton, president of the Pharmaceutical Society of Australia and professor of pharmacy at the University of Canberra who did not contribute to the study, said he was not "totally surprised".

He said central business districts attracted more foot traffic and pharmacies naturally clustered around other health points such as hospitals or medical services.

Sometimes outer suburbs had fewer pharmacies as it took time for infrastructure and populations to grow, he added.

Patients also typically had different needs as well, he said, with inner city pharmacies typically seeing younger people who took fewer medicines.

Professor Naunton said a key limitation of the study was that it simply counted community pharmacies but access to services also depended on the number of pharmacists employed in those businesses.

If a pharmacy in a regional area only included one pharmacist, this reduced the hours that people can have medicines dispensed.

"A more even distribution of pharmacy staffing, pharmacists and pharmacy assistants would be beneficial," he said.

"The key issue for the profession … is a more even distribution of pharmacy staffing, pharmacists and pharmacy assistant.

"The distribution of pharmacies is less relevant."

Mark Naunton said not all community pharmacies were the same size or had the same patient profiles. (Supplied: Mark Naunton)

Staffing was also a key concern for Simon Blacker, national vice president of the Pharmacy Guild of Australia, who did not contribute to the study.

"Like many industries, community pharmacies in regional and rural areas struggle to attract talent from metropolitan centres," he said.

Mr Blacker said although the study raised "important questions about healthcare access in Australia", the central findings should be "interpreted cautiously".

He noted the study didn't take into account factors such as trading hours, workforce capacity or the range of services provided.

"Pharmacy density alone does not necessarily reflect patient access to pharmacy care," he said.

Filling gaps in care

Pharmacy Guild of Australia NT branch president Peter Hatswell who did not contribute to the study, said there used to be a community pharmacy on the Tiwi Islands, but even with substantial government funding, it wasn't "commercially viable" and was forced to close.

"You need about 2,500 to 3,000 people for a pharmacy to be viable," he said.

People who live in towns or communities with no local community pharmacy often have to travel long distances to fill scripts, or have medications sent by post.

In the Northern Territory, remote residents who don't have a community pharmacy can fill some urgent scripts through the local health centre, he explained.

Peter Hatswell is a prescribing pharmacist and has managed pharmacies around the Northern Territory for more than 30 years. (Supplied: The Pharmacy Guild of Australia)

But over the past few decades, Alice Springs-based Mr Hatswell said he'd taken many calls from remote clinics to arrange for emergency medications to be sent in at very short notice.

"I was supplying 32 different communities that stretched all the way down into South Australia and up to Tennant Creek and beyond," he said.

"We had a huge, huge area to cover and I used to go out into these communities two or three times a year to see if there was anything more I could do to make sure that their supply was trouble-free and reliable and needs were being met."

Kelly Abbott is funded to visit about 30 people in their homes, but says there is much higher demand. (Supplied: Kelly Abbott)

Kelly Abbott, an independent consultant pharmacist, visits patients in their homes to review their medications, many of whom aren't able to drive themselves to a physical pharmacy.

She said pharmacists were the "most accessible health professional" available to most Australians.

"Someone can to walk into a pharmacy and just ask a question rather than having a book an appointment," she said.

"That's a fantastic asset to have … and the thinner they get on the ground, the harder it is for people to actually get these benefits."

World.title: Albanese's career mirrors Howard's in two important ways
World.content:
Point of view: You are the Australian prime minister. You've been elected for a second term, an outcome barely anyone would have predicted back when you were grinding your way through desolate years of opposition. You've just introduced a tax you once promised not to. You're staring down an intense scare campaign on that tax, while — in other news — Pauline Hanson is steaming in off a long run.

You are, of course, Anthony Albanese in 2026. But you could just as easily be John Howard in 1998.

We all, at some level, know that Australia has burned through a few too many political leaders of late. But it's genuinely rattling to realise that in the last 30 years, Anthony Albanese and John Howard are the only two prime ministers to win two elections in a row. The only two.

The only two to get a clear run at a second term. The only two afforded the opportunity to overcome the invariable hiccups of a first term as prime minister, then to get better at it, and to introduce and bed down the changes they want to make.

The vast majority of the Labor and Liberal leaders this century have been surprise arrivals who announce big plans and are then swiftly consigned to the woodchipper by their nearest and dearest. This is why the Australian policy landscape is haunted by the ghosts of carbon pricing schemes, dams that were never built, nuclear power plants smothered in their cradles. All this, surely, is a contributor to the dank mood of Australian voters.

Former Prime Minister John Howard, was the second longest serving PM, holding the position for 11 years. (ABC News: Simon Beardsell)

'This bloke is truly one out of the box'

Only Albanese and Howard have enjoyed what once was thought to be more or less a certainty for a newly-elected prime minister: A second term in which to really make things happen.

It takes some dark cosmic humorist to design a club of which only Howard and Albanese are members: The two men have traditionally loathed one another.

One of the most vitriolic speeches ever delivered in the House of Representatives about a serving prime minister was given by Albanese on April 5, 1998 — a contribution still listed in his archived speeches simply as "Grievance Debate, Prime Minister".

Over lunch at The Lodge for ABC TV's Kitchen Cabinet, Albanese is 63 years old and says he's "grown up" since that famous speech. (Supplied: ABC TV)

The chamber footage of this speech captures Albanese at 35 years of age. He's been in parliament less than two years. He wears a gawky grey suit, a tie excusable only thanks to the passage of time, and slightly owlish glasses. The earring that once graced his left earlobe is already gone, but the hard-left backbencher speaks with the defiant vitriol of a lad accustomed to picking fights with the NSW Right at Sussex St, and losing. He gets stuck straight into the physical appearance of Howard, who'd recently had his teeth fixed.

"In the pantheon of chinless blue bloods and suburban accountants that makes up the Australian Liberal Party, this bloke is truly one out of the box," Albanese says.

"You can trim the eyebrows; you can cap the teeth; you can cut the hair; you can put on different glasses," sneers the younger man.

"You can give him a ewe's milk facial, for all I care! But, to paraphrase a gritty Australian saying, 'Same stuff, different bucket'."

Lessons learned on migration

Over lunch at The Lodge for ABC TV's Kitchen Cabinet, Albanese is 63 years old and says he's "grown up" since that speech.

He's obliged to be diplomatic, seeing as he himself in the intervening years has had his fangs fixed and invested in some snazzier glasses.

But Albanese's reinvention goes far further.

The hard-left Labor MP who once took joy in "fighting Tories" is now studiously, perhaps even performatively respectful of the Coalition prime minister.

Asked to nominate an act of great political courage he's witnessed in his political career, he plumps for not Keating's economic reforms, or Hawke's Accord, but Howard and Tim Fischer's embrace of gun controls after Port Arthur.

And after years of railing in opposition against Howard's GST and harsh border protection measures, Albanese now administers both of them without a murmur.

Watch Kitchen Cabinet on ABC iview Join Annabel Crabb for a brand new season as she breaks bread with six of the federal parliament's most fascinating and powerful figures from across the political spectrum.

"We've strengthened them!" he says brightly, of the boat turnbacks and offshore processing measures that he once denounced as inhumane.

Albanese says he's learned the lessons of opposition in this particular policy area.

"If you want to run a migration system that's respectful of the contribution that migrants make, it has to be orderly," he says.

"And that's the lesson that the British Labor government is dealing with at the moment. It's a lesson that the US Democrats should have learnt but didn't. And it's something that we have [learned]."

Albanese expresses respect for Howard.

"He had control of the caucus," he says. "Howard as well, I think, understood that the 24-hour media cycle isn't what you have to be focused on. Credit where credit's due. It's a substantial achievement to govern for 11 years."

Does losing make you better at politics?

Albanese's use of the term "caucus" may be a Freudian slip, but there's no doubt that the Labor leader has achieved, over time, a similar dominance over the Labor Party to that enjoyed by Howard over the Liberal Party at his zenith.

By the time they finally won office, both Howard and Albanese had weathered long and miserable apprenticeships in opposition. It made both of them hungrier for government, and far more strategic and resilient than newer colleagues.

Does losing — a lot — make you better at politics?

"It certainly does," says Albanese.

"I'm someone who analyses things. How did it go? How could it have been done better? "

Long experience has also taught Albanese not to panic when bad polls roll around. He recalls — because he was there — that while Howard's four terms as prime minister are now recalled in the Liberal Party as a golden age, there were points in every term at which the Coalition was deemed by pollsters to be gone for all money.

Albanese was elected to parliament on his birthday in 1996. (ABC News: Nic MacBean)

Control is central to the project. Albanese's taste for it is evident in everything he does. He manages his own diary ("it drives my staff mad!") so that he can bring appointments forward and deal with them earlier if a gap opens up. If he's cooking, no-one is allowed to help.

As a child, Albanese was often left alone to manage the home while his chronically ill mother was in hospital. He was doing laundry, paying bills, getting himself to school and sport, from an early age. So he's accustomed to doing things for himself. And he's also known, from childhood, that life can go badly wrong from time to time. If you're organised and prepared, you're better placed to cope with unexpected disasters as and when they occur.

"Life's busy," he says.

"Never do something tomorrow you can do today. Never do something this afternoon if you can do it in the morning."

Here's another thing Albanese has in common with Howard: he's perceived as ordinary. Boring, even. A greyish man in a suit, not noticeably burdened with rhetorical talent. Who could blame citizens for failing to clock him among the more eye-catching figures who've ridden the carousel of political leadership this century — Tony the Endorphin Addict, Mellifluous Malcolm, Bill "Showbags" Shorten?

But there's nothing ordinary about Albanese's life. Until he was 14 years old, he was told by his mother, Marianne, that his father had died in a car accident. But he wasn't dead at all; Carlo Albanese, whose name the prime minister still carries, was alive and well and building another family in Italy all that time. Albanese was meant to be adopted out to spare Marianne's shame, but a nun at the hospital judiciously placed the infant in his mother's arms, and Marianne switched to Plan B.

The bond between mother and son was so close that Albanese did not seek out his father until after Marianne's death; he did not want her ever to think she hadn't been enough.

Loading

Survival against the odds

Ironically, Albanese has himself been in near-fatal vehicle accidents not once, but three times. Politically, his is also a story of survival against the odds.

Albanese is a graduate of NSW Labor's hard left faction, whose sheer unkillability, determination and — where required — ruthlessness has ensured his near-total colonisation of a party once unquestionably dominated by the NSW Right.

It's extraordinary. It really is.

According to one pollster, the three most common descriptors that surface about Albanese in polling sessions are "weak", "liar", and "means well".

ABC Politics in your inbox Sign up to the ABC Politics newsletter with Courtney Gould

It's a collection of descriptors that would elicit yays and nays from both Albanese and his detractors. But of them all, "weak" is the one that seems most off-beam for an old leftie who has not only brought the famously restive Labor caucus under his control, but now is taking the opportunity of disarray in the Liberal Party of Australian politics to munch his way even further rightwards, invoking language and concepts once claimed as conservative territory.

"We respect institutions as well and traditions," he says. "I am a traditionalist. I follow all of the protocols, all of that, I think is really important."

When it's suggested that student activist Albanese — chained to a Sydney University clock tower in the 1980s protesting against the capitalist bent of the Economics faculty — would be horrified by this 63-year-old version of himself, Prime Minister Albanese demurs.

"No, no, no. What you can hear is my mum saying that's the way he was brought up, to respect people and respect those institutions. It's a working-class phenomenon to do that."

World.title: The 'precious' bond driving the Stingers to success
World.content:
They say the truest test of a team's culture is what they do away from the glare of public scrutiny.

How they show their respect for each other, those little moments unseen by the public and imperceptible until you see it with your own eyes.

At St Rita's College, a week out from the World Aquatics World Cup Finals, which get underway in Sydney on Wednesday, the Australian women's water polo team, the Stingers, delivered one of those little moments that underline why they epitomise everything great about sport — to be revealed in a moment.

Water polo is not one of the nation's bigger sports, which is why it so often slides under the radar of many fans.

But at the Paris Olympics of 2024, the public could not help but be carried along in the eddies of success and enthusiasm as the Stingers smiled their way to a sensational silver medal, the best result by any Australian team at those Games.

Australia won a superb silver medal in Paris, their best Olympic result in 24 years. (Getty Images: Andy Cheung)

"At the Paris Olympics, because we got that silver medal, it kind of brought the whole of Australia on board with how close we are as a team," Tilly Kearns told ABC Sport during the team's staging camp in Brisbane.

"It made everyone kind of see that special connection that we have."

Stingers meet success and failure with the same, indomitable spirit How you respond to missing out is just as important as how you respond to success. On that measure alone, these Aussie Stingers are true champions.

That special connection could have been strained to breaking point.

The Stingers not only had to embrace the general chaos of an Olympic tournament that was as fiercely competitive as any in history, but did so while negotiating a COVID outbreak pre-Games that had the potential to derail their campaign.

Such an injustice could have shattered the carefully cultivated bonds of any team. But not these Stingers.

"I think what's so cool about our team is our connection and the culture that we've built," Abby Andrews told ABC Sport.

"That tournament in Paris was so up and down; we had so many highs together … I think we were playing to the best of our ability and we were lifting each other as a team."

Paris silver stung for a minute, but the smiles were never far from the Stingers' faces. (Getty Images: RvS.Media/Monika Majer)

Bronte Halligan, the team's captain, said the connection was built on a genuine shared love of their sport.

"We just love what we do," she said.

"We're so passionate about what we do, and we have such a great bunch that enjoys being together day-in, day-out and working hard together. I think that's the key.

"We play a hard sport. Every sport is tough, but our sport particularly. You've got people jumping on you, pulling you down, drowning you in the water.

"But you find the fun in the moments, and we just laugh, and we smile, and when you see a teammate giggling about something in the pool, even though you're working as hard as you can and you just want to get out and go home, you think, yeah, this is why I love being here.

"This is what's awesome about this group, we can do that, we can have a smile in those really tough moments.

"I think that's so precious and I hope that never leaves the team."

'Authentic' Stingers

The Stingers are a tight bunch. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

Australia is hosting the World Aquatics Water Polo World Cup Finals for the first time at the Sydney Olympic Park Aquatic Centre this week.

Eight of the world's top teams — including a Russian side, competing for the first time on Australian soil since their international exile was controversially ended by World Aquatics in April — are set to duke it out.

The Stingers open their campaign against Italy on Wednesday at 6:30pm AEST.

There is a chance that Australia could meet Spain, the team that beat Australia to gold at the Paris Olympics in 2024, later in the competition.

There, the Aussies suffered the uniquely bittersweet heartbreak of winning a silver medal at a major tournament.

Standing on that podium alongside gold medallists Spain and bronze medallists the Netherlands, both revelling in the euphoria of their victories that day, the Stingers had to juggle the success of a silver medal with the leaden-hearted feeling of defeat.

They did so with lion-hearted stoicism, staring down their anguish to embrace triumph — a testament to their togetherness.

The Stingers hope to inspire others with their success and their togetherness. (Getty Images: Adam Pretty)

"I think that stuff's hard to manufacture," Kearns told the ABC.

"It's authentic, and it's really us.

"I started playing water polo for the friendship aspect and still, to this day — I'm almost 26 now — the reason why I'm still playing is because of my teammates and especially my Aussie Stingers teammates; they're just the best.

"I truly love them so much."

Talk is cheap, they say, but you don't have to spend long in the company of the team to realise that they truly live by the ideals they espouse.

One of the newest members of the team, 17-year-old student Bless Daly, was the last to give an interview to ABC Sport following the Stingers' training session in Brisbane.

While the teenage sporting prodigy — more than adept at hockey, softball and tennis as well as swimming and water polo — spoke to the ABC, her more senior teammates, obligations over, milled around the pool deck, waiting for her to finish, so she wouldn't have to make her way to lunch on her own.

It's a small thing, tiny in the overall scheme, but a moment that perfectly illustrated their togetherness.

Tilly Kearns is one of Australia's most powerful shooters. (Supplied)

"Bless is doing just such an amazing job," Kearns said of her young teammate.

"She just fits our vibe so perfectly as Aussie Stingers; she gets in there and has a laugh and works hard when she's in the pool."

Daly, for her part, is desperately soaking up all the knowledge her experienced teammates — 10 of the 15 squad members won silver in Paris — can give her.

"This group of girls is so supportive … They have your back through thick and thin," she said.

"I think when you see it outside of the pool and outside of the group, you don't quite understand the culture, but stepping into it, it's honestly amazing.

"It's something that's so cool and so special, and I think being a part of it is something I've always dreamed of."

Stingers performing at apex of the sport

Abby Andrews was named MVP in the Champions League, which she won with Olympiacos. (Supplied: Instagram)

Daly slots into a squad brimming with talent.

Halligan recently won her fifth-straight Italian Serie A title for Ekipe Orizonte, while Kearns claimed the Spanish league crown with Mataró.

Andrews is fresh off winning the LEN Champions League title with Greek club Olympiacos, while fellow Aussies Alice Williams and Kearns also played in the exclusive and prestigious Final Four tournament for Barcelona-based teams Sant Andreu and Mataró, respectively.

"Every time — I mean every time — we're having a big game, there's always another Aussie in the other team," Kearns said with a beaming smile.

"In the semifinal and third place game in the Champions League, I was playing against my teammates, my Aussie Stingers teammates.

"I'm so close to them; they're my sisters and, at the end of the day, we lost both games, but they won, and that was just — I was stoked for them.

"And Abby, winning MVP, all of us Aussies were just so insanely proud of her, and same with the others that were there."

How this Champions League winner aims to ignite Stingers Winning the Champions League with Greek giants Olympiacos was "one of the coolest moments" of Abby Andrews's life. She wants to use that experience to push the Stingers to the next level.

Having her players excel at the pinnacle of the sport is all part of the plan for Bec Rippon, the Olympic medal-winning coach.

"Those players are playing in some amazing European clubs, and they've really earned the right to do that," Rippon said.

"And it's exciting to watch them go and be outstanding ambassadors for us and great players in those leagues.

"When they get together from all the different places, wherever they are, overseas or in Australia … how do we bring all of that knowledge together and all of that experience together?

"It's great having them everywhere, but it also presents a bit of a challenge in terms of building a team.

"That's a challenge I'm happy to have, because we've got amazing players."

Coach Bec Rippon is intensely proud of her squad. (Supplied: Zac Hudson)

Playing on different teams, often against each other in such a fiercely competitive and physical sport as water polo, could also pose a problem to some groups. But not these Stingers.

"Look, they're competitive with each other, but they actually care a lot about each other, which is something that we value a lot in the team," Rippon said with obvious pride.

"We're trying to create a team that really lifts each other, not through just trying to tell each other that they're good, but genuinely supporting each other when it's tough.

"I just love seeing them get around each other."

Alice Williams also played in the Champions League Final Four this year. (Getty Images: Dean Mouhtaropoulos)

And it is clearly not for show. Even a cursory glance across social media posts from these athletes reveals heartfelt messages of support.

"I think you just want to celebrate your teammates' wins, even if that's not your own team," Hannigan said.

"It's not just about winning though. We want to put ourselves in really tough competition that gets us better day-in, day-out to be the best in the national team.

"I'm so proud of all the girls, overseas and in Australia.

"So the girls in Spain, myself in Italy, other girls in Italy, there's girls in Greece, there's girls over in America playing in the college system, and then there's the Australian League; I think all of that combines together, and we're playing at the highest level ever now.

"All the girls [in the squad] are up in the top one, two, three teams of every league in every season.

"I think that that's the most important thing, putting ourselves in really high quality competition which means that then we can perform on the big stage when we come together. I think that's a great thing."

Now attention turns to the biggest tournament to take place in Sydney since the Olympic Games in 2000.

'I couldn't be more blessed to play for an Australian women's team'

Bronte Halligan is thrilled to be captaining the team in her home pool. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

Challenging for a medal will, of course, be the biggest litmus test of whether this team is building successfully towards the LA Games of 2028.

But for Kearns, the way they do it is just as important.

"What I really love about us is, sure, we're performing, and we're scoring goals and doing all the right things in the pool, but the fact is that we're doing it with smiles on our faces," Kearns said.

"We just respect each other so much and push each other and work hard for each other.

"I think it sets such a great example."

Water polo can be a physically testing sport. (Getty Images: Adam Pretty)

It's an example that Kearns said will, hopefully, drive others to follow in their footsteps.

"I love talking to the girls and all the kids that are coming to watch afterwards because I remember when I was their age, and I was the kid with a pen and paper chasing signatures.

"I didn't even know the girls' names, but I didn't care; I saw they were wearing green and gold, so I wanted a signature.

"And now I'm playing with players like Bronte, and I still have a little poster that I had her sign when I was young, and now we're teammates.

"So hopefully, maybe one day, one of those girls will be in the mix with me and with us.

"To be on home soil and playing in front of them is great, but also to invite them into our special team, to give people insights into truly how special the culture is here and hopefully put up some good water polo is really exciting."

Bec Rippon and Bronte Halligan will lead the Stingers at the Sydney Olympic Park Aquatic Centre. (Supplied: Zac Hudson)

Halligan agreed.

"I think this is what it's about. It's about creating a fun, exciting game that people want to watch," she said.

"And if we can do that, then we're creating a community around us that wants to be a part of our story, that wants to be a part of our journey.

"I think there's just so much joy in the water and there's joy to be a part of it.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

The end goal for the current squad is the Los Angeles Olympic Games, where they will once again strive for a medal.

But the captain acknowledged there is a bigger picture.

"Yes, we're building for LA and LA is the end goal for this group, but you've got to enjoy it every day. If you don't enjoy it, then there's no point in being there," she said.

"We bring that joy and that fun in the water. And if you can do that and do it in a way that you're competing with the best in the world, then I think that's a phenomenal thing, and I think that's what this group is really doing at the moment.

"I think we started that in Paris and we're building on that momentum.

'When we get these opportunities on home soil … that's what creates the real excitement and momentum behind us. We feel it, and we love it.

"Australian culture is really getting behind women in sport now.

"I don't want to leave ever … it's so great, and I couldn't be more blessed to be an Australian and to play for an Australian women's team."

World.title: ASX set to advance, tech stocks push Wall Street higher; Google’s new AI offerings
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to advance, tech stocks push Wall Street higher; Google’s new AI offerings Stan Choe July 22, 2026 — 5:13am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

More gains for makers of computer chips and other winners of the artificial-intelligence boom are carrying Wall Street higher. The S&P 500 climbed 0.9 per cent. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 361 points, or 0.7 per cent, i mid-afternoon trade, and the Nasdaq composite was 1.4 per cent higher. AI stocks once again were at the centre of the action on Wall Street, and they rose for a second straight day after tumbling the week before. AP The Australian sharemarket is set to advance, with futures at 4.53am AEST pointing to a gain of 16 points or 0.2 per cent, at the open. The ASX closed flat on Tuesday. The Australian dollar was trading at US70.05¢. AI stocks once again were at the centre of the action on Wall Street, and they rose for a second straight day after tumbling the week before.



After rocketing higher because of the boom in investment in AI chips and data centres, they’ve come under pressure in recent weeks on worries that they shot too high. Concerns are also weighing that investment in AI may fall off if it doesn’t produce as much profit and productivity as hoped. Related Article Opinion

Trade wars Trump wants to make his trade wall bigger and better than ever before Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Micron Technology jumped 12.7 per cent and added to its 1.9 per cent gain from the day before, coming off its 13.3 per cent drop from last week. Nvidia added 1.5 per cent, and they were the two strongest forces lifting the S&P 500. The gains came despite more climbs for oil prices, and Brent crude oil topped $US90 per barrel because of continued attacks between the United States and Iran. It rose 2 per cent to $US91.01 and briefly got near $US92 for the first time in more than five weeks. That’s up from less than $US72 early this month, which is roughly where it was before the war with Iran. Rising oil prices are threatening a reacceleration of inflation, just as increases for prices were slowing more than economists expected. That in turn could push the Federal Reserve and other central banks to raise interest rates to keep a lid on inflation, which would slow economies and undercut prices for stocks and other investments.



The yield on the 10-year Treasury edged up to 4.63 per cent from 4.60 per cent late Monday and from just 3.97 per cent before the war with Iran began. On Wall Street, several stronger-than-expected profit reports from big US companies helped stocks to strengthen despite the added pressure. 3M climbed 6.9 per cent after topping analysts’ expectations for both profit and revenue in the latest quarter. It also raised its forecast for profit over the full year of 2026. Hasbro rallied 7.9 per cent after the toy maker said its Magic: The Gathering game topped $US500 million in revenue for a quarter for the first time. It also raised its revenue forecast for the year. General Motors cruised 4.8 per cent higher after the automaker’s profit and revenue for the latest quarter beat analysts’ expectations and CEO Mary Barra said demand in North America remains strong.



They helped offset a drop for Danaher, which slid 11.4 per cent even though it likewise topped analysts’ expectations for profit and revenue. Analysts pointed to its forecast for an underlying measure of revenue growth for the summer, which was weaker than Wall Street expected. Alphabet slid 0.9 per cent after Google released a trio of cheaper versions of its Gemini AI model, but shared no timing updates for the flagship Pro model that has already seen its launch delayed by several weeks. The new model lineup includes Gemini 3.6 Flash and Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite, updated versions of its lightweight offerings, designed for use cases that do not require the most cutting-edge technology. Google also unveiled a new lightweight variant, Gemini 3.5 Flash Cyber, which is tailored towards cybersecurity applications. Homebuilder D.R. Horton slipped 0.8 per cent despite topping profit and revenue expectations for the latest quarter. Executive Chairman David Auld said it’s still feeling the effects of affordability concerns in the housing market and caution among potential home buyers. Mortgage rates have already climbed to their highest level in nearly a year because of higher Treasury yields in the bond market. That could force D.R. Horton to offer more incentives to homebuyers in the current quarter, which would cut into its profits.



Related Article Opinion

Online shopping $900 million fines look like the cost of doing business for giant shopping apps Elizabeth Knight Business columnist Companies broadly are under pressure to deliver strong growth in profit and revenue because of how high their stock prices have shot. Indexes are near their records, even with the recent shakiness for AI stocks. In stock markets abroad, indexes rose modestly in Europe. The United Kingdom’s FTSE 100 added 0.6 per cent as new Prime Minister Andy Burnham hosted his first Cabinet meeting. In Asia, stocks swung more. South Korea’s Kospi jumped 3.6 per cent on strong gains for its two dominant stocks. Both Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix have been big beneficiaries of the AI boom, and the Kospi has soared 60 per cent so far this year even with its 20 per cent drop for July so far. Tokyo’s Nikkei 225 climbed 3.3 per cent after returning from Monday’s holiday, while indexes rose 1.8 per cent in Shanghai and edged down by less than 0.1 per cent in Hong Kong.

World.title: I earn $80,000 a year in dividends. Should I reinvest, or add it to my super?
World.content:
MoneyPlanning & budgetingAsk an expert Opinion I earn $80,000 a year in dividends. Should I reinvest, or add it to my super? Noel Whittaker Money columnist July 22, 2026 — 5:08am

July 22, 2026 — 5:08am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

I am 58 and have a portfolio of blue-chip shares worth about $1.67 million, producing about $80,000 a year in fully franked dividends. I have owned the shares for 20 years, and they have unrealised capital gains of about $1.3 million. All dividends are re-invested. I expect to retire in two years. My salary is about $130,000 including overtime and penalty rates, and with my dividend income, my taxable income is about $205,000 to $210,000 a year. I salary-sacrifice $20,800 into super each year, with employer contributions of about $11,500, bringing me close to the concessional contribution cap. I also pay Division 293 tax. My super consists of about $715,000 in a government PSS defined benefit scheme and $805,000 in another account, giving me total super of about $1.52 million. With Labor’s capital gains tax changes due to commence on July 1, 2027, I am concerned about the future CGT implications for my share portfolio. Should I continue reinvesting my dividends through DRPs, or would I be better off taking the dividends in cash and making non-concessional contributions to super instead? A healthy portfolio of blue-chip shares can produce plenty of tasty dividends. Simon Letch There is no doubt the coming changes have introduced a whole new level of complexity for investors with diversified share portfolios. Fortunately, you’ve held your shares for a long time, so the post-2027 treatment of any capital gains should not be too onerous. As capital gains are added to your taxable income, it makes sense to defer any major sales until after you retire, when your taxable income will be much lower. Meanwhile, if you have capital losses available, consider using them to offset gains and crystallise some gains before June 30, 2027.



I agree you should take future dividends in cash and maximise non-concessional contributions to super. The amount you can contribute will depend on the notional value of your defined benefit entitlement. Editor's pick Opinion

Ask an expert Should we delay our retirement to help pay our daughter’s uni fees? Paul Benson Money contributor I have read on several social media sites that, before passing away, you should remove your children (even adults in their thirties) as direct beneficiaries of your assets. Instead, you should place all your assets, including bank accounts, jewellery and super, into a revocable trust and name your children as beneficiaries of the trust. Supposedly, this allows them to bypass the lengthy probate process and gain immediate access to the assets. Does this also apply to irrevocable trusts and testamentary trusts? Estate planning solicitor Rachael Rofe tells me the short answer is that this advice is generally incorrect in an Australian context. Much of what circulates on social media is based on US estate planning, where revocable living trusts are commonly used. Australia has a very different legal system. In Australia, assets already owned by a trust are generally not personally owned by you and therefore do not usually form part of your estate on death. However, transferring all your assets into a trust shortly before death is rarely straightforward.



It can trigger tax and stamp duty consequences, affect asset protection and create practical complications, so it is often inappropriate. Revocable trusts are not commonly used in Australia as an estate-planning vehicle as they are in the United States. Assets genuinely owned by an irrevocable trust generally do not form part of your estate, but establishing one is a major decision with significant legal and tax implications. Testamentary trusts are different again. They are created by your will and come into existence only after your death. They do not avoid probate because the will generally must first be admitted to probate before the estate can be administered and the testamentary trusts established. It is also worth remembering that not every estate requires probate. Whether probate is needed depends on the nature of the assets and the requirements of the institutions holding them. For most Australians, good estate planning is not about avoiding probate at all costs. It is about ensuring assets pass to the right people in the most tax-effective and asset-protective manner, while minimising the risk of family disputes.



I am 61, retired, and have just sold my investment property. Since retiring, I have withdrawn more than $100,000 from my super. Tax-wise, would it be beneficial to contribute some of the sale proceeds back into super? I haven’t made any super contributions since 2020, and my super balance is well under $1 million, so I am wondering whether non-concessional contributions are an option. How much could I contribute without exceeding the limits, and how can I determine the amount that would be most tax-effective? Editor's pick Opinion

Hip pocket Hoarding receipts? These are the ones you actually need to keep Dominic Powell Money Editor Since the taxation changes announced in the recent budget, superannuation has become by far the most tax-effective investment vehicle for older Australians. Given you are 61 and retired, you have no problems accessing your super. And because your super balance is well under the $2.1 million threshold, you have considerable flexibility. You can contribute $32,500 as a tax-deductible concessional contribution, but I doubt you would need to do this unless you have taxable income you wish to reduce. The more appropriate option appears to be non-concessional contributions. These are limited to $130,000 a year, but you can bring forward three years’ worth of contributions and contribute up to $390,000. There is no contributions tax or withdrawal tax on these non-concessional contributions.



My mother recently passed away and my sibling and I inherited her home. She bought the property in 1990 and lived in it as her principal place of residence until 2014. She then moved into my apartment, where she lived with me rent-free for the next 12 years until her death in 2026. She owned no other property during that time but rented out her home after moving out. We understand that if we sell the property, there may be capital gains tax because it was rented. However, we have also been told that if we do not sell the property within two years of our mother’s death, any later sale would attract capital gains tax on the entire ownership period from 1990 until 2026. Is that correct? No, that is wrong. That section protects the deceased’s home from CGT if sold within two years of death. It cannot apply to your mother’s circumstances because it was not covered with her main residence exemption at the date of death. Even utilising the six-year rule will not bring you up to her date of death. The CGT calculation goes back to the time it was first rented, starting with the market value then. As she was not covering another property with her main residence exemption, she can continue to cover that property for six years after it was rented out, so only half of the gain you calculate will be taxable and then half that amount for the 50 per cent CGT discount. Noel Whittaker is author of Retirement Made Simple and other books on personal finance. Questions to: noel@noelwhittaker.com.au



Advice given in this article is general in nature and is not intended to influence readers’ decisions about investing or financial products. They should always seek their own professional advice that takes into account their own personal circumstances before making any financial decisions.
