World.title: Investors could be $600k worse off when buying new builds
World.content:
MoneyInvestingProperty investment Investors could be $600k worse off when buying new builds Sue Williams July 22, 2026 — 5:06am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Property investors rushing to negatively gear new build homes in light of the looming budget changes have been warned they could be making a huge mistake, with modelling suggesting buyers of older, established homes will be far better off. Research by Get Rare Properties found that, when comparing two $700,000 properties held for 20 years, the owner of the established build will be $592,000 ahead, even after all the tax advantages given to the new build. New builds will be the only ones eligible for buyers to negatively gear from next July. Natalie Boog Founder Rasti Vaibhav, who previously spent 15 years managing $2 billion of institutional portfolios at Westpac and AMP Capital, said there’s no situation here where a new build ends up the better option. As part of a sweeping range of new tax measures revealed in this year’s Federal Budget, investors will no longer be able to negatively gear properties bought after July 1 next year, unless they are new builds. Existing properties that are already owned and negatively geared will be unaffected.



Vaibhav crunched the figures considering the tax benefit of a new build of about $231,000 over 20 years, from both negative gearing and depreciation. Against that, however, he used data from long-run analysis from the Property Investment Professionals of Australia that found capital growth from new builds averaged 3 to 5 per cent, against that of established properties of 5 to 8 per cent, leaving a growth shortfall of around $1.17 million. Editor's pick Investing ‘The days of multiple properties are over’: How to invest after the budget Then there was the capital gains tax (CGT) with the older property paying $445,000 more. The net outcome, however, was still that the established wins by $592,000, while, at CoreLogic’s actual decade growth rates – 3.4 versus 5.8 per cent – it comes out top by $430,000. “The reality is, if you want to avoid tax, then lose money,” Vaibhav says. “But a tax strategy isn’t as good as one that concentrates on building wealth. The government wanted to keep negative gearing for new property to encourage demand and then the supply.” “The consumer should really be concentrating more on making their money work harder long-term than on saving tax short-term. They should instead be buying established property in good locations, close to job hubs and shopping centres where people want to live rather than new builds on the city fringes, and as their equity grows quicker, they can reinvest that to create exponential compounding benefits.”



That’s a view that’s supported by a number of buyers’ agents. Kane Dury, principal of Discover Buyers Agency, for instance, says the Government has created a powerful tax incentive that should still not override sound investment judgement. “It puts us at risk of the tail wagging the dog,” Dury said. “What makes a good investment is where demand is greater than supply and so much of the value of an investment lies in the scarcity of land, which appreciates while the building on it depreciates.” [Tax breaks are] not so attractive if the property underperforms for a long period. Kane Dury, principal of Discover Buyers Agency “So you want more land and less house, or an older house, rather than a new build where you’re paying more for the dwelling on less land. And tax benefits and depreciation – for which you can substitute the word ‘loss’ – aren’t going to fix that.” One problem with some new builds too, Dury says, is that the area in which they’re constructed is often, as a result, saturated with supply, making it difficult to sell the property when it comes time to get out. As a result, established properties in popular locations are usually a much better bet.



“Tax is a big pain point, so if someone says we’re going to minimise it for you, that’s very attractive,” Dury said. “But it’s not so attractive if the property underperforms for a long period.” Of course, the investment in an established property needs to be sound in order for it to work, Vaibhav points out. “You always want less risk and better returns and not every market is good,” he said. “There might be another reason you want to save on tax, too. But for most people, the aim is to build wealth for their retirement years, to support their kids with education and live off passive income. So it’s critical they make sound judgements now.” Expert tips on how to save, invest and make the most of your money delivered to your inbox every Sunday.

World.title: One-pan 30-minute pork, sage and fennel lasagne
World.content:
Step 1 Preheat the oven grill to high. Heat the oil in a large deep oven-proof frying pan over high heat. Add the sage leaves and cook for 30 seconds or until crisp. Remove the sage and set aside. Add the fennel, sausage mince and garlic, breaking up the mince with the back of a wooden spoon. Cook for 5 minutes or until the fennel is caramelised.

Step 2 Add the tomatoes and stock and bring the mixture to a simmer. Add the pasta sheets, submerging them in the liquid, and cook for 15 minutes, covered, until they are just tender and the sauce has reduced.

Step 3 Meanwhile, combine the mascarpone, parmesan, mozzarella and 60ml of water in a medium bowl. Season with salt and mix well. Spoon the cheese mixture over the lasagne. Place the frying pan on a baking tray and place it under the grill, then cook for 6-8 minutes or until the top is bubbling and golden.

World.title: How Adriano put up a small home in a day - and made it fire-resistant
World.content:
PropertyNewsConstruction How Adriano put up a small home in a day - and made it fire-resistant Sue Williams July 22, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The morning after a ferocious bushfire tore through a NSW South Coast community, architect Adriano Pupilli returned to find out what was left of his holiday cottage and the innovative prefab flatpack bush cabin he’d invented, designed and built himself. Both were still standing but, as he set about doing repairs, he decided he’d pivot to creating an easy-to-construct modular tiny house that would also be bushfire resistant instead. Adriano and his family at their tiny home. Adriano Pupilli Architects “My pregnant wife and our three-year-old son escaped when they were picked up by a fishing group from down the coast at Ulladulla,” said Pupilli. “Then I had to get out when everything was on fire just before the front came. It was pretty scary. “I went back, thinking everything will have gone, but the fire jumped over the site, so the buildings were damaged and charred but, crazily, had survived. So this time, I thought I’d design a self-contained cabin that was highly resistant to bushfire.”



The final Casa Manyana tiny house prototype has been rated a lofty Bushfire Attack Level (BAL) 40 – suitable for a very high bushfire-risk environment, capable of withstanding extreme radiant heat and probably direct exposure to flames. Just like his first IMBY (in my back yard) model, it continues the same spirit of DIY assembly, sustainable materials and a modular kit of parts that all slot perfectly together, with no need for nails, screws or glue in the structure. The home is made from a modular kit. Adriano Pupilli Architects As such, it could be an adjunct to a regular house in a bushfire area, increasing space or providing safe accommodation for guests, or could be used after a fire when a family needs somewhere to live while rebuilding. “It’s a great idea,” said Dr Hugo Moline, lecturer in architectural practice & design at Newcastle University, who has followed the progress of the project. “With the housing crisis, we really need a lot more dwellings, and this can be erected quickly on a little plot of land, can work for multi-generational families and can help people back onto their land after a disaster.



“It’s so much more comfortable and dignified and safe than a caravan or camping or living out of a shipping container. The components can be brought easily onto a site, it’s affordable and accessible and you don’t have to be massively skilled to put it together.” The retail price for a Casa Manyana – named after the village 215km south of Sydney where Pupilli built it after the devastating fires of 2019-2020 – would be about $75,000 to $120,000 depending on size and design options. The kitchenette and sleeping loft. Adriano Pupilli Architects The form of his own 18-square-metre cabin, with a two-square-metre deck, a living space with a sofa bed, sleeping loft, a kitchenette and bathroom was put up, with the help of two friends, in a day, and turned into a fully clad structure in four. Tiling, electrical work and plumbing took extra. A protective outer layer of zincalume-rolled cladding and fibre cement creates a resilient structure, while plantation pine and plywood ensure a warm, welcoming interior. There’s high-performance insulation for thermal comfort, and operable louvre windows are meshed for bushfire resistance and cross-ventilation.



At Ember Bushfire Consulting, Peter Hague says much of his work lies in assessing the risks of new development in bushfire zones. “But this could be a good idea and, with such a high BAL rating, especially for people already affected by bushfires,” he said. Archicentre Australia director Peter Georgiev says anything that can assist people in bushfire-prone areas is welcome. The home is fast to construct but plumbing took extra time. Adriano Pupilli Architects “That’s especially if it’s something that keeps the cost down, and allows them to keep a foothold on their property,” he said. “We’re really trying to deal with these sorts of issues, so anything we can do to encourage these kind of innovations.” Dr Iftekhar Ahmed, associate professor in construction management/disaster resilience at the School of Architecture and Built Environment at Newcastle University, says it’s important to have structures that can minimise bushfire damage, give people time to escape and help them to return and rebuild.



Related Article Residential property How two architects reimagined their own homes “We need better options than what’s already available in the market,” he said. “This could be a good idea but it needs testing in bushfire conditions and needs to be explored in greater detail to see if it’s a viable option.” Pupilli is keen to cooperate with national or state organisations looking for good options in bushfire areas. “I wanted to do emergency housing or additional housing that would be different to the typical dongas and shipping container pods,” he said. “At the same time, they are also resilient to danger and more sympathetic to the landscape and a delight to be inside. “They are architect-designed, site-specific options that allow people to get back on the land and rebuild quicker and be safer in the elements.”

World.title: What’s Brisbane’s identity beyond the old Queenslander? Izzie White has an idea
World.content:
Welcome to CityChats, where Brisbane Times meets our city’s most interesting characters on our most iconic form of transport. This week, architecture influencer Izzie White tells us why she’s passionate about Brisbane being pink, and how we should rethink our relationship with public space. We meet White at Riverside ferry terminal near Eagle Street on a drizzly overcast day after she ducked out of work to chat with us. Architect Izzie White. Fairfax Media How did you get into making social media content? I make short-form videos explaining how to understand modern architecture and modern city making. I studied my bachelor and masters of architecture in Brisbane. I’ve been between Melbourne and Brisbane over the last couple of years, when I’ve really got to see the difference in city making.



About a year ago, I decided the public should really know about this too, and I started making videos. I’ve had the most amazing journey being able to talk to the public online about how to understand the city going up around them. Architecture feels like something that we all love and are exposed to, and it’s around us, but it feels a little bit unattainable. Has that been your experience? Architecture has a very tough relationship with the media. A lot of what makes it into mainstream media is very expensive houses that not a lot of us are ever going to live in. If you’ve ever seen the stats, about 97 per cent of homes in Australia are done without architects, so the portion of architecture that gets covered by mainstream media is incredibly narrow. Big commercial work is very hard to talk to the media about when you’re an architect because you really have to protect your client relationships, so when you’re working for an architecture firm and you do want to put out media, you are held really tightly with what you can say.



That’s not unusual, it’s just the way of the world, but that is why we have this incredible comms bubble between what architects know and what they’re working on, and what the general public get to see and understand about their city. Related Article City life Tivoli creative director on protecting Brisbane’s iconic (and haunted) venues You’ve lived between Brisbane and Melbourne in the past few years. What is your experience watching a city like Melbourne grow compared to Brisbane? Almost every city in Australia right now is facing a similar housing conversation, and almost every city is approaching the solution in a similar way. We are increasing density to allow for more supply in our inner-city areas, and that makes a lot of sense. I think Melbourne has more pressure, with more people. It’s also a much less forgiving climate. And so they’ve had a lot of tension in where they put this new housing.



The lesson out of that, which I hope Brisbane can avoid, is that long-term planning with communities and being able to bring them on board with where more housing is going to go is a much better solution than rapid rezoning and sending out panic alarms. It can absolutely be done, it takes longer, and in a public conversation that focuses mainly on housing supply, there’s much less focus on master-planning for livable communities. Do you think we need to be cautious of sprawl, and is it being addressed? What we have to be cautious of is relying on houses and apartments to do everything. Australia has the lowest-density cities in the world. There is a direct relationship between how much time you spend in the private home and how much time you spend in the public realm. If you don’t have that third bedroom, chances are you’re going to the park, or you’re looking for a studio that you can rent in the civic realm, and that’s what’s so cool about big cities.



When you do travel to the Tokyos, Londons, New Yorks, they have this jam-packed street life. That is what density supports and facilitates, but it also needs that public realm built in. Related Article Arts ‘We thought it might go straight in the bin’: The design rule the architects of GOMA ignored So I think the lesson is that the infrastructure has to come with the housing to support that, because otherwise, where does everyone go if they don’t have the backyard and there’s no park being built? Do you think we’re doing that well enough? Are we building the parks and the extra elements around supporting that density? Everyone could do it better. Brisbane is lucky in the sense that it has this built-in public space – being the river – along almost the whole length of it.



Our weather also facilitates being able to pop down for free, go for a bike ride in a big outdoor public open space, so we’re very lucky that we have that. Once we get away from those inner-city areas with that already good and built-up amenity, we do need to be really mindful that we’re building in civic and community facilities to facilitate that public life. Without it, you risk exacerbating urban challenges that are already felt, like traffic, isolation, things like that. We’re about to go through, I guess, a bit of an identity change, to reshape our identity somewhat, with starting the Olympics build. There’s going to be quite a lot of transformation of the river itself. It just feels like we’re about to embark on something that’s going to change it quite dramatically. Are you worried about that? I’m not worried about the Olympics speeding up development. I think the Olympics have been going around for a long time now for a lot of major cities, and there are a lot of amazing lessons to be learnt from all of those. I have full faith that the architects that are being selected are going to take on board everything that has been documented and already tried before.



I do hope that we get good public amenity out of it and not just new private spaces. South Bank is a great example of doing a massive piece of urban renewal. Some people might call it gentrification but 30 years on, everyone seems to think it’s a great thing. It’s a very tough line to walk. As we’re returning to the Riverside ferry terminal, White points out one of her favourite apartment buildings in Brisbane – 443 Queen Street – a collaboration between WOHA Architects, Architectus, TCL, and RPS Landscape Architecture. Do you think we’re skipping over generations of design because of our love of the Queenslander? Totally. It’s an amazing thing to sort of not learn from past mistakes. Everyone seems to look back on old projects, saying, “I wish we kept that”, without realising that we’re doing the same thing now.



I would say there’s very little incentive for developers to be able to keep those buildings. A lot of extra work has to go into peeling apart a building and seeing what’s usable. Without the policy to incentivise that shift in thinking to building sustainably, thinking about material and energy of life, we’re probably not going to see it if we just rely on the market. It does come back to better policy and people putting the pressure on what they want to see in their city. Loading White and her mother are behind the renovation of Miss Midgley’s, a pink heritage-listed boutique hotel on James Street in New Farm – and she has strong opinions about colour on Brisbane streets. You’ve spoken online about the colour of Queenslanders and the heritage aspect of them. Why are you so passionate about this?



I’m incredibly passionate about keeping Brisbane’s identity. Of course, housing is going to change and we’re going to have a big city, of course we are, but there are lessons in our architecture that we shouldn’t lose, colour being one of them. I’m a big believer that Brisbane should be pink – the whole city. Because when we come in and we paint everything white, it’s an incredibly anonymous colour. It doesn’t say anything about our landscapes, our flora or our fauna. Related Article City life Pub Choir queen on why singing is ‘the closest to magic we can get’ Queenslanders were always colourful, and it’s to do with shifting glare in our hot, hot Brisbane sun. You can keep all of our colours light and bright, you can do sage greens and pastel blues and beautiful buttercup yellows, you’re still going to reflect a lot of heat, but we’re keeping that core Brisbane identity. The reason I’m so passionate about that, aside from the fact that I think it’s beautiful, is that if we really want to be a global city, we need an identity that is ours. And when we import things that didn’t come from this place, we risk looking like, and feeling like, everything else.



Brisbane was built on this incredible stone bed called the Brisbane tuff. It’s this beautiful pink sandstone that was used to build all of our heritage buildings. It was cut by convicts. It’s also a beautiful relationship with a landscape that we built over the top of, and there’s this idea in design called a sense of place, making sure that what you’re developing responds to the very specific location it’s being built in. Should the Olympic stadium be pink? I think the Olympic stadium should be pink, and not just with lighting, do it permanent. World.title: On board the best ship in ‘the world’s most luxurious fleet’
World.content:
InspirationCruises On board the best ship in ‘the world’s most luxurious fleet’ Julietta Jameson July 22, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It’s night four of a 12-night cruise aboard Seven Seas Grandeur when, at precisely 6pm, a bell rings out across the ship’s PA system signalling the beginning of the “block party”, a Regent Seven Seas Cruises’ tradition. Guests in varying states of dress, from bathrobes to cocktail wear, spill out of their suites and into the hallways where cheery room attendants serve drinks and canapes. The captain and cruise director are making their way deck by deck, corridor by corridor, shaking hands with passengers as they go, attempting to break the captain’s own record of 24-odd minutes to cover the entire vessel. The Regent Seven Seas Grandeur carries 744 passengers and three Picassos. Our hallway on deck six is the final stop. While we wait, a bubbly woman with a broad New Jersey accent makes friends with everyone and, when the captain arrives, hugs him like a long-lost brother. With familiarity like that, it’s no wonder the record is not broken tonight. New Jersey tells me she and her husband have accumulated some 350 nights onboard various Regent ships. I’ll later encounter others who have clocked up hundreds as well. Repeat customers are so plentiful, in fact, it seems newbies such as me are very much in the minority. “How many Regent cruises have you done?” becomes such a common conversation starter this feels less like a cruise cohort and more like a well-heeled cult.



From the get-go, I can easily see why the cruise line inspires such fervent devotion. When I first sight the 744-passenger Seven Seas Grandeur awaiting us at Civitavecchia (Rome), her gracious, classical all-white exterior gleaming in the sun impresses mightily. 



There’s a spa deck but no waterslides on a ship that caters to adults first and foremost. There’s also a walk-in closet, which is handy, because I’ve packed like I’m European royalty in response to a stated dress code of “elegant casual” with higher sartorial requirements in the evening. Still, my suite has hanging space, drawers and shelves enough for four times what I’ve brought with me. As sartorially prepared as I am, I am also one of those “very happy with my own company” types, so while revelling in discovering the myriad features of what will be my digs for nearly two weeks, an invitation on the bed from hostess Carlotta to join the “solo travellers’ social” that first evening gives me pause. In the spirit of good cruising etiquette, however, I attend, and I’m pleasantly surprised, becoming a regular at the nightly get-togethers. We’re a group of 10 or so women and just one man, John from the north of England, who’s on his 81st cruise – not all on Regent Seven Seas Cruises. Like many older guests, he doesn’t get off the ship and tells me the things he loves most about being on Regent are not having to cook, clean or do his own washing. Laundry is – blissfully for John, and me for that matter – included. The theatrical interior of main restaurant Compass Rose.



The art collection includes a life-sized glass cherry blossom tree. Out of the mostly American and English passenger list (with a smattering of Australians, New Zealanders and other nationalities) there are plenty of livelier guests who take in the shows, prop up the late-night bars, make friends and memories. In that, it’s a horses for courses kind of cruise, catering for the quiet to the extrovert, the night owl to the early riser. I am the latter – and find my tribe at the buffet breakfast eaten outside at La Veranda as we take in our destinations in the morning light. Perhaps the only type it doesn’t fully cater for is the kid. Regent Seven Seas welcomes them, but there are no dedicated children’s programs or facilities other than on select sailings. There are certainly no waterslides or other rides. It’s a classic, adult kind of ship. On this cruise, I quickly notice there are none younger than mid-teens and then only a few of those, some of them travelling with grandparents. One granddad tells me that while Regent is undeniably expensive, he did the maths, and figured it to be value for money for his holiday, because of its all-inclusive model. Premium spirits and cocktails, free-flowing wines, speciality dining and quality shore excursions are all included, as well as the aforementioned laundry. Extra costs come in the form of special wines, spa treatments, sessions in the cooking school, liquor tastings and premium excursions. But for those who want to splash the extra cash, the boutique is full of Fendi, Hermes and Gucci.



Chartreuse restaurant serves classic French fare with a modern twist. On this sailing, it’s also selling jewellery in line with the itinerary’s theme: “spotlight on Faberge”. Sarah Faberge is onboard. She’s the godmother of Seven Seas Grandeur and the steward of the modern-day incarnation of the eponymous jewellery house, her ancestors having founded it in pre-revolution Russia. She features in a series of talks, together with other Faberge experts including Dorothy McFerrin, owner of one of the world’s greatest private collections. The synergy is a bespoke-to-Grandeur Faberge egg on display in the ship’s main reception area, a frothy confection made as an ode to the oceans, with fine blue lacquering and ripples of diamonds and pearls set to resemble waves. It’s worth more than $US1 million ($1.4 million). (Soon, the whole Faberge thing has me a bit obsessed. I start using the ship’s Wi-Fi to trawl eBay and Facebook Marketplace for hidden Russian treasure. You never know your luck, after all.) Grandeur’s own Faberge egg may be a special piece, but it is far from out of place. This ship is pimped. Deckchairs await passengers drawn to the infinity-edge plunge pool.



Nearly 140,000 kilograms of marble, along with shining chrome, gleaming glass, upholstery and drapery befitting the most upmarket residence and 503 stunning crystal chandeliers feature in a contemporary decor scheme that manages to be both homely and awe-inspiring. A multimillion-dollar art collection comprising 1600 pieces, including three Picassos, helps. Sculptures surprise at every turn, including a life-sized glass cherry blossom tree in the entrance to speciality dining restaurant Pacific Rim. The Picassos hang in another – the New York-style steakhouse Prime 7 – underlining the meticulous attention to detail that has gone into creating restaurants that play into high-end big-city establishments more than a shipboard fantasy of what such an eatery might be. Even the French restaurant, Chartreuse, resists twee as it achieves exquisiteness. The main restaurant, Compass Rose, is perhaps the most theatrical, with an art nouveau-style scheme of organic forms that cleverly divide the cavernous space into zones while providing glamour. That’s complemented by ocean-themed Versace crockery and luxury glassware. The Grandeur’s soaring atrium.



I eat most nights at Compass Rose with the social solos – and note how many of my friends order the Dover sole. It looks plain and boring to me. Then someone mentions it’s fancy – I Google it and discover it’s been called “the poshest fish in the world”. I figure I’m on the poshest ship in the world, I may as well try it. It is delicious – as are desserts. The latter are thankfully reasonably portioned because I do not hold back. With that in mind, my strategy for picking shore excursions should be finding those most likely to invite the highest step count. But the main motivator behind my choices is actually to find the least touristy. It means I join buses with like-minded travellers who favour curiosity over checklist tourism. Serendipitously, it also often means high step counts. In Barcelona, we walk for a solid three hours exploring Montjuic with its green parklands, quiet monuments and expansive views over the city. Out of Livorno, I head to the Ligurian village of Lerici, famous for being the place where Romantic poet Percy Bysshe Shelley was living before he drowned, and where his mate, Lord Byron, legendarily swam the 7.5 kilometres across from Portovenere for a visit.



It’s not exactly off the beaten track, but it’s not the main game on the Ligurian coast either, and the feeling there is relaxed, real and casually welcoming. The Grandeur Suite’s spacious living room. The Concierge Suite boasts a king-size bed and private balcony. We jump in rubber runabouts and cruise the Bay of Poets, admiring fortifications, old marble quarries and a waterbound statue of the Virgin Mary revered by fishermen. The Cinque Terre is nearby. Other excursions from our ship have gone there. Before our guide drops us off in stunning, gelati-coloured Portovenere for free-time wandering, he says, “I go to the Cinque Terre, I get bored. But every time I come here, it is like coming for the first time.”



Those of us from the ship, his guests, congratulate ourselves on our choice. In Monte Carlo, while other ships lay at anchor away from port, we dock in front of the casino. This is entertainment enough: preparations for the F1 Grand Prix are in their final stages, an armada of superyachts are our direct neighbours, and the buzz of the tiny city’s waterfront is palpable. Related Article Cruises It’s the ultimate autumn trip, but this cruise is brilliant any time My excursion takes me out of town to Saint-Jean-Cap-Ferrat in France, where I roam the pink palace and nine themed gardens of the Villa Ephrussi de Rothschild, a romantic interlude in the belle epoque. Further gorgeous days in A Coruna, Spain, Honfleur, France and the English countryside from Southampton, plus sea days spent doing trivia, playing board and card games, lying by the pool, enjoying the spa’s wet areas and taking in shows and talks, make life onboard Grandeur a lovely slice of la dolce vita.



For me, this is the perfect way to cruise the Mediterranean and North Atlantic, in step with the things I love about the Continent: its vintage glamour, cultivated ease and enduring sense of style. In fact, I could easily clock up hundreds of days on Regent Seven Seas myself. I just need to find a forgotten Faberge to fund them. THE DETAILS CRUISE

Regent Seven Seas Cruises will carry out a number of European sailings in 2027 (and still some in 2026). One is on board Seven Seas Grandeur: “A Grecian Summer Venice (Fusina) to Barcelona”, an 11-night journey departing June 2, 2027. From $12,910 a person. Additional inclusions to those mentioned are specialty coffees, customised in-suite mini bar, pre-paid gratuities, Wi-Fi and 24-hour in-suite dining.

MORE

World.title: Adam Liaw’s simple stove-top trick for a richer, deeper lamb stew
World.content:
This comforting classic English lamb stew might be simple, but it relies on doing the basics well. A little patience and attention to detail will go a long way to achieving a rich, brown hot pot with deliciously golden potatoes on top.

When the potatoes are tender, uncover the pot and dot with the remaining 20g of butter then grill until the potatoes are golden and crisp at the edges. Remove from the oven and stand for at least 10 minutes before serving.

Bring to a simmer, then layer the top of the dish with the potatoes, starting at one side of the dish and moving to the other so the potatoes overlap in a fish-scale pattern. Dot the top of the potatoes with another 20g of the butter, scatter with the remaining thyme leaves and season well with salt. Cover and transfer to the oven for 1½ hours.

Add another 20g of the butter, reduce the heat slightly and fry the onions for about 10 minutes until softened and browned. Stir in the flour and fry for another 5 minutes until the flour starts to brown. Add the carrots and return the lamb and any juices to the pot and mix to combine. Add the stock, Worcestershire sauce, bay leaves and thyme and season with salt.

Heat your oven to 160C fan-forced (180C conventional). Heat a large, low, double-handled casserole dish over medium heat. Add 20g of the butter and fry the lamb in small batches until well browned (see notes), seasoning each batch with salt and black pepper. Remove to a plate.

Masterclass

Brown meat in multiple, smaller batches

The Maillard reactions that turn meat brown add deep complexity to a hot pot, but too often we don’t take the time to do it right. In previous columns, I’ve shared tips such as browning meat in larger pieces, or browning over medium heat for a more even colour. The goal here is to get a beautiful sear on the meat before it starts releasing liquid and cooling down your pot.

Arguably, the easiest way to achieve this is simply to brown less meat at a time.

The best recipes from Australia's leading chefs straight to your inbox. Sign up

Some recipes call for browning in two or three batches, but I often do it in many more. Smaller batches allow your pot to retain more heat; five or six small batches of just a few pieces each will often give you better results, faster, than overloading the pan.

As a rule of thumb, I keep half of the surface area at the base of the pot uncovered for each batch. This prevents overcrowding that drops the pan’s temperature and causes the meat to stew in its own juices rather than brown.

In Adam's French onion beef stew, he cooks the onions, stirring occasionally, for up to 40 minutes to coax out their sweetness. William Meppem

Browning onions puts you in control

How you brown your onions is one of the most effective ways to control the finished stew’s flavour. We can thank the delicious chemistry of onions and other alliums for this. Cook them fast, and they will brown quickly through Maillard reactions between carbohydrates and sulfurous peptides, giving the dish a savouriness and rich mouthfeel. Cook them slowly, and the starches will convert enzymatically to simple sugars, which brown through slightly different chemical pathways to deliver a mellow sweetness.

Cooking onions quickly over medium heat results in a stew that is savoury and less sweet, while cooking them slowly over low heat produces a sweeter base. You see this principle in action with caramelised onions, which take upwards of 40 minutes to become richly sweet.

But for a Lancashire hot pot, we can actually have the best of both worlds. A quicker fry of about 10 minutes gives us that baseline savouriness, and then the long braise in the oven brings out the sweetness. If you want even more sweetness, you can always cook your onions for longer at the start to caramelise them further.

Grill Adam’s roasted scalloped potatoes at the end to give them a golden glow. William Meppem

Browning applies to potatoes, too

I know you’re probably sick of me going on about browning by now, but the final step you need for a spectacular Lancashire hot pot is a layer of golden-brown potatoes on top. Using a good pot with a solid, heavy lid allows the potatoes to steam beautifully on top of the stew while the lamb cooks. However, once the pot is uncovered, you need dry, direct heat to crisp them up.

This can be difficult to achieve in modern electric ovens, which infuriatingly often won’t let you force the overhead grill to stay on if the oven has already reached its target temperature. Even if you crank the oven to its maximum, the grill element will shut off the moment the oven reaches that ambient temperature.

If you’re lucky enough to have two ovens, you can transfer the pot from its hot, steamy oven into a cold, dry one; this gives the overhead grill plenty of time to directly brown the top before the oven heats up. If you only have one oven, simply leave the oven door cracked open for a minute or two to let the ambient heat escape. This cools the oven down enough for the grill element to stay on a little longer.

Serve pickled cucumber and lingonberry jam with rich dishes such as Adam's Swedish meatballs. William Meppem

On the side

Nearly all rich, braised dishes need a bright, tangy side dish to cut through the fat. It’s a pairing we see time and time again in global cuisines – from Indian curries served with tangy pickles and chutneys to Swedish meatballs paired with pickled cucumbers.

The classic accompaniment for a Lancashire hot pot is pickled red cabbage. You can easily pickle it yourself ahead of time, but if you’re short on time, saute or braise shredded red cabbage with a little butter, sugar and apple cider vinegar for a brilliant, fast alternative.

World.title: ASX set to advance, tech stocks push Wall Street higher; Google’s new AI offerings
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to advance, tech stocks push Wall Street higher; Google’s new AI offerings Stan Choe July 22, 2026 — 5:13am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

More gains for makers of computer chips and other winners of the artificial-intelligence boom are carrying Wall Street higher. The S&P 500 climbed 0.9 per cent. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 361 points, or 0.7 per cent, i mid-afternoon trade, and the Nasdaq composite was 1.4 per cent higher. AI stocks once again were at the centre of the action on Wall Street, and they rose for a second straight day after tumbling the week before. AP The Australian sharemarket is set to advance, with futures at 4.53am AEST pointing to a gain of 16 points or 0.2 per cent, at the open. The ASX closed flat on Tuesday. The Australian dollar was trading at US70.05¢. AI stocks once again were at the centre of the action on Wall Street, and they rose for a second straight day after tumbling the week before.



After rocketing higher because of the boom in investment in AI chips and data centres, they’ve come under pressure in recent weeks on worries that they shot too high. Concerns are also weighing that investment in AI may fall off if it doesn’t produce as much profit and productivity as hoped. Related Article Opinion

Trade wars Trump wants to make his trade wall bigger and better than ever before Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Micron Technology jumped 12.7 per cent and added to its 1.9 per cent gain from the day before, coming off its 13.3 per cent drop from last week. Nvidia added 1.5 per cent, and they were the two strongest forces lifting the S&P 500. The gains came despite more climbs for oil prices, and Brent crude oil topped $US90 per barrel because of continued attacks between the United States and Iran. It rose 2 per cent to $US91.01 and briefly got near $US92 for the first time in more than five weeks. That’s up from less than $US72 early this month, which is roughly where it was before the war with Iran. Rising oil prices are threatening a reacceleration of inflation, just as increases for prices were slowing more than economists expected. That in turn could push the Federal Reserve and other central banks to raise interest rates to keep a lid on inflation, which would slow economies and undercut prices for stocks and other investments.



The yield on the 10-year Treasury edged up to 4.63 per cent from 4.60 per cent late Monday and from just 3.97 per cent before the war with Iran began. On Wall Street, several stronger-than-expected profit reports from big US companies helped stocks to strengthen despite the added pressure. 3M climbed 6.9 per cent after topping analysts’ expectations for both profit and revenue in the latest quarter. It also raised its forecast for profit over the full year of 2026. Hasbro rallied 7.9 per cent after the toy maker said its Magic: The Gathering game topped $US500 million in revenue for a quarter for the first time. It also raised its revenue forecast for the year. General Motors cruised 4.8 per cent higher after the automaker’s profit and revenue for the latest quarter beat analysts’ expectations and CEO Mary Barra said demand in North America remains strong.



They helped offset a drop for Danaher, which slid 11.4 per cent even though it likewise topped analysts’ expectations for profit and revenue. Analysts pointed to its forecast for an underlying measure of revenue growth for the summer, which was weaker than Wall Street expected. Alphabet slid 0.9 per cent after Google released a trio of cheaper versions of its Gemini AI model, but shared no timing updates for the flagship Pro model that has already seen its launch delayed by several weeks. The new model lineup includes Gemini 3.6 Flash and Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite, updated versions of its lightweight offerings, designed for use cases that do not require the most cutting-edge technology. Google also unveiled a new lightweight variant, Gemini 3.5 Flash Cyber, which is tailored towards cybersecurity applications. Homebuilder D.R. Horton slipped 0.8 per cent despite topping profit and revenue expectations for the latest quarter. Executive Chairman David Auld said it’s still feeling the effects of affordability concerns in the housing market and caution among potential home buyers. Mortgage rates have already climbed to their highest level in nearly a year because of higher Treasury yields in the bond market. That could force D.R. Horton to offer more incentives to homebuyers in the current quarter, which would cut into its profits.



Related Article Opinion

Online shopping $900 million fines look like the cost of doing business for giant shopping apps Elizabeth Knight Business columnist Companies broadly are under pressure to deliver strong growth in profit and revenue because of how high their stock prices have shot. Indexes are near their records, even with the recent shakiness for AI stocks. In stock markets abroad, indexes rose modestly in Europe. The United Kingdom’s FTSE 100 added 0.6 per cent as new Prime Minister Andy Burnham hosted his first Cabinet meeting. In Asia, stocks swung more. South Korea’s Kospi jumped 3.6 per cent on strong gains for its two dominant stocks. Both Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix have been big beneficiaries of the AI boom, and the Kospi has soared 60 per cent so far this year even with its 20 per cent drop for July so far. Tokyo’s Nikkei 225 climbed 3.3 per cent after returning from Monday’s holiday, while indexes rose 1.8 per cent in Shanghai and edged down by less than 0.1 per cent in Hong Kong.

World.title: I earn $80,000 a year in dividends. Should I reinvest, or add it to my super?
World.content:
MoneyPlanning & budgetingAsk an expert Opinion I earn $80,000 a year in dividends. Should I reinvest, or add it to my super? Noel Whittaker Money columnist July 22, 2026 — 5:08am

July 22, 2026 — 5:08am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

I am 58 and have a portfolio of blue-chip shares worth about $1.67 million, producing about $80,000 a year in fully franked dividends. I have owned the shares for 20 years, and they have unrealised capital gains of about $1.3 million. All dividends are re-invested. I expect to retire in two years. My salary is about $130,000 including overtime and penalty rates, and with my dividend income, my taxable income is about $205,000 to $210,000 a year. I salary-sacrifice $20,800 into super each year, with employer contributions of about $11,500, bringing me close to the concessional contribution cap. I also pay Division 293 tax. My super consists of about $715,000 in a government PSS defined benefit scheme and $805,000 in another account, giving me total super of about $1.52 million. With Labor’s capital gains tax changes due to commence on July 1, 2027, I am concerned about the future CGT implications for my share portfolio. Should I continue reinvesting my dividends through DRPs, or would I be better off taking the dividends in cash and making non-concessional contributions to super instead? A healthy portfolio of blue-chip shares can produce plenty of tasty dividends. Simon Letch There is no doubt the coming changes have introduced a whole new level of complexity for investors with diversified share portfolios. Fortunately, you’ve held your shares for a long time, so the post-2027 treatment of any capital gains should not be too onerous. As capital gains are added to your taxable income, it makes sense to defer any major sales until after you retire, when your taxable income will be much lower. Meanwhile, if you have capital losses available, consider using them to offset gains and crystallise some gains before June 30, 2027.



I agree you should take future dividends in cash and maximise non-concessional contributions to super. The amount you can contribute will depend on the notional value of your defined benefit entitlement. Editor's pick Opinion

Ask an expert Should we delay our retirement to help pay our daughter’s uni fees? Paul Benson Money contributor I have read on several social media sites that, before passing away, you should remove your children (even adults in their thirties) as direct beneficiaries of your assets. Instead, you should place all your assets, including bank accounts, jewellery and super, into a revocable trust and name your children as beneficiaries of the trust. Supposedly, this allows them to bypass the lengthy probate process and gain immediate access to the assets. Does this also apply to irrevocable trusts and testamentary trusts? Estate planning solicitor Rachael Rofe tells me the short answer is that this advice is generally incorrect in an Australian context. Much of what circulates on social media is based on US estate planning, where revocable living trusts are commonly used. Australia has a very different legal system. In Australia, assets already owned by a trust are generally not personally owned by you and therefore do not usually form part of your estate on death. However, transferring all your assets into a trust shortly before death is rarely straightforward.



It can trigger tax and stamp duty consequences, affect asset protection and create practical complications, so it is often inappropriate. Revocable trusts are not commonly used in Australia as an estate-planning vehicle as they are in the United States. Assets genuinely owned by an irrevocable trust generally do not form part of your estate, but establishing one is a major decision with significant legal and tax implications. Testamentary trusts are different again. They are created by your will and come into existence only after your death. They do not avoid probate because the will generally must first be admitted to probate before the estate can be administered and the testamentary trusts established. It is also worth remembering that not every estate requires probate. Whether probate is needed depends on the nature of the assets and the requirements of the institutions holding them. For most Australians, good estate planning is not about avoiding probate at all costs. It is about ensuring assets pass to the right people in the most tax-effective and asset-protective manner, while minimising the risk of family disputes.



I am 61, retired, and have just sold my investment property. Since retiring, I have withdrawn more than $100,000 from my super. Tax-wise, would it be beneficial to contribute some of the sale proceeds back into super? I haven’t made any super contributions since 2020, and my super balance is well under $1 million, so I am wondering whether non-concessional contributions are an option. How much could I contribute without exceeding the limits, and how can I determine the amount that would be most tax-effective? Editor's pick Opinion

Hip pocket Hoarding receipts? These are the ones you actually need to keep Dominic Powell Money Editor Since the taxation changes announced in the recent budget, superannuation has become by far the most tax-effective investment vehicle for older Australians. Given you are 61 and retired, you have no problems accessing your super. And because your super balance is well under the $2.1 million threshold, you have considerable flexibility. You can contribute $32,500 as a tax-deductible concessional contribution, but I doubt you would need to do this unless you have taxable income you wish to reduce. The more appropriate option appears to be non-concessional contributions. These are limited to $130,000 a year, but you can bring forward three years’ worth of contributions and contribute up to $390,000. There is no contributions tax or withdrawal tax on these non-concessional contributions.



My mother recently passed away and my sibling and I inherited her home. She bought the property in 1990 and lived in it as her principal place of residence until 2014. She then moved into my apartment, where she lived with me rent-free for the next 12 years until her death in 2026. She owned no other property during that time but rented out her home after moving out. We understand that if we sell the property, there may be capital gains tax because it was rented. However, we have also been told that if we do not sell the property within two years of our mother’s death, any later sale would attract capital gains tax on the entire ownership period from 1990 until 2026. Is that correct? No, that is wrong. That section protects the deceased’s home from CGT if sold within two years of death. It cannot apply to your mother’s circumstances because it was not covered with her main residence exemption at the date of death. Even utilising the six-year rule will not bring you up to her date of death. The CGT calculation goes back to the time it was first rented, starting with the market value then. As she was not covering another property with her main residence exemption, she can continue to cover that property for six years after it was rented out, so only half of the gain you calculate will be taxable and then half that amount for the 50 per cent CGT discount. Noel Whittaker is author of Retirement Made Simple and other books on personal finance. Questions to: noel@noelwhittaker.com.au



Advice given in this article is general in nature and is not intended to influence readers’ decisions about investing or financial products. They should always seek their own professional advice that takes into account their own personal circumstances before making any financial decisions. World.title: Investors could be $600k worse off when buying new builds
World.content:
MoneyInvestingProperty investment Investors could be $600k worse off when buying new builds Sue Williams July 22, 2026 — 5:06am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Property investors rushing to negatively gear new build homes in light of the looming budget changes have been warned they could be making a huge mistake, with modelling suggesting buyers of older, established homes will be far better off. Research by Get Rare Properties found that, when comparing two $700,000 properties held for 20 years, the owner of the established build will be $592,000 ahead, even after all the tax advantages given to the new build. New builds will be the only ones eligible for buyers to negatively gear from next July. Natalie Boog Founder Rasti Vaibhav, who previously spent 15 years managing $2 billion of institutional portfolios at Westpac and AMP Capital, said there’s no situation here where a new build ends up the better option. As part of a sweeping range of new tax measures revealed in this year’s Federal Budget, investors will no longer be able to negatively gear properties bought after July 1 next year, unless they are new builds. Existing properties that are already owned and negatively geared will be unaffected.



Vaibhav crunched the figures considering the tax benefit of a new build of about $231,000 over 20 years, from both negative gearing and depreciation. Against that, however, he used data from long-run analysis from the Property Investment Professionals of Australia that found capital growth from new builds averaged 3 to 5 per cent, against that of established properties of 5 to 8 per cent, leaving a growth shortfall of around $1.17 million. Editor's pick Investing ‘The days of multiple properties are over’: How to invest after the budget Then there was the capital gains tax (CGT) with the older property paying $445,000 more. The net outcome, however, was still that the established wins by $592,000, while, at CoreLogic’s actual decade growth rates – 3.4 versus 5.8 per cent – it comes out top by $430,000. “The reality is, if you want to avoid tax, then lose money,” Vaibhav says. “But a tax strategy isn’t as good as one that concentrates on building wealth. The government wanted to keep negative gearing for new property to encourage demand and then the supply.” “The consumer should really be concentrating more on making their money work harder long-term than on saving tax short-term. They should instead be buying established property in good locations, close to job hubs and shopping centres where people want to live rather than new builds on the city fringes, and as their equity grows quicker, they can reinvest that to create exponential compounding benefits.”



That’s a view that’s supported by a number of buyers’ agents. Kane Dury, principal of Discover Buyers Agency, for instance, says the Government has created a powerful tax incentive that should still not override sound investment judgement. “It puts us at risk of the tail wagging the dog,” Dury said. “What makes a good investment is where demand is greater than supply and so much of the value of an investment lies in the scarcity of land, which appreciates while the building on it depreciates.” [Tax breaks are] not so attractive if the property underperforms for a long period. Kane Dury, principal of Discover Buyers Agency “So you want more land and less house, or an older house, rather than a new build where you’re paying more for the dwelling on less land. And tax benefits and depreciation – for which you can substitute the word ‘loss’ – aren’t going to fix that.” One problem with some new builds too, Dury says, is that the area in which they’re constructed is often, as a result, saturated with supply, making it difficult to sell the property when it comes time to get out. As a result, established properties in popular locations are usually a much better bet.



“Tax is a big pain point, so if someone says we’re going to minimise it for you, that’s very attractive,” Dury said. “But it’s not so attractive if the property underperforms for a long period.” Of course, the investment in an established property needs to be sound in order for it to work, Vaibhav points out. “You always want less risk and better returns and not every market is good,” he said. “There might be another reason you want to save on tax, too. But for most people, the aim is to build wealth for their retirement years, to support their kids with education and live off passive income. So it’s critical they make sound judgements now.” Expert tips on how to save, invest and make the most of your money delivered to your inbox every Sunday.

World.title: One-pan 30-minute pork, sage and fennel lasagne
World.content:
Step 1 Preheat the oven grill to high. Heat the oil in a large deep oven-proof frying pan over high heat. Add the sage leaves and cook for 30 seconds or until crisp. Remove the sage and set aside. Add the fennel, sausage mince and garlic, breaking up the mince with the back of a wooden spoon. Cook for 5 minutes or until the fennel is caramelised.

Step 2 Add the tomatoes and stock and bring the mixture to a simmer. Add the pasta sheets, submerging them in the liquid, and cook for 15 minutes, covered, until they are just tender and the sauce has reduced.

Step 3 Meanwhile, combine the mascarpone, parmesan, mozzarella and 60ml of water in a medium bowl. Season with salt and mix well. Spoon the cheese mixture over the lasagne. Place the frying pan on a baking tray and place it under the grill, then cook for 6-8 minutes or until the top is bubbling and golden.

World.title: How Adriano put up a small home in a day - and made it fire-resistant
World.content:
PropertyNewsConstruction How Adriano put up a small home in a day - and made it fire-resistant Sue Williams July 22, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The morning after a ferocious bushfire tore through a NSW South Coast community, architect Adriano Pupilli returned to find out what was left of his holiday cottage and the innovative prefab flatpack bush cabin he’d invented, designed and built himself. Both were still standing but, as he set about doing repairs, he decided he’d pivot to creating an easy-to-construct modular tiny house that would also be bushfire resistant instead. Adriano and his family at their tiny home. Adriano Pupilli Architects “My pregnant wife and our three-year-old son escaped when they were picked up by a fishing group from down the coast at Ulladulla,” said Pupilli. “Then I had to get out when everything was on fire just before the front came. It was pretty scary. “I went back, thinking everything will have gone, but the fire jumped over the site, so the buildings were damaged and charred but, crazily, had survived. So this time, I thought I’d design a self-contained cabin that was highly resistant to bushfire.”



The final Casa Manyana tiny house prototype has been rated a lofty Bushfire Attack Level (BAL) 40 – suitable for a very high bushfire-risk environment, capable of withstanding extreme radiant heat and probably direct exposure to flames. Just like his first IMBY (in my back yard) model, it continues the same spirit of DIY assembly, sustainable materials and a modular kit of parts that all slot perfectly together, with no need for nails, screws or glue in the structure. The home is made from a modular kit. Adriano Pupilli Architects As such, it could be an adjunct to a regular house in a bushfire area, increasing space or providing safe accommodation for guests, or could be used after a fire when a family needs somewhere to live while rebuilding. “It’s a great idea,” said Dr Hugo Moline, lecturer in architectural practice & design at Newcastle University, who has followed the progress of the project. “With the housing crisis, we really need a lot more dwellings, and this can be erected quickly on a little plot of land, can work for multi-generational families and can help people back onto their land after a disaster.



“It’s so much more comfortable and dignified and safe than a caravan or camping or living out of a shipping container. The components can be brought easily onto a site, it’s affordable and accessible and you don’t have to be massively skilled to put it together.” The retail price for a Casa Manyana – named after the village 215km south of Sydney where Pupilli built it after the devastating fires of 2019-2020 – would be about $75,000 to $120,000 depending on size and design options. The kitchenette and sleeping loft. Adriano Pupilli Architects The form of his own 18-square-metre cabin, with a two-square-metre deck, a living space with a sofa bed, sleeping loft, a kitchenette and bathroom was put up, with the help of two friends, in a day, and turned into a fully clad structure in four. Tiling, electrical work and plumbing took extra. A protective outer layer of zincalume-rolled cladding and fibre cement creates a resilient structure, while plantation pine and plywood ensure a warm, welcoming interior. There’s high-performance insulation for thermal comfort, and operable louvre windows are meshed for bushfire resistance and cross-ventilation.



At Ember Bushfire Consulting, Peter Hague says much of his work lies in assessing the risks of new development in bushfire zones. “But this could be a good idea and, with such a high BAL rating, especially for people already affected by bushfires,” he said. Archicentre Australia director Peter Georgiev says anything that can assist people in bushfire-prone areas is welcome. The home is fast to construct but plumbing took extra time. Adriano Pupilli Architects “That’s especially if it’s something that keeps the cost down, and allows them to keep a foothold on their property,” he said. “We’re really trying to deal with these sorts of issues, so anything we can do to encourage these kind of innovations.” Dr Iftekhar Ahmed, associate professor in construction management/disaster resilience at the School of Architecture and Built Environment at Newcastle University, says it’s important to have structures that can minimise bushfire damage, give people time to escape and help them to return and rebuild.



Related Article Residential property How two architects reimagined their own homes “We need better options than what’s already available in the market,” he said. “This could be a good idea but it needs testing in bushfire conditions and needs to be explored in greater detail to see if it’s a viable option.” Pupilli is keen to cooperate with national or state organisations looking for good options in bushfire areas. “I wanted to do emergency housing or additional housing that would be different to the typical dongas and shipping container pods,” he said. “At the same time, they are also resilient to danger and more sympathetic to the landscape and a delight to be inside. “They are architect-designed, site-specific options that allow people to get back on the land and rebuild quicker and be safer in the elements.”

World.title: What’s Brisbane’s identity beyond the old Queenslander? Izzie White has an idea
World.content:
Welcome to CityChats, where Brisbane Times meets our city’s most interesting characters on our most iconic form of transport. This week, architecture influencer Izzie White tells us why she’s passionate about Brisbane being pink, and how we should rethink our relationship with public space. We meet White at Riverside ferry terminal near Eagle Street on a drizzly overcast day after she ducked out of work to chat with us. Architect Izzie White. Fairfax Media How did you get into making social media content? I make short-form videos explaining how to understand modern architecture and modern city making. I studied my bachelor and masters of architecture in Brisbane. I’ve been between Melbourne and Brisbane over the last couple of years, when I’ve really got to see the difference in city making.



About a year ago, I decided the public should really know about this too, and I started making videos. I’ve had the most amazing journey being able to talk to the public online about how to understand the city going up around them. Architecture feels like something that we all love and are exposed to, and it’s around us, but it feels a little bit unattainable. Has that been your experience? Architecture has a very tough relationship with the media. A lot of what makes it into mainstream media is very expensive houses that not a lot of us are ever going to live in. If you’ve ever seen the stats, about 97 per cent of homes in Australia are done without architects, so the portion of architecture that gets covered by mainstream media is incredibly narrow. Big commercial work is very hard to talk to the media about when you’re an architect because you really have to protect your client relationships, so when you’re working for an architecture firm and you do want to put out media, you are held really tightly with what you can say.



That’s not unusual, it’s just the way of the world, but that is why we have this incredible comms bubble between what architects know and what they’re working on, and what the general public get to see and understand about their city. Related Article City life Tivoli creative director on protecting Brisbane’s iconic (and haunted) venues You’ve lived between Brisbane and Melbourne in the past few years. What is your experience watching a city like Melbourne grow compared to Brisbane? Almost every city in Australia right now is facing a similar housing conversation, and almost every city is approaching the solution in a similar way. We are increasing density to allow for more supply in our inner-city areas, and that makes a lot of sense. I think Melbourne has more pressure, with more people. It’s also a much less forgiving climate. And so they’ve had a lot of tension in where they put this new housing.



The lesson out of that, which I hope Brisbane can avoid, is that long-term planning with communities and being able to bring them on board with where more housing is going to go is a much better solution than rapid rezoning and sending out panic alarms. It can absolutely be done, it takes longer, and in a public conversation that focuses mainly on housing supply, there’s much less focus on master-planning for livable communities. Do you think we need to be cautious of sprawl, and is it being addressed? What we have to be cautious of is relying on houses and apartments to do everything. Australia has the lowest-density cities in the world. There is a direct relationship between how much time you spend in the private home and how much time you spend in the public realm. If you don’t have that third bedroom, chances are you’re going to the park, or you’re looking for a studio that you can rent in the civic realm, and that’s what’s so cool about big cities.



When you do travel to the Tokyos, Londons, New Yorks, they have this jam-packed street life. That is what density supports and facilitates, but it also needs that public realm built in. Related Article Arts ‘We thought it might go straight in the bin’: The design rule the architects of GOMA ignored So I think the lesson is that the infrastructure has to come with the housing to support that, because otherwise, where does everyone go if they don’t have the backyard and there’s no park being built? Do you think we’re doing that well enough? Are we building the parks and the extra elements around supporting that density? Everyone could do it better. Brisbane is lucky in the sense that it has this built-in public space – being the river – along almost the whole length of it.



Our weather also facilitates being able to pop down for free, go for a bike ride in a big outdoor public open space, so we’re very lucky that we have that. Once we get away from those inner-city areas with that already good and built-up amenity, we do need to be really mindful that we’re building in civic and community facilities to facilitate that public life. Without it, you risk exacerbating urban challenges that are already felt, like traffic, isolation, things like that. We’re about to go through, I guess, a bit of an identity change, to reshape our identity somewhat, with starting the Olympics build. There’s going to be quite a lot of transformation of the river itself. It just feels like we’re about to embark on something that’s going to change it quite dramatically. Are you worried about that? I’m not worried about the Olympics speeding up development. I think the Olympics have been going around for a long time now for a lot of major cities, and there are a lot of amazing lessons to be learnt from all of those. I have full faith that the architects that are being selected are going to take on board everything that has been documented and already tried before.



I do hope that we get good public amenity out of it and not just new private spaces. South Bank is a great example of doing a massive piece of urban renewal. Some people might call it gentrification but 30 years on, everyone seems to think it’s a great thing. It’s a very tough line to walk. As we’re returning to the Riverside ferry terminal, White points out one of her favourite apartment buildings in Brisbane – 443 Queen Street – a collaboration between WOHA Architects, Architectus, TCL, and RPS Landscape Architecture. Do you think we’re skipping over generations of design because of our love of the Queenslander? Totally. It’s an amazing thing to sort of not learn from past mistakes. Everyone seems to look back on old projects, saying, “I wish we kept that”, without realising that we’re doing the same thing now.



I would say there’s very little incentive for developers to be able to keep those buildings. A lot of extra work has to go into peeling apart a building and seeing what’s usable. Without the policy to incentivise that shift in thinking to building sustainably, thinking about material and energy of life, we’re probably not going to see it if we just rely on the market. It does come back to better policy and people putting the pressure on what they want to see in their city. Loading White and her mother are behind the renovation of Miss Midgley’s, a pink heritage-listed boutique hotel on James Street in New Farm – and she has strong opinions about colour on Brisbane streets. You’ve spoken online about the colour of Queenslanders and the heritage aspect of them. Why are you so passionate about this?



I’m incredibly passionate about keeping Brisbane’s identity. Of course, housing is going to change and we’re going to have a big city, of course we are, but there are lessons in our architecture that we shouldn’t lose, colour being one of them. I’m a big believer that Brisbane should be pink – the whole city. Because when we come in and we paint everything white, it’s an incredibly anonymous colour. It doesn’t say anything about our landscapes, our flora or our fauna. Related Article City life Pub Choir queen on why singing is ‘the closest to magic we can get’ Queenslanders were always colourful, and it’s to do with shifting glare in our hot, hot Brisbane sun. You can keep all of our colours light and bright, you can do sage greens and pastel blues and beautiful buttercup yellows, you’re still going to reflect a lot of heat, but we’re keeping that core Brisbane identity. The reason I’m so passionate about that, aside from the fact that I think it’s beautiful, is that if we really want to be a global city, we need an identity that is ours. And when we import things that didn’t come from this place, we risk looking like, and feeling like, everything else.



Brisbane was built on this incredible stone bed called the Brisbane tuff. It’s this beautiful pink sandstone that was used to build all of our heritage buildings. It was cut by convicts. It’s also a beautiful relationship with a landscape that we built over the top of, and there’s this idea in design called a sense of place, making sure that what you’re developing responds to the very specific location it’s being built in. Should the Olympic stadium be pink? I think the Olympic stadium should be pink, and not just with lighting, do it permanent. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: On board the best ship in ‘the world’s most luxurious fleet’
World.content:
InspirationCruises On board the best ship in ‘the world’s most luxurious fleet’ Julietta Jameson July 22, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It’s night four of a 12-night cruise aboard Seven Seas Grandeur when, at precisely 6pm, a bell rings out across the ship’s PA system signalling the beginning of the “block party”, a Regent Seven Seas Cruises’ tradition. Guests in varying states of dress, from bathrobes to cocktail wear, spill out of their suites and into the hallways where cheery room attendants serve drinks and canapes. The captain and cruise director are making their way deck by deck, corridor by corridor, shaking hands with passengers as they go, attempting to break the captain’s own record of 24-odd minutes to cover the entire vessel. The Regent Seven Seas Grandeur carries 744 passengers and three Picassos. Our hallway on deck six is the final stop. While we wait, a bubbly woman with a broad New Jersey accent makes friends with everyone and, when the captain arrives, hugs him like a long-lost brother. With familiarity like that, it’s no wonder the record is not broken tonight. New Jersey tells me she and her husband have accumulated some 350 nights onboard various Regent ships. I’ll later encounter others who have clocked up hundreds as well. Repeat customers are so plentiful, in fact, it seems newbies such as me are very much in the minority. “How many Regent cruises have you done?” becomes such a common conversation starter this feels less like a cruise cohort and more like a well-heeled cult.



From the get-go, I can easily see why the cruise line inspires such fervent devotion. When I first sight the 744-passenger Seven Seas Grandeur awaiting us at Civitavecchia (Rome), her gracious, classical all-white exterior gleaming in the sun impresses mightily. 



There’s a spa deck but no waterslides on a ship that caters to adults first and foremost. There’s also a walk-in closet, which is handy, because I’ve packed like I’m European royalty in response to a stated dress code of “elegant casual” with higher sartorial requirements in the evening. Still, my suite has hanging space, drawers and shelves enough for four times what I’ve brought with me. As sartorially prepared as I am, I am also one of those “very happy with my own company” types, so while revelling in discovering the myriad features of what will be my digs for nearly two weeks, an invitation on the bed from hostess Carlotta to join the “solo travellers’ social” that first evening gives me pause. In the spirit of good cruising etiquette, however, I attend, and I’m pleasantly surprised, becoming a regular at the nightly get-togethers. We’re a group of 10 or so women and just one man, John from the north of England, who’s on his 81st cruise – not all on Regent Seven Seas Cruises. Like many older guests, he doesn’t get off the ship and tells me the things he loves most about being on Regent are not having to cook, clean or do his own washing. Laundry is – blissfully for John, and me for that matter – included. The theatrical interior of main restaurant Compass Rose.



The art collection includes a life-sized glass cherry blossom tree. Out of the mostly American and English passenger list (with a smattering of Australians, New Zealanders and other nationalities) there are plenty of livelier guests who take in the shows, prop up the late-night bars, make friends and memories. In that, it’s a horses for courses kind of cruise, catering for the quiet to the extrovert, the night owl to the early riser. I am the latter – and find my tribe at the buffet breakfast eaten outside at La Veranda as we take in our destinations in the morning light. Perhaps the only type it doesn’t fully cater for is the kid. Regent Seven Seas welcomes them, but there are no dedicated children’s programs or facilities other than on select sailings. There are certainly no waterslides or other rides. It’s a classic, adult kind of ship. On this cruise, I quickly notice there are none younger than mid-teens and then only a few of those, some of them travelling with grandparents. One granddad tells me that while Regent is undeniably expensive, he did the maths, and figured it to be value for money for his holiday, because of its all-inclusive model. Premium spirits and cocktails, free-flowing wines, speciality dining and quality shore excursions are all included, as well as the aforementioned laundry. Extra costs come in the form of special wines, spa treatments, sessions in the cooking school, liquor tastings and premium excursions. But for those who want to splash the extra cash, the boutique is full of Fendi, Hermes and Gucci.



Chartreuse restaurant serves classic French fare with a modern twist. On this sailing, it’s also selling jewellery in line with the itinerary’s theme: “spotlight on Faberge”. Sarah Faberge is onboard. She’s the godmother of Seven Seas Grandeur and the steward of the modern-day incarnation of the eponymous jewellery house, her ancestors having founded it in pre-revolution Russia. She features in a series of talks, together with other Faberge experts including Dorothy McFerrin, owner of one of the world’s greatest private collections. The synergy is a bespoke-to-Grandeur Faberge egg on display in the ship’s main reception area, a frothy confection made as an ode to the oceans, with fine blue lacquering and ripples of diamonds and pearls set to resemble waves. It’s worth more than $US1 million ($1.4 million). (Soon, the whole Faberge thing has me a bit obsessed. I start using the ship’s Wi-Fi to trawl eBay and Facebook Marketplace for hidden Russian treasure. You never know your luck, after all.) Grandeur’s own Faberge egg may be a special piece, but it is far from out of place. This ship is pimped. Deckchairs await passengers drawn to the infinity-edge plunge pool.



Nearly 140,000 kilograms of marble, along with shining chrome, gleaming glass, upholstery and drapery befitting the most upmarket residence and 503 stunning crystal chandeliers feature in a contemporary decor scheme that manages to be both homely and awe-inspiring. A multimillion-dollar art collection comprising 1600 pieces, including three Picassos, helps. Sculptures surprise at every turn, including a life-sized glass cherry blossom tree in the entrance to speciality dining restaurant Pacific Rim. The Picassos hang in another – the New York-style steakhouse Prime 7 – underlining the meticulous attention to detail that has gone into creating restaurants that play into high-end big-city establishments more than a shipboard fantasy of what such an eatery might be. Even the French restaurant, Chartreuse, resists twee as it achieves exquisiteness. The main restaurant, Compass Rose, is perhaps the most theatrical, with an art nouveau-style scheme of organic forms that cleverly divide the cavernous space into zones while providing glamour. That’s complemented by ocean-themed Versace crockery and luxury glassware. The Grandeur’s soaring atrium.



I eat most nights at Compass Rose with the social solos – and note how many of my friends order the Dover sole. It looks plain and boring to me. Then someone mentions it’s fancy – I Google it and discover it’s been called “the poshest fish in the world”. I figure I’m on the poshest ship in the world, I may as well try it. It is delicious – as are desserts. The latter are thankfully reasonably portioned because I do not hold back. With that in mind, my strategy for picking shore excursions should be finding those most likely to invite the highest step count. But the main motivator behind my choices is actually to find the least touristy. It means I join buses with like-minded travellers who favour curiosity over checklist tourism. Serendipitously, it also often means high step counts. In Barcelona, we walk for a solid three hours exploring Montjuic with its green parklands, quiet monuments and expansive views over the city. Out of Livorno, I head to the Ligurian village of Lerici, famous for being the place where Romantic poet Percy Bysshe Shelley was living before he drowned, and where his mate, Lord Byron, legendarily swam the 7.5 kilometres across from Portovenere for a visit.



It’s not exactly off the beaten track, but it’s not the main game on the Ligurian coast either, and the feeling there is relaxed, real and casually welcoming.
