The Grandeur Suite’s spacious living room. The Concierge Suite boasts a king-size bed and private balcony. We jump in rubber runabouts and cruise the Bay of Poets, admiring fortifications, old marble quarries and a waterbound statue of the Virgin Mary revered by fishermen. The Cinque Terre is nearby. Other excursions from our ship have gone there. Before our guide drops us off in stunning, gelati-coloured Portovenere for free-time wandering, he says, “I go to the Cinque Terre, I get bored. But every time I come here, it is like coming for the first time.”



Those of us from the ship, his guests, congratulate ourselves on our choice. In Monte Carlo, while other ships lay at anchor away from port, we dock in front of the casino. This is entertainment enough: preparations for the F1 Grand Prix are in their final stages, an armada of superyachts are our direct neighbours, and the buzz of the tiny city’s waterfront is palpable. Related Article Cruises It’s the ultimate autumn trip, but this cruise is brilliant any time My excursion takes me out of town to Saint-Jean-Cap-Ferrat in France, where I roam the pink palace and nine themed gardens of the Villa Ephrussi de Rothschild, a romantic interlude in the belle epoque. Further gorgeous days in A Coruna, Spain, Honfleur, France and the English countryside from Southampton, plus sea days spent doing trivia, playing board and card games, lying by the pool, enjoying the spa’s wet areas and taking in shows and talks, make life onboard Grandeur a lovely slice of la dolce vita.



For me, this is the perfect way to cruise the Mediterranean and North Atlantic, in step with the things I love about the Continent: its vintage glamour, cultivated ease and enduring sense of style. In fact, I could easily clock up hundreds of days on Regent Seven Seas myself. I just need to find a forgotten Faberge to fund them. THE DETAILS CRUISE

Regent Seven Seas Cruises will carry out a number of European sailings in 2027 (and still some in 2026). One is on board Seven Seas Grandeur: “A Grecian Summer Venice (Fusina) to Barcelona”, an 11-night journey departing June 2, 2027. From $12,910 a person. Additional inclusions to those mentioned are specialty coffees, customised in-suite mini bar, pre-paid gratuities, Wi-Fi and 24-hour in-suite dining.

MORE

See RSSC.com The writer travelled as a guest of Regent Seven Seas Cruises.

World.title: Adam Liaw’s simple stove-top trick for a richer, deeper lamb stew
World.content:
This comforting classic English lamb stew might be simple, but it relies on doing the basics well. A little patience and attention to detail will go a long way to achieving a rich, brown hot pot with deliciously golden potatoes on top.

When the potatoes are tender, uncover the pot and dot with the remaining 20g of butter then grill until the potatoes are golden and crisp at the edges. Remove from the oven and stand for at least 10 minutes before serving.

Bring to a simmer, then layer the top of the dish with the potatoes, starting at one side of the dish and moving to the other so the potatoes overlap in a fish-scale pattern. Dot the top of the potatoes with another 20g of the butter, scatter with the remaining thyme leaves and season well with salt. Cover and transfer to the oven for 1½ hours.

Add another 20g of the butter, reduce the heat slightly and fry the onions for about 10 minutes until softened and browned. Stir in the flour and fry for another 5 minutes until the flour starts to brown. Add the carrots and return the lamb and any juices to the pot and mix to combine. Add the stock, Worcestershire sauce, bay leaves and thyme and season with salt.

Heat your oven to 160C fan-forced (180C conventional). Heat a large, low, double-handled casserole dish over medium heat. Add 20g of the butter and fry the lamb in small batches until well browned (see notes), seasoning each batch with salt and black pepper. Remove to a plate.

Masterclass

Brown meat in multiple, smaller batches

The Maillard reactions that turn meat brown add deep complexity to a hot pot, but too often we don’t take the time to do it right. In previous columns, I’ve shared tips such as browning meat in larger pieces, or browning over medium heat for a more even colour. The goal here is to get a beautiful sear on the meat before it starts releasing liquid and cooling down your pot.

Arguably, the easiest way to achieve this is simply to brown less meat at a time.

The best recipes from Australia's leading chefs straight to your inbox. Sign up

Some recipes call for browning in two or three batches, but I often do it in many more. Smaller batches allow your pot to retain more heat; five or six small batches of just a few pieces each will often give you better results, faster, than overloading the pan.

As a rule of thumb, I keep half of the surface area at the base of the pot uncovered for each batch. This prevents overcrowding that drops the pan’s temperature and causes the meat to stew in its own juices rather than brown.

In Adam's French onion beef stew, he cooks the onions, stirring occasionally, for up to 40 minutes to coax out their sweetness. William Meppem

Browning onions puts you in control

How you brown your onions is one of the most effective ways to control the finished stew’s flavour. We can thank the delicious chemistry of onions and other alliums for this. Cook them fast, and they will brown quickly through Maillard reactions between carbohydrates and sulfurous peptides, giving the dish a savouriness and rich mouthfeel. Cook them slowly, and the starches will convert enzymatically to simple sugars, which brown through slightly different chemical pathways to deliver a mellow sweetness.

Cooking onions quickly over medium heat results in a stew that is savoury and less sweet, while cooking them slowly over low heat produces a sweeter base. You see this principle in action with caramelised onions, which take upwards of 40 minutes to become richly sweet.

But for a Lancashire hot pot, we can actually have the best of both worlds. A quicker fry of about 10 minutes gives us that baseline savouriness, and then the long braise in the oven brings out the sweetness. If you want even more sweetness, you can always cook your onions for longer at the start to caramelise them further.

Grill Adam’s roasted scalloped potatoes at the end to give them a golden glow. William Meppem

Browning applies to potatoes, too

I know you’re probably sick of me going on about browning by now, but the final step you need for a spectacular Lancashire hot pot is a layer of golden-brown potatoes on top. Using a good pot with a solid, heavy lid allows the potatoes to steam beautifully on top of the stew while the lamb cooks. However, once the pot is uncovered, you need dry, direct heat to crisp them up.

This can be difficult to achieve in modern electric ovens, which infuriatingly often won’t let you force the overhead grill to stay on if the oven has already reached its target temperature. Even if you crank the oven to its maximum, the grill element will shut off the moment the oven reaches that ambient temperature.

If you’re lucky enough to have two ovens, you can transfer the pot from its hot, steamy oven into a cold, dry one; this gives the overhead grill plenty of time to directly brown the top before the oven heats up. If you only have one oven, simply leave the oven door cracked open for a minute or two to let the ambient heat escape. This cools the oven down enough for the grill element to stay on a little longer.

Serve pickled cucumber and lingonberry jam with rich dishes such as Adam's Swedish meatballs. William Meppem

On the side

Nearly all rich, braised dishes need a bright, tangy side dish to cut through the fat. It’s a pairing we see time and time again in global cuisines – from Indian curries served with tangy pickles and chutneys to Swedish meatballs paired with pickled cucumbers.

The classic accompaniment for a Lancashire hot pot is pickled red cabbage. You can easily pickle it yourself ahead of time, but if you’re short on time, saute or braise shredded red cabbage with a little butter, sugar and apple cider vinegar for a brilliant, fast alternative.

World.title: Kids do feel the cold, so why won’t they wear jumpers?
World.content: But our movement and behaviour also play an important role in maintaining this balance. When we’re cold we may walk into sunshine, curl up, or add a layer; when we’re hot we take one off. A child who keeps running may already be generating the warmth they need.

World.title: 'Sensible' or 'unpopular' - Auckland's housing intensification compromise
World.content:
Council approves major housing intensification plan Morning Report Download MP3 4m

Auckland is going up.

In an act of compromise pretty much no-one is completely happy with, Auckland councillors voted in favour of allowing buildings of up to 15 storeys near transport hubs in central suburbs, and up to six storeys outside a 10-kilometre radius of the CBD.

Plan Change 120 has for five years incited passionate debate about the future of Auckland's skyline, eliciting over 10,000 submissions to local boards and iwi authorities across the city.

On Tuesday, the plan at last got sign off, meaning taller buildings would be allowed within walking distance from transport hubs, the CBD and other metropolitan centres.

Buildings up to 15 storeys high could go up in inner-Auckland suburbs like Kingsland, Mt Eden and Morningside.

Opponents decried what taller buildings would mean for their suburbs and the loss of protections for some 500 special character homes. Supporters of intensification said it was essential for growth and to house the city's spiralling population.

The plan councillors eventually voted on was a combination of two options sent out for public consultation - one which offered more intensification, the other less.

Councillor Richard Hills. RNZ / Alexia Russell

Richard Hills chaired Tuesday's extraordinary meeting of the Policy, Planning and Development Committee.

"I hope that we move forward to the compromise position. Do I support everything in here? No. But do any of us support anything perfectly, 100 percent ever? No we can't, it's like the budget," he said.

The plan was a response to a government requirement for the council to allow for more than 1.4 million homes to be built in Auckland.

Councillor Mike Lee tabled an amendment to pause the "extremely unpopular" proposal until after November's general election.

"This plan is very much the personal creature of the Minister for Housing," he said.

"Pause this right now and put people out of their agony because a lot of people are extremely adversely affected."

The amendment failed, as did another by councillor John Gillon seeking to reduce the extent of intensification.

Councillor John Gillon. Supplied / Auckland Council

Waitakere councillor Shane Henderson supported the hybrid plan but would have preferred if it went further.

He said he did not understand why so much energy was expended trying to slow down growth through intensification.

"We talked about harbour views earlier. Harbour views, I think, to the exclusive enjoyment of those wealthy enough and lucky enough to have been born at the right time."

The plan also had the support of Mayor Wayne Brown.

"Eighty-five percent of Aucklanders aren't affected and we are making the most of where we have sunk a lot of cash into public transport," he said.

"It seems unbelievably sensible."

From left: Christopher Luxon, Chris Bishop and Wayne Brown in April 2026. RNZ

Councillor Daniel Newman pointed the finger at the government for the policy taking so long.

"I can assure people in this room that I am no vassal of the Minister of Housing, Minister for RMA Reform, Minister of Transport, Chris Bishop. This process obviously has been a shambolic process and it does start with that minister."

Plan Change 120 includes provisions for down-zoning in areas predicted to be hardest hit by flooding, based on new rainfall data.

Councillors voted in favour of the plan by 17 to five.

Outside of the council chamber, Sally Hughes of the Character Coalition said the group was "deeply disappointed" that councillors did not address its concerns.

"This new hybrid does provide some relief from intensification in areas outside of the 10km circle that the council invented, but they haven't provided any relief for some of those inner suburbs that will really suffer from 15 storey buildings being able to be built on one side of the road when there are special character houses on the other side of the road. That's how crazy the plan is."

Patrick Reynolds. Supplied / City Vision

However, Patrick Reynolds from Greater Auckland said upzoning around these rapid transport stations in the inner suburbs was critical.

"I think there is a condition that I call 'height fright' that is extremely endemic. It's almost like the only thing that people can picture about the future being different is taller buildings, so they focus on that.

"The much more important thing to focus on is the quality of the design of the building and the places between them, whatever height they are."

World.title: From 'achievable' to 'unlikely' in nine days: Immigration NZ's botched $35m project
World.content:
Documents reveal officials ignored minister's office Morning Report Download MP3 8m

Senior Immigration New Zealand officials repeatedly ignored requests from the minister's office and progressed work on a project the minister hadn't agreed to extra funding for, according to new documents released to RNZ.

The hundreds of pages of correspondence paint a picture of the processes the Ministry of Business, Innovation, and Employment (MBIE), which the Immigration department sits within, used to pursue a now abandoned IT upgrade.

Public Service Commissioner Sir Brian Roche has appointed Michael Heron KC to investigate "integrity concerns" after Immigration Minister Erica Stanford revealed last month her officials "deliberately witheld" information from both her and the previous government.

That and accusations of "creative accounting" were laid out in a damning review into the department's handling of the project.

At least $35 million of taxpayers' money was wasted after the biometric capability upgrade (BCU) was ultimately stopped in 2025 after years of red flags, delays, and missed milestones.

In an unusual move Stanford has released documents to RNZ she would normally withhold under the "free and frank" provision, given the "significant public interest considerations and the fact that my recollections of the conversations are consistent with what is noted in the timeframe".

Public Service Commissioner Sir Brian Roche. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

One of those documents, a timeline developed by her specialist ministerial advisor, Kara Isaac, clearly lays out the many emails, conversations, and meetings between the minister's office and her ministry officials, including the chief executive, between 21 February and 30 April 2024.

In that timeline, there were five requests by Stanford's office for previous independent quality assurance reports (IPAs) analysing the project to be sent in full - it was six days before the ministry provided two of them.

Based on notes kept at the time and released to RNZ, it immediately became clear what officials had verbally told Stanford in meetings about the progress of the upgrade, and what the independent analysis showed were very different.

In a project update to the minister on 19 March 2024 it stated: "The latest IQA confirmed the project approach was sound and robust, the build is achievable, and the risk management practice is effective."

Yet, on receiving the IQAs nine days later the minister's office found it stated: "Given the projects poor delivery history, and its inability to meet agreed milestones, we have doubts as to whether the project will in fact deliver at all, and we question its continuation."

On realising this Isaac contacted the acting chief executive at the time, Nic Blakely, formally raising the misleading advice to the minister.

In a closed door meeting later that same day with Blakely, Stanford raised the "concerning significant discrepancies" and was told the issue would be raised with chief executive, Carolyn Tremain, as soon as she returned from leave.

Michael Heron KC has been appointed to investigate "integrity concerns" at Immigration NZ. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Report into IT upgrade 'damning'

An aide memoire of everything known about the discrepancies, produced on 28 March 2024 by Isaac and released to RNZ, detailed "free and frank opinion" to the minister.

In it, Isaac notes Stanford was alerted via a written briefing on 19 March 2024 that the project was tracking well, yet in a meeting with officials less than a week later, on 25 March, officials advised Stanford the previous IQA report was "damning".

Isaac's aide memoire makes clear that only came to light after probing from Stanford's office and "at my continued insistence that we received the IQA reports to review for ourselves".

She went on to say the most recent IQA report gave the project a delivery rating of 'unlikely' to deliver.

"So we are now in a situation where it appears a number of people have deliberately mislead [sic] you about the status of a $32m (and counting) project," she wrote.

Isaac suggested the issues be raised immediately with Tremain when she returned from leave, and that a new urgent IQA be commissioned to get an updated status, as well as an investigation into the "deliberate provision to you of misleading advice on a significant IT project".

At the same time Isaac had been raising questions about an "unexpected attempt" from the ministry to include in a cabinet paper an increase in the project's total costs from $35m to $40m.

She recommended the investigation include who "instigated the attempt in mid-March to add into the Fees and Levies Cabinet paper agreement" a funding increase to $40m "without proper scrutiny".

An email released to RNZ from 5 March 2024 shows MBIE deputy secretary and chief security officer Greg Patchell describing the project as "well in flight" and "likely to need to exceed the current spending limit of an all-of-life total of $35m".

The email, to a number of other senior MBIE staff, notes a meeting Patchell and Tremain had with Stanford a week earlier and the minister's "preference to address the approval to an all of life cost over $35m" in the fees and levies cabinet paper.

That "preference" is not a recollection held by Stanford, and there is no record of her discussing or agreeing to an increase in costs at that point, according to the documents released to RNZ.

Immigration chief executive Carolyn Tremain. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

More than a week later MBIE officials, including Patchell, met with Stanford and were asked about the project whole-of-life costs - Patchell advised "it would be weeks before further analysis would be completed".

Isaac notes in her timeline at this point there was still no record or mention of using the cabinet paper to get sign-off for increased funding.

It wasn't until 19 March that Stanford's office has any record of officials requesting that, despite the earlier 5 March email already detailing what Patchell said was the minister's preference on the matter.

Isaac advised it was a "firm no" to including the request as the cabinet paper was two days from lodgement and "it had never been raised with the office" before now.

RNZ asked Stanford a series of questions about the time taken for information to be passed onto her office, and whether she had received an acceptable explanation as to why Patchell had instructed his colleagues she was keen to increase the project's costs through the fees and levies cabinet paper.

She told RNZ "matters relating to the provision of information and the accuracy and adequacy of the advice I received will be investigated as part of the Michael Heron KC inquiry that is now underway".

She said she was unable to comment further to "preserve the integrity of the inquiry, including procedural fairness".

Likewise, the ministry associate deputy secretary Stephen Vaughan told RNZ it would be inappropriate to comment on specific matters while the inquiry is underway.

World.title: Older people facing impossible choices as cost of living continues to bite
World.content:
Older people hardest hit by inflation, says Grey Power Morning Report Download MP3 4m

Age Concern Auckland says older people are facing impossible choices as the surging cost of living crisis continues to bite.

Annual inflation had risen to 4.1 percent, the highest level in more than two years.

Power prices were up 12 percent annually and rates increased by 8.8 percent.

Age Concern Auckland's chief executive Kevin Lamb said a lot of older people were existing on superannuation alone.

"These latest increases, and particularly at this time of year, when they're having to make those awful decisions of whether or not to heat their home or go and buy groceries, they are now living almost beyond their means where they simply can't make ends meet," he said.

Lamb said that, in the past year, Age Concern Auckland had seen a 20 to 30 percent increase in calls for help.

"We're dealing with potentially vulnerable older people who don't have support networks around them, they don't have a family to support them, they're living in loneliness and isolation," he said.

Lamb added that climbing rates bills were putting a lot of pressure on superannuants and it was too hard for older people to get rates relief.

"If you are living in a multi-generational home where you have an older person, for example, you've also got younger children and a family's living there where you might not get those rebates. It's incredibly difficult to just sort of cope with an increase of the sorts of levels we're seeing. It's just putting too much pressure on people," he said.

Lamb said that many seniors who asked Age Concern for help didn't know that they could claim a rates rebate.

Households not benefitting from low wholesale electricity prices

Powerswitch general manager Paul Fuge. Supplied / Consumer NZ

Meanwhile, Consumer NZ said it was seeing record levels of interest in its electricity comparison website.

"We've been going 25 years, and last year was the busiest year by far," said Powerswitch manager, Paul Fuge.

"We had over a million users of our site last year, and that's continued into this year. What it indicates is people are really struggling with the cost of living and electricity prices are a big part of that, and they're seeking relief through trying to find a cheaper provider," he said.

Fuge said the "lion's share" of the increase in power prices was due to an increase in transmission and distribution costs.

He said those costs were regulated and were therefore unavoidable.

But, Fuge said households were not seeing the benefit of record low wholesale electricity prices.

"In terms of procuring electricity in the wholesale market, those costs have actually fallen. So, the costs of purchasing electricity in the wholesale market are less. And those costs, those savings, should be being passed through to consumers now," he said.

"What electricity companies are saying is they'll, you know, likely result in lower prices or flat prices in the future. We're saying that in any other market, when those input costs fall, consumers in a competitive market would see the benefits of that more immediately."

Fuge said power bills should drop "soon".

World.title: 27 missing, including 11 children, after two boats capsize off Papua New Guinea
World.content:
Concern is mounting for up to 27 people missing at sea in Papua New Guinea's Islands region.

Bad weather has hampered the search for the crew on at least two boats who were registered as missing on Saturday.

The incident involved several staff of the East New Britain Provincial Health Authority and their families and friends - totalling 27 people including 11 children.

They were reportedly voyaging on two boats from Pangpang Island in the Duke of York group to Kokopo, the capital of East New Britain, a journey of around 20 kilometres.

The East New Britain Provincial Disaster Committee said that on Saturday afternoon, the capsized vessels were reported, and a search was immediately initiated.

It said that on Saturday night, two survivors, who described as skippers, were reported to have gone ashore on the mainland at Baii Village, Kombiu, which is north of where their journey to Kokopo would have taken them.

Police reportedly retrieved the pair and took them to Kokopo Police Station, where they were kept and interviewed as part of the ongoing response.

The national broadcaster NBC reported on the update given by the chairman of East New Britain's Disaster Committee, Levi Mano, before a concerned crowd in windy conditions in Kokopo.

He said a number of agencies have been involved in the search, including police, a helicopter courtesy of National Government through the National Disaster Office and Maritime Safety Authority, and numerous local sea vessels.

Eventually on Monday one of the boats was spotted far to the north drifting upturned with no apparent sign of people off the west coast of Namatanai, in neighbouring New Ireland Province.

Levi Mano said that rough seas and bad weather hampered both sea and air search efforts, causing a temporary pause to the search operation.

Gazelle MP Jelta Wong told RNZ Pacific the aerial search resumed Tuesday.

Meanwhile, Mano said authorities were doing what they could in tough conditions across a wide region.

He emphasised to the crowd that police were involved as the search operation required "all agencies" to be engaged.

The East New Britain government has urged all travellers to check weather and sea conditions before going out to sea, and to take precautions.

World.title: Former judge says proposed move on orders are careless and callous
World.content:
A retired district court judge who for almost two decades dealt with homeless offenders says the proposed move on orders are careless, callous and will not work.

The Summary Offences Amendment Bill is before a select committee and will give police the power to ask people as young as 14 years old who are begging or rough sleeping to move elsewhere.

The Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith has defended the bill, saying it covers behaviour which is problematic, that isn't already enshrined in legislation.

Tony Fitzgerald hung up his gavel in March after serving 27 years on the bench in the criminal, family and youth courts.

Each month for more than 15 years, he also presided over Auckland's Te Kooti o Timatanga Hou - The Court of New Beginnings - which holds homeless people accountable for low-level offending and helps to get them off the streets and into housing and work.

It has been more than a job - 10 years after the very first court participant got back on her feet, Tony Fitzgerald was the celebrant for her wedding.

"She's just one of many who just needed a helping hand to get out of the trap they were in. And that word trap, which I've used in my written submissions and I use now, doesn't come from me," Fitzgerald said.

"It was a word that often came up when I was talking to people about their situation and most described being homeless as a trap they just needed help to get out of."

Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

He has written a letter to every person who graduated from the Court of New Beginnings - over the years that's around 300 people.

Fitzgerald opposes the proposed move on orders and has written a submission laying out his concerns - among them, that it is legally unnecessary, inconsistent with the Bill of Rights Act, careless towards the people being moved on and callous.

"Why I've described this bill as callous is that having, by policies, created the increase in homelessness and its visibility, to deal with the inevitable consequences of that, make people liable for imprisonment for nothing more than sleeping or inhabiting public spaces, which are the only spaces a homeless person can sleep or inhabit."

He said it was especially callous to include children as young as 14 who should be offered help, if they are sleeping rough.

"I thought the very inclusion of them was emblematic of the callousness that instead of recognising that a 14-year-old begging and sleeping on the street would raise significant concerns for their care and protection, which would be the obvious pathway to take, they propose immediately progressing to a criminal justice statute and police powers," Fitzgerald said.

"So for me, that's callous."

Another opponent who has made submissions on the bill is Danielle LeGallais, the co-founder of Sunday Blessings, a charity that hands out 250 takeaway meals in central Auckland every Sunday.

She's a criminal barrister and is worried the homeless do not understand what's proposed in the move on orders.

"One of the responses that I heard very clearly was that some people thought the move on orders were already in effect. They didn't understand that this was a new proposal from the government in terms of like legislative framework," she said.

"Rough sleepers are really confused about the implications of the bill."

Danielle LeGallais. Supplied / Hamlin Law

LeGallais said many rough sleepers had already been reprimanded by police or the court for disorderly behaviour and wanted to avoid getting into further trouble.

But she said they faced ongoing disadvantages and questioned how a person with a tent for shelter and belongings not easily carried, could be easily moved on.

"The drafters of the bill and our government haven't taken into consideration all the intersecting factors relating to homelessness and extreme poverty, including very simple things like having access to a phone that is charged, having access to credit, having access to the internet."

Decades ago when in her 20s, LeGallais experienced hidden homelessness and had a serious run-in with the law for a theft that resulted in sentencing - money she paid off in full at the time.

She said that had shaped her decision to become a criminal barrister and drove her to help others.

Many charities say homelessness is a growing problem and LeGallais said her organisation is finding it harder to meet the demand for the Sunday meals.

The Salvation Army is expected to release its six-montly national update on homelessness this month, after its December update showed homeless was rising with roughly one in every 1000 people without shelter.

"The Sunday that's just gone, five people missed out on kai packs. Now, that may not sound like a big number, but for those five people that spent 45 minutes lining up and to have that happen to them at the end of that, that is heartbreaking," she said.

"We one hundred percent are finding it difficult to keep up with demand but we're doing the very best that we can."

Te Kooti o Timatanga Hou - The Court of New Beginnings

When the court dealing with homeless offenders was set up, Fitzgerald said there was concern from retailers and police about disorderly behaviour, the frequency of petty crime and what to do about it.

Retired district court judge Tony Fitzgerald. RNZ / Amy Williams

Two people came to see him.

"One was the officer in charge of the downtown police station, Senior Sergeant Ben Offner, and the other was John McCarthy, who was then the general manager of Lifewise," he said.

"They had heard about work I was doing in the Youth Court, working collaboratively with not only professionals but with the community, and this was producing really good results, and there was some publicity around that."

The pair spent a day in court and asked Fitzgerald if it would be possible to set up a similar court for homeless people.

"I can remember the conversation, Ben Offner was explaining that he was really concerned about the frequency with which people who were homeless and committing low-level nuisance offending in Auckland were just being processed frequently through the court," Fitzgerald said.

"It was not only frustrating for him, but for the retailers and the business owners," he said.

"If it was necessary, they would arrest and charge and people would go to court, but it only seemed a very short period of time before they were back out on the street again, regardless of whatever sentence they got."

At the time, Fitzgerald had been sitting in the conventional courts for 12 years.

"I had seen the hopeless situation faced by those people frequently coming in on low-level offending, for whom the very short list of conventional options does nothing constructive for them."

He was interested in stopping that cycle.

"I had already found great benefits in working more collaboratively with a wider range of professionals than often had been happening in the conventional court process in the Youth Court, but also more collaboratively with the community and seeing firsthand just how much better outcomes could be for everybody if the collaboration between courts and communities was able to improve."

The New Beginnings Court started in 2010 and Fitzgerald credited the many volunteers from social services and Community Law for helping it succeed till this day.

Whaea, social worker Michelle Kidd, retired in 2023 after 13 years with the court.

Michelle Kidd. RNZ / Edward Gay

Evaluations have shown that its approach reduced reoffending rates by 66 percent, nights spent in prison by 78 percent and hospital admissions, also by 78 percent.

Fitzgerald said since those early evaluations, he believed from what he saw each month that all the rates of rehabilitation have improved but there is no current data.

"It was very satisfying to become involved in a process where you could see good things happening for everyone concerned."

The pathways to homelessness and how to support people out of that "trap" was a subject that concerns him greatly; he has written papers and articles and spoken at conferences both here and overseas.

He was frustrated that move on orders are on the table.

"The debate currently is almost identical to the debate in that period before Ben and John came to see me and I feel concerned and frustrated that here we are again going through exactly the same debate."

Fitzgerald said the difference more than 15 years on, was the evidence from both here and overseas about what works and what does not.

"I oppose the [move on] orders because I know, based on the evidence and the research here and overseas, what this bill proposes cannot possibly work for anybody."

He said that included retailers, business owners, tourists, taxpayers and the general public.

"There is no place in the world where the use of police and criminal justice powers and facilities has ever succeeded in achieving the types of aims this bill has. Nowhere."

World.title: Two need medical treatment after chemical scare in Waikato
World.content:
Two people have been treated by ambulance officers at the scene of an unknown chemical incident in the Waikato town of Tuakau.

Emergency services were called to the area on Tuesday afternoon when the chemical was detected in water, causing a strong fuel or LPG smell.

Fire and Emergency (FENZ) said firefighters responded to the "hazardous substances incident" at 4pm.

It said 10 homes were evacuated, and two other households self-evacuated.

FENZ flushed out drains and returned the atmosphere to safe levels.

Residents were allowed to return home around 10:30pm last night.

An ambulance spokesperson said two people received medical treatment at the scene, but did not need to be taken to hospital.

In an update at 10.30pm, Assistant District Commander Brad Harvey said firefighters had been flushing the drains and atmospheric readings showed the air quality in and around them had returned to safe levels.

"Residents who were evacuated earlier this evening are able to return home. The advice to other residents to stay inside with doors and windows shut has also been lifted," Harvey said.

"The scene will be left in the hands of local water management staff. The nature and source of the substance which prompted the emergency response has not yet been established."

No impact on drinking water

Aksel Bech Supplied / Waikato District Council

Waikato District Council said there was no impact on drinking water or stormwater networks, and no issues with drinking water quality.

Specialist advice has been sought from the Queensland Fire Department to help identify the substance and FENZ was working with the Waikato District Council and Watercare to develop a plan to flush the drains safely.

Waikato mayor Aksel Bech said a strong fuel or LPG smell was detected near the water treatment plant.

He said the chemical substance was suspected to be from an underground petrol or LPG type of storage tank.

"[That] led us to believe that perhaps there might have been an issue from inside of one of the petrol stations in Tuakau, it would have to be somewhere with a bit of volume in order to actually be able to produce a smell. Very quickly when that smell was detected the water that goes into the watercare facility was diverted off into a pump so as not to contaminate anything within the plant. That is under control."

World.title: First round of Northland power pylon collapse case to begin in court
World.content:
The first round in a class action case relating to a pylon collapse that cut power to Northland is due to start in the High Court in Wellington on Thursday.

An investigation found the pylon toppled over in June 2024 when contractors unbolted three of the tower's four legs at once.

The resulting outage left 180,000 people and around 20,000 businesses without power, in some cases for several days.

Legal firms Lee Salmon Long and Piper Alderman have launched a class action on behalf of Northland businesses to recoup their losses, on a no win, no fee basis.

The defendants are Transpower, the state-owned national grid operator, and Omexom, the French-owned maintenance contractor.

This week's hearing will determine whether the case is "opt-in" or "opt-out".

If it is opt-out, all Northland businesses will automatically be part of the proceedings.

If it is opt-in, businesses will have to actively sign up to take part.

Among those who have affidavits supporting the claim, and the opt-out order, are iwi leaders Dame Naida Glavish and Harry Burkhardt.

Glavish said the pylon fell next to her marae, Puatahi, north of Auckland.

Dame Naida Glavish. RNZ / Lucy Xia

"It was completely avoidable. When infrastructure of this scale fails because of negligence, there must be consequences. We need to lift the standard of accountability nationally, so this never happens again," she said.

Burkhardt said Northland was home to many Māori-owned and operated businesses without access to significant funding.

Without class action, those businesses would be unable to challenge large companies such as Transpower and Omexom.

Burkhardt said backing the class action was about strengthening standards for the future.

"We talk about deliberate investment in Northland, in our people and our infrastructure. What happened here was the opposite. It reflected complacency and a lack of care," he said.

The iwi leaders' affidavit stated an opt-out case would provide greater access to justice, given Northland's isolation.

It said it would be difficult to make Māori business owners in remote areas aware of the claim and what they needed to do to join it.

The defendants were seeking an opt-in case.

The legal firms pursuing the class action did not say how much money they were seeking.

The losses suffered by Northland businesses were estimated at $60 million by economic consultants Infometrics, and $80m by the Northland Chamber of Commerce.

The class action was being paid for by litigation funding company Omni Bridgeway.

World.title: McRae sends special message to Hill before Pies head west
World.content:
Coach Craig McRae says Bobby Hill will always be welcome at Collingwood despite the troubled star looking to cut short his contract.

Hill was the hero of the Magpies' 2023 premiership under McRae, winning the Norm Smith Medal after a four-goal grand final showing against Brisbane.

But taking stretches of personal leave, the 26-year-old small forward has not played for almost a year and is unlikely to wear Collingwood colours again.

With the club and Hill's management dealing with the issue of a contract that runs until the end of 2030, McRae said he was more concerned for Hill's wellbeing, and sent a message of support.

Magpies admit Hill is 'a long way away from playing footy' Bobby Hill returns to Collingwood training, but coach Craig McRae says it will be some time before the 2023 Norm Smith medallist is ready to play in the AFL again.

"I haven't seen Bobby in the building for a while … if you're out there, Bobby, we've got a lot of love and care for you, we'll never waver in our love and support for the young man," McRae said.

"And then the other part is completely out of my hands, conversations around management and other things, so I'll leave others to do those things.

"He's a premiership player, and Norm Smith medallist, and he'll forever be welcome in our four walls."

McRae was speaking ahead of the Magpies' clash with Adelaide on Thursday night, which he expected to have a finals-like atmosphere.

The teams squared off in a qualifying final at Adelaide Oval last year, with Collingwood triumphant by 24 points.

"We've got some good memories, that game last year, the final, a big crowd there, it was a highlight of the year for me and the team. It was a huge game, and we played the ground well," he said.

"We anticipate this game to be like a final; big crowd and we're anticipating a big game."

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

The Magpies had only a five-day turnaround between games but surprised McRae with their training intensity, which meant he was unlikely to rest any veteran players, including Scott Pendlebury.

Gun midfielder Josh Daicos skipped training with an ankle injury but is expected to be available, while defender Jeremy Howe is also set to be named after overcoming a calf injury.

"We trained today, and we played Saturday night, and if you watch training you go, 'No way that group just played three days ago,'" he said.

"There's a huge energy in the building right now … at this stage, I don't think we've got a reason to rest too many players or manage players."

AAP

World.title: How this Champions League winner aims to ignite Stingers
World.content:
Australia's women's water polo team, the Stingers, are no strangers to success.

Winning a silver medal at the Paris Olympics, the best performance by any Australian team at those Games, put the Stingers right in the upper echelons of their field.

It's what makes the World Aquatics Water Polo World Cup finals, being hosted in Australia from July 22-26 at the Sydney Aquatics Centre at Homebush, so exciting.

But the fact the Stingers are challenging at the top of the world rankings is no accident.

The entire team is packed with genuine superstars, playing in some of Europe's biggest clubs in the biggest competitions in the world.

Abby Andrews has proven herself to be one of the very best.

Abby Andrews's first major trophy was the biggest in club water polo. (Supplied: Instagram)

The 25-year-old left-handed shooter won the LEN European Champions League title with Greek giants Olympiacos earlier this year.

Not only that, but the Brisbane native was named the most valuable player in the Final Four tournament, scoring four goals in the semifinal and a fabulous five in the final.

"It was definitely an out-of-body experience," the 25-year-old told ABC Sport ahead of this week's World Aquatics Water Polo World Cup event in Sydney.

"I mean, as an Australian, we always look and we watch the Champions League finals every year and we always think, 'Oh, how cool would it be to be in that, let alone win?'

"I said to some of my [Stingers] teammates here in Australia when I got back, I don't think I've ever won anything.

"Actually being able to lift a cup and just the feeling of euphoria with that, and the celebrations and our massive fan base in Europe is insane …

"That was probably one of the coolest moments of my life. It was awesome."

Abby Andrews scored nine goals across the semifinal and final. (Supplied: LEN European Aquatics)

Andrews's Olympiacos side beat Barcelona-based CN Mataró, featuring Stingers teammate Tilly Kearns, 14-12 in the semifinal, before downing Hungarian giants Ferencvárosi TC in the final by a score of 17-14.

"As the season went on, our team was really gaining strength," Andrews said.

"The semifinal was tough, but I think it was a great stepping stone for us.

"And then the final was brutal. We had lots of momentum swings but honestly, until the very end, we just completely stuck together."

The Final Four, held on the Mediterranean island of Malta, was an enormous occasion, the first time the men's and women's competitions were held at the same venue at the same time.

That allowed the women's teams to truly benefit from the enormous and fanatical support of their ultras.

Loading Instagram content

"It's insane," Andrews admitted of the enormous support.

"I mean, certain games that we play will have flares. They'll have this massive police presence and you just never know like what the crowd's going to do; when they're going to start chanting, if they'll go quiet for a bit.

"It's just something we don't experience here.

"I think what's so cool about the European multi-sport organisations is that they're just fanatics, like, they are absolutely mad, but ultimately their presence is so lifting and we love playing in front of them.

"It's just such a different experience.

"And for women's water polo to get that kind of attention as well, both our men's and women's teams were in the Final Four and the men unfortunately lost the semi, so all the attention shifted to us and the fans just went, 'you know what, let's give [the support] to the women'."

Abby Andrews has been a mainstay in the Stingers team. (Getty Images: James Worsfold)

Andrews joined Olympiacos, the enormous multi-sport club based in the Piraeus region of Athens better known for its football team, soon after winning Olympic silver in 2024.

Having already played overseas in the American college system and in Italy, Andrews has been exposed to the very best of the best for her entire career.

Being able to cap her second season by winning the biggest prize in club water polo underlines the fact that she is on the right track personally.

"I think each experience teaches you something different," Andrews said.

"Having that exposure against the European powerhouses and just playing them regularly, having camps with them is honestly so invaluable and it's been a huge addition to my game.

"I love bringing the new techniques that they have, because obviously some Europeans are different in size, strength, skill and you kind of just adopt new methods as you see them. So it's really fun.

"I think my latest one in Olympiacos, it being my second year, I was able to establish myself more in the systems that the Greek teams play and really settle into that, as well as just realising that I can also step up and have a really big attacking presence.

"It's just such a cool environment to be in and I love like learning about myself in those environments and how I can step up."

Abby Andrews is expecting pressure at her first-ever home World Cup finals. (Getty Images: DeFodi Images/Marcel ter Bals)

Andrews did accept that playing at such a huge club comes with enormous pressure, but that it was "kind of a good extra pressure to have".

Extra pressure is something that Andrews is hoping to embrace over the next week, as the Stingers look to show off their status as genuine world challengers in the World Aquatics Water Polo World Cup, starting in Sydney on Wednesday.

The world's top eight men's and women's national water polo teams will all compete at the event at the Sydney Aquatic Centre, the first time the city has hosted a major global water polo competition since the 2000 Olympics.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Sydney has twice hosted the World Cup finals before: the men's edition in 1999, won by Hungary; and the women's in 1995, won by the Aussies.

The Women's World Cup has also been hosted in Brisbane (1981) and Perth (2002).

But as much as the overall goal is to win the title in Sydney, emulating the Australian women's water polo team that won gold in the same Sydney Olympic Pool at the Sydney Games of 2000, filling the stands and inspiring others to follow in the Stingers' wake is just as important.

"I think this new generation coming through is so eager, I've never seen this kind of excitement from the younger kids coming through," Andrews said.

"I think it's already got such a good momentum and I think if we can really build on that and just fill the stands, get everyone there.

"You're going to be seeing some high-quality water polo from every team around the world, and being able to have this at home, who knows when we'll have this again, maybe not until Brisbane [2032].

"So while we've got this, let's use it. Everyone come down. I just think it's going to be such a spectacle."

World.title: Vaughters says night tests would have saved cycling '25 years of drama'
World.content:
Former professional cyclist and Cannondale-EF team boss Jonathan Vaughters has weighed in on the row over pre-dawn doping tests at the Tour de France, arguing such controls ​could have exposed cycling's blood-doping era decades earlier had they existed at the time.

Riders including race leader Tadej Pogačar and Jonas Vingegaard were woken in the early hours of Sunday for unannounced doping checks ahead of ​the 15th stage, prompting ‌complaints that the disruption to sleep was unfair and potentially dangerous.

Vaughters, who rode professionally through the late 1990s and early 2000s, defended the practice.

"2am testing is one of the very effective ways ‌to prevent peptide (EPO, hGH) and testosterone micro dosing," Vaughters wrote on social media.

"If ⁠UCI [Union Cycliste Inter]ationale) had tested us in 2001 at 2am? We'd all have ‌been suspended and saved the sport ​25 years of drama."

His comments ‌carry particular weight given his own history with doping.

Jonathan Vaughters (right) was teammates with Lance Armstrong (left) on the US Postal team. (Getty Images: Graham Watson)

Vaughters was a teammate of Lance Armstrong on the US Postal Service team and later admitted using performance-enhancing drugs, including EPO, during his career.

When Lance met Oprah Lance Armstrong had successfully doped for years. But when the evidence backed him into a corner, he took control of the narrative and confessed live on Oprah's couch, martyring himself to cycling's EPO era.

He subsequently testified in the US Anti-Doping Agency's (USADA) investigation into ​Armstrong, ‌who was stripped of his seven Tour titles in 2012 after the agency concluded he ran what it called the most sophisticated doping program the sport had seen.

Vaughters ⁠went on to found the team now ‌known as Cannondale-EF, positioning it as ‌an advocate for clean racing.

His remarks come as riders pushed back on the timing of ‌Sunday's tests.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Vingegaard, tested at 2 am, said the visit cost him about 40 minutes of sleep before a mountain stage on which he later ‌crashed ​and broke his collarbone.

Pogačar, ⁠tested at 5 am, said he managed only four hours of sleep. Stage winner Remco Evenepoel called the practice "inhuman".

The International Testing Agency, which oversees doping controls for the UCI, said it was "conscious that night-time testing may be disruptive ⁠to riders' rest and recovery" but that effective testing must, "in limited and justified circumstances," occur outside daytime hours.

Micro-dosing of substances ‌such as EPO ‌and human growth hormone, which can clear the body within ​hours, has long concerned anti-doping authorities, who say predictable daytime-only testing makes such practices easier to evade.

Reuters

World.title: Weatherald retains Australian Test spot despite middling Ashes returns
World.content:
Opening batsman Jake Weatherald has retained his spot in Australia's Test squad for the looming series against Bangladesh.

Despite a middling Ashes campaign last summer, Weatherald is among a 13-man squad bolstered by the return of a trio of big guns.

Captain Pat Cummins, paceman Josh Hazlewood and spinner Nathan Lyon all return after recovering from injury.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"They have worked extremely hard, individually and with the [fitness] teams, over the past few months to return from their respective injuries," Australia's chairman of selectors George Bailey said.

"While this is a 13-player squad, we have players prepared and available should any adjustments be required in the lead-up to these matches.

"The volume of cricket and schedule across the next 12 months are likely to present further opportunities across all formats for many players."

Missing from Australia's squad for the final Test against England last January are Usman Khawaja (retired), Michael Neser, Todd Murphy and Brendan Doggett.

The Australians host Bangladesh in Darwin from August 13-17 and Mackay from August 22-26, the start of a gruelling 12 months featuring 20 Test matches.

Weatherald will resume his opening batting partnership with Travis Head after playing all five Tests last summer against England.

The Darwin-born left-hander made only 201 runs at an average of 22.33 but has been given another chance to enhance his Test credentials.

AAP

World.title: Buckley opts out of Dons, Blues coaching races after Tasmania snub
World.content:
A disappointed Nathan Buckley is ruling out bidding for other vacant AFL head coaching jobs after being overlooked by the Tasmania Devils.

While Buckley, who openly coveted the Tasmanian post that went to Ken Hinkley, says he wants to be a head coach again, he is unlikely to pitch for the vacant positions at Essendon and Carlton.

"I haven't really reflected on where those roles sit, and I don't think I would enter those processes," Buckley told Fox Footy on Monday night.

Loading...

Buckley said his most likely outcome next year was to remain at Geelong, where he is an assistant to Chris Scott.

"I am absolutely focused on the next six to 10 weeks with Geelong and how that plays out," he said.

"I will take some time to reassess what is after that."

Buckley was committed to winning the Devils job that instead was given to former Port Adelaide boss Hinkley.

"I went home, kicked the dog, threw the toys out of the cot … because I was really keen on it," he said.

"If you're going to go for a job, you have got to decide if you're absolutely all in on it — and I was.

"And I absolutely respect the process that the Devils have run, and I respect their decision with Ken as well. I am glad they have found their man, and they're really clear that Kenny is the guy for them."

However, the former Collingwood boss said the Devils' decision was a personal "fork in the road".

"I was really deliberate in getting back into Geelong, and that was as much to give myself the very best chance to be ready to go for the Tasmania role," he said.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"Now that is off the table, so I will be absolutely committed to what is going on at Geelong. I have got an option for next year there and that is probably the most likely outcome.

"There are no guarantees in this, and you have got to put yourself out there, and you have got to have a crack.

"So there's disappointment."

Asked if he remained steadfast in wanting to be a head coach again, Buckley replied: "Yeah. I determined that about 12 months ago.

"That is what I believe I am capable of doing. It's what I want to do."

AAP

World.title: Millions greet Spain's WC heroes as FIFA probes ugly post-match fights
World.content:
Spain's World Cup-winning team has been met with an estimated two million fans at a raucous championship parade through the streets of Madrid.

The 26 players and their coaching staff met with the country's royals, and then with Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, after arriving in the Spanish capital a day after beating Argentina 1-0 in the final in New Jersey.

"Thank you to the coaches and players for the style of play, the effort and the victory," Sánchez said. "We have truly enjoyed watching you play."

Spain's World Cup win a reminder collective spirit trumps solo stars As some of football's biggest names lit up the World Cup, Spain flew under the radar all the way to hoisting the trophy on its final day.

The squad then boarded an open-top bus for a raucous parade through central Madrid. "Stars shine together" was written on the bus, which also carried photos of the footballers.

Players — carrying the World Cup trophy and wearing shirts with the words Somos Campeones (We Are Champions) — danced and interacted with the fans along the route.

"It's been an emotional and proud experience to represent a wonderful country with such passionate and devoted fans," Spain coach Luis de la Fuente said before the parade started. "We are filled with joy."

The squad travelled down Madrid's historic avenues from near Moncloa Palace, the prime minister's official residence, to Cibeles Square, where authorities told local media that some 120,000 people were on hand for a ceremony.

Players were introduced one by one before entering the stage set up at the square. Each picked the song to be played when they came in. Álex Baena, celebrating his 25th birthday, entered with the World Cup trophy.

Coach De la Fuente was thrust into the air by his players after being introduced. The coach was among those who sang along to the song being played for them.

Striker Borja Iglesias featured as a DJ at one point, with his teammates dancing on the stage.

Singers Aitana, Ana Mena and Lola Índigo were among those entertaining the crowd and the players.

Thousands of Spanish fans gathered around the Cibeles Fountain (Fuente de Cibeles) in Madrid to celebrate their World Cup win. (Ruben Albarran/Anadolu via Getty Images)

The ceremony ended with the whole Spain squad lifting the trophy again, just like at the awards ceremony on Sunday, but now in front of the local crowd.

Groups of fans had begun securing their spots near Cibeles late Monday morning local time ahead of the team's arrival, bringing umbrellas to protect against the sun and temperatures of up to 35 degrees Celsius.

The square is where previous Spain teams and their supporters have typically gathered to celebrate. It is also the traditional celebration spot for Real Madrid when it wins titles.

FIFA launches investigation into ugly post-game fracas

Argentina's Leandro Paredes was given a red card after fighting Spain's Gavi following the final whistle. (Getty Images: Marvin Ibo Guengoer - GES Sportfoto/Getty Images)

FIFA opened an investigation Monday after Spain's celebrations on beating Argentina in the World Cup final took an ugly turn when players briefly clashed on the field.

Video replays showed several players involved in a scuffle, including Argentina midfielder Leandro Paredes.

He appeared to shove Spain's Eric Garcia by the throat. When Spain substitute Gavi jumped in to intervene, Paredes pushed him to the ground.

Spain captain Rodri also seemed to be hit in the stomach by Argentina defender Nahuel Molina as he ran past to join teammates celebrating the title win.

Molina later crowded Rodri, who was the target of a verbal confrontation by his former Manchester City teammate Nicolas Otamendi.

Argentina coach Lionel Scaloni and other players rushed in to de-escalate the situation.

FIFA said in a statement its "disciplinary committee has appointed a Disciplinary and Ethics Prosecutor to investigate potential breaches of the [FIFA disciplinary code] with regard to the post-match incidents".

The brief statement gave no timetable for an investigation and did not name Paredes, who was not shown a red card after the game yet could face a suspension.

Spain needed extra time to win Sunday's final 1-0 after Argentina was reduced to 10 men. Enzo Fernandez was sent off with a second yellow card in stoppage time at the end of 90 minutes.

The Argentina players stood facing their fans, with their backs to the podium, when Spain's squad lifted the trophy. It was an unusual show of disrespect to the new champions, who had given their opponents a guard of honour to collect their medals.

AP

World.title: Aussie world champs name new rugby sevens coach for LA Olympics
World.content:
Reg Tayler has been named head coach of the world champion Australian women's rugby sevens team, as the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics loom on the horizon.

The decision completes a succession plan following Tim Walsh's departure from the position after Australia clinched the World Championship in France last month.

Tayler was an assistant coach to Walsh, who has since become Rugby Australia's (RA) director of women's high performance.

New Australia coach Reg Tayler (right) pictured with Tim Walsh. (Rugby Australia)

Tayler will guide Australia through its two-year build-up to the Olympics.

"The squad is determined for continued success through to the Olympics in Los Angeles," Tayler said in an RA statement.

Rugby Australia setting high standards Only three years out from hosting the Women's Rugby World Cup, Australia makes a key appointment it hopes will help deliver success on the international stage.

"Our players are professional and dedicated to achieving a gold medal, and I am confident we will have the squad capable of that in 2028."

Tayler, who joined the Australian sevens program last year, has big shoes to fill.

Walsh not only led Australia to its recent World Championship victory but was also in charge when it won the inaugural Olympic gold in women's rugby sevens at the 2016 Rio de Janeiro Games.

It is the only time Australia has won Olympic gold in the sport.

Australia won the first women's Olympic rugby sevens gold on offer in 2016. (Getty Images/World Rugby: Dan Mullan)

Walsh, who coached Australia across two stints, will still have input through his newly created role as part of RA's strategy to align the sevens and Wallaroos programs.

He is confident Tayler will leave his mark as head coach, describing the appointment as a "seamless acquisition" for the squad.

"Reg is highly knowledgeable of the World Series circuit and has worked with many of our players coming through the pathways system," Walsh said.

"He's not going in cold, he completely understands the game and his expertise is going to be fully utilised by the program.

"It's a privilege and honour to retain Reg."

Tayler has previously coached the Australia A women's sevens team.

He also spent time working with Ireland's women's and men's squads between 2023-25.

Australia claimed the World Championship with victories in the final two legs of the series in Valladolid and Bordeaux.

World.title: Football world 'devastated' by death of English icon Keegan
World.content:
Former England captain and manager Kevin Keegan has died aged 75.

Keegan's family and Newcastle United revealed in January that the two-time European Footballer of the Year was undergoing cancer treatment, without disclosing details of his illness. His death was confirmed by Newcastle overnight.

Last month, Keegan, who was nicknamed "King Kev" and "Mighty Mouse" and was one of the most influential figures of his generation in English football, revealed he had stage four cancer.

Fans lay flowers at St James' Park, Newcastle United's home ground, in memory of Keegan after his death. (Getty Images: Owen Humphreys)

"We are devastated to learn of the passing of Kevin Keegan, one of the most iconic, influential and deeply loved figures in our club's history," Newcastle said in a statement.

"As a player, he brought world-class talent, ambition and belief to St. James' Park, helping to transform perceptions of what Newcastle United could be.

"As a manager, he ignited our city. Kevin gave supporters hope and pride, and led a team whose style, spirit and passion captured the imagination of football fans around the world. He was so much more than an entertainer."

Glittering career as player and manager

Keegan became one of English football's biggest superstars in his time with Liverpool from 1971-77. (Getty Images: Harry Ormesher)

Keegan began his career at Scunthorpe United before joining Liverpool in 1971.

He made 323 appearances for Liverpool in all competitions, scoring 100 goals over six seasons. He won three First Division titles, the FA Cup, two UEFA Cups and the 1977 European Cup during a glittering spell at Anfield.

After moving to Hamburg, Keegan was named European Footballer of the Year in 1978 and 1979, becoming the only British player to win the Ballon d'Or twice. He later returned to England to play for Southampton and Newcastle before retiring in 1984 at the age of 33.

Keegan scored 21 goals in 63 appearances for England between 1972 and 1982, captaining the side 31 times.

He moved into management at Newcastle in 1992, guiding the club into the Premier League and transforming it into one of England's most entertaining sides.

Keegan's team came agonisingly close to winning the 1995-96 Premier League title before they were overtaken by Manchester United.

Although the title race did not go Keegan's way, his rant aimed at United manager Sir Alex Ferguson in the heat of the race went down in football folklore.

After leaving St James' Park in January 1997, he had a brief spell at Fulham before taking charge of England in 1999 following Glenn Hoddle's departure.

He resigned after Euro 2000 and a defeat by Germany at Wembley Stadium, famously saying he was "not good enough" to do the job, at a media conference. He won seven of his 18 matches in charge.

Keegan later managed Manchester City before leaving the club in March 2005 and initially announcing his retirement from football. He made an emotional return to Newcastle in 2008, though his second spell at the club lasted only eight months.

A lasting legacy

A statement from Keegan's family, quoted by British media, said on Monday: "It is with immense sadness that we announce that Kevin Keegan has passed away at the age of 75.

"The former England player and manager had been battling cancer and was surrounded by his wife and daughters in his final moments."

Tributes poured in for Keegan, with Liverpool saying in a statement: "Our 'Mighty Mouse', his legacy at Liverpool will be forever etched in history."

England Football wrote on X: "We are incredibly saddened by the news that Kevin Keegan OBE has passed away," while former Newcastle striker Alan Shearer wrote: "My Hero. My manager. My friend. Sleep easy Boss".

Reuters

Tech.title: Peak Design’s modular Field Bracket has a finder tag built-in
Tech.content:
is a technology reporter who has been covering the industry since 2007. He co-hosts the Waveform podcast with MKBHD. A former engineer, he now specializes in topics like computational photography and social media protocols.

I am a very clumsy man. So clumsy, that I have AirTags hanging off practically every camera I own. Have I left my camera in an Uber? Yes. Have I left it on an airplane? Also yes. For me, finder tags are essential for my cameras.

The problem is, strapping a finder tag to a camera is always cumbersome. I currently have them hanging off my camera straps like a phone charm circa 2001. They’re ugly, and very much get in the way when I’m trying to focus on shooting. But Peak Design thinks it has a solution in its new Field Bracket system, which it launched today on Kickstarter, starting at $150 for early birds.

Image Credit: Peak Design

The Peak Design Field Bracket is part L-Bracket, part hand grip, part cheese plate. It’s made for photographers and videographers who want to quickly switch between landscape and portrait orientation on their tripod, or sometimes want to mount a light or mic to their camera when there isn’t a dedicated place to do so. But possibly the most enticing thing, to me at least, is that the bracket comes with a slot for a dedicated Finder Tag.

Peak’s Beacon Finder Tag is a Peak Design-branded finder that works with Apple Find My and Google Find Hub. That means it’ll work with both Apple and Android phones, so you don’t have to worry about losing access to your camera finder if you switch ecosystems. The tag uses a standard CR2025 battery, and Peak says it’s rated to last up to 6 months. It’s also rated for IP67 water and dust resistance, and it fits flush inside the base plate of the L-bracket.

The Beacon Finder Tag is just one of the accessories Peak Design is selling alongside the Field Bracket. The base product you’ll be buying is in fact an L-bracket, but once that’s on your camera, you’ll have access to other add-on accessories like a hand grip, finger grip, and cheese plate. Peak says the Field Bracket will work with most ARCA-compatible tripods, and won’t get in the way if you use it with its own capture clip or camera straps. In fact, the bracket itself has dedicated slots to attach your Peak Design camera strap, so you won’t have to sacrifice the strap you own to use the bracket.

Peak calls the vertical attachment to the L-bracket the Field Latch, and it uses the company’s new locking system to quickly attach and detach it without any tools. This is the same place you attach the optional cheese plate, which pulls out in adjustable stops in case you need to access ports or run cables from the camera.

Image Credit: Peak Design

Of course, you’ll have to choose the exact bracket you want for the camera you own, considering it’s molded specifically to that body. At launch, most cameras supported are the newest, or near-newest models of each camera line. You can see a compatibility list here. And if you want to see your camera supported, Peak has a dedicated feedback page to submit the camera you own.

The bracket itself will MSRP at $149.95, and if you want a bundle of all the accessories currently offered, you can get everything for $269.80. As usual, though, Peak Design is offering a Kickstarter discount, which puts the bracket at $125 and the bundle at $199, while supplies last at least.
